I   do   not  think   you   put   me   into   this   ofÏce   so   that   I,   too,   should   lie   to   you.  Our   country   is   not   prospering.   The   great   creative   and  spiritual   potential   of   our   nation   is   not   being   used   to   its   fullest.  Whole   sectors   of   industry   are   producing   things   in   which   no   one  is   interested,   while   things   we   need   are   in   short   supply.  The   state,   which   calls   itself   a   state   of   the   working   people,  is  humiliating  and  exploiting  the  workers.  Our  outdated  economy   is   squandering   energy...A   country   which   could   once  be   proud   of   the   standard   of   education   of   its   people   spends   so  little   on   education   that   today   it   ranks   72nd   in   the   world.   We  have  laid  waste  to  our  soil  and   the  rivers  and  the  forests   our  forefathers   bequeathed   us,   and   we   have   the   worst   environment in   all  of  Europe  today...  The   worst   thing   is   that   we   are   living   in   a   decayed   moral  environment.   We   have   become   morally   ill,   because   we   have  become   accustomed   to   saying   one   thing   and   thinking   another.  We   have   learned   not   to   believe   in   anything,   not   to   care   about  one   another   and   only   to   look   after   ourselves.   Notions   such   as  love,  friendship,  compassion,  humility  and  forgiveness  have  lost   their   depth   and   dimension,   and   for   many   of   us   they  represent   merely   some   kind   of   psychological   idiosyncrasy,   or  appear   as   some   kind   of   stray   relic   from   times   past,   something  rather   comical   in   the   era   of   computers   and   space   rockets...  The   previous   regime,   armed   with   its   arrogant   and   intoler-  ant   ideology,   denigrated   man   into   a   production   force   and  nature   into   a   production   tool.   In   this   way   it   attacked   their   very  essence   and   the   relationship   between   them.   It   made   talented  people   who   were   capable   of   managing   their   own   affairs...into  cogs   in   some   kind   of   monstrous,   ramshackle,   smelly   machine  whose   purpose   no   one   can   understand.   It   can   do   nothing   more  than   slowly   but   surely   wear   itself   down,   along   with   all   the   cogs  init.  When   I   talk   about   a   decayed   moral   environment...I   mean  all   of   us,   because   all   of   us   have   become   accustomed   to   the  totalitarian   system,   accepted   it   as   an   inalterable   fact   and  thereby   kept   it   running.   In   other   words,   all   of   us   are   respon-  sible,   each   to   a   different   degree,   for   keeping   the   totalitarian  machine   running.   None   of   us   is   merely   a   victim   of   it,   because  all   of   us   helped   to   create   it   together.  Why   doI   mention   this?   It   would be   very   unwise   to   see   the  sad   legacy   of   the   past   40   years   as   something   alien,   handed  down   to   us   by   some   distant   relatives.  On   the   contrary,   we   must   accept   this   legacy   as   something  which   we   have   brought   upon   ourselves.   If   we   can   accept   this,  then   we   will   understand that   it   is   up   to   all   of   us   to   do   something  about   it.   We   cannot   lay   all   the   blame   on   those   who   ruled   us  before,   not   only   because   this   would   not be   true   butalso   because  it   could   detract   from   the   responsibility   each   of   us   now   faces   -  the   responsibility   to   act   on   our   own   initiative,   freely,   sensibly  and   quickly...  Throughout   the   world,   people   are   surprised   that   the   acqui-  escent,   humiliated,   skeptical   Czechoslovak   people   who   appar-  ently   no   longer   believed   in   anything   suddenly   managed   to   find  the   enormous   strength   in   the   space   of   a   few   weeks   to   shake   off  the   totalitarian   system   in   a   completely   decent   and   peaceful  way.   We   ourselves   are   also   surprised   at   this,   and   we   ask   where  the   young   people,   in   particular,   who   have   never   known   any  other   system,   find   the   source   of   their   aspirations   for   truth,  freedom   of   thought,   political   imagination,   civic   courage   and  civic   foresight.   How   is   it   that   their   parents,   the   generation  which   was   considered   lost,   also   joined   in   with   them?   How   is  it   possible   that   so   many   immediately   grasped   what   had   to   be  done?  Of   course,   for   our   freedom   today   we   also   had   to   pay   a  price.   Many   of   our   people   died   in   prison   in   the   50s,   many   were  executed,   thousands   of   human   lives   were   destroyed,   hundreds  of   thousands   of   talented   people   were   driven   abroad....   Those  who   resisted   totalitarian   government   were  persecuted,  [as  were]   those   who   simply   managed   to   remain   true   to   their   own  principles   and   think   freely.   None   of   those   who   paid   the   price  in   one   way   or   another   for   our   freedom   today   should   be  forgotten...  Neither   should   we   forget   that   other   nations   paid   an   ever  higher   price   for   their   freedom   today,   and   thus   also   paid   indi-  rectly   forus,   too.   Therivers   of   blood   which   flowed   in   Hungary,  Poland,   Germany   and   recently   in   such   a   horrific   way   in  Romania,   as   well   as   the   sea   of   blood   shed   by   the   nations   of   the  Soviet   Union,   should   not   be   forgotten...it   was   these   great  sacrifices   which   wove   the   tragic   backdrop   for   today’s   freedom  or   gradual   liberation   of   the   Soviet-bloc   nations,   and   the   back-  drop   of   our   newly   charged   freedom,   too...  This,   it   seems   to   me,   is   the   great   moral   stake   of   the   present  moment.   It   contains   the   hope   that   in   the   future   we   will   no  longer   have   to   suffer   the   complex   of   those   who   are   perma-  nently   indebted   to   someone   else.   Now   it   is   up   to   us   alone  whether   this   hope   comes   to   fruition,   and   whether   our   civic,  nation   and   political   self-confidence   reawakens   in   a   historically  new   way.  4/1/92

ORLOFF CONSULTING, INC.   2  Mastery of Business Leadership (MBL)   teaches the specific skills and personal disciplines of leadership. MBL is about self-mastery through business knowledge, emotional literacy and authenticity.   The program supports the leader’s personal and professional development, which grows  confidence, superior performance and high effectiveness. The organization  benefits directly and immediately from the leader's new capabilities.  A major premise for MBL is that merely having top-notch business skills or emotional intelligence and authenticity is not enough. Among other things, the leader must know himself/herself and have the ability and willingness to see change and building relationships as a natural process in a successful organization The MBL program treats leadership as a learned set of skills both externally and internally and emphasizes the leader’s functions as role model, empowerer and coach, as well as setter of  direction, manager, and strategic thinker.  Orloff Consulting’s methodology is the foundation of the MBL. It teaches how to recognize and  focus on the   strengths of the the individual and the organization in order to create the desired  results. A Crisis in Corporate Leadersnip  Today's CEO must be a mapper, a thinker,  a mentor, and a storyteller.  It takes a strong  leader to bring a business  through a major transformation—and build  new bonds  between lop management and staff.  In CEO: Corporate Leadership in Action,  consultants Harry Levinson and Stuart  Rosenthal profile six successful leaders who  changed the direction of  their companies and  inspired a new camaraderie based on their  values and ideals.  CEO (Basic Books, $19.95) explores the  challenges faced by Walter Wriston at Citicorp,  Thomas J. Watson, Jr. at IBM, Reginald  Jones of  General Electric, Arthur 0.  ‘Sulzberger, Jr. of The New York  Times, John  Hanley of Monsanto, and lan K. MacGregor of AMAX. Here are some illuminating ex-  cerpts:  Mapping Out a  Strong  Identity  None of the CEOs we interviewed had a  specific  charge from  a  board of  directors;  nor did any start out with a vision. Each had  * define his own problems and methods for  olving them.  Jones laid out the six problems he faced at  3; Hanley the  three major issues at Mon-  santo, Sulzberger the four prominent con-  cerns at the Times. Each set out ona path  of resuscitation and recovery.  Wriston saw *  the world as one economic unit and the need  to prepare  to  compete  in those terms.  MacGregor saw a world of declining natural  resources and rising inflation, and therefore  advocated  acquiring  more mines, Watson  discovered that Univac had taken the com-  puter  lead  and threatened IBM's customer  arthur Ochs Sulzberger of The  New  York Times  base; at his  insistence, IBM engineers over:  took Univac in two years. Sulzberger saw no  adequate management and looming im-  poverishment that  would  follow a continuous urson drain on Times’ resources. All were clear about what they were going to do and  how they were going to doit.  Thinkers as well as Doers  Although much is said,  particularly by Peters  and Waterman, about companies being ac-  tion-oriented, what we've seen is a great deal of thinking.  GE asked for  conceptualization by  out-  siders. Walter  Wriston emphasized the Lay  making,  he had thought his position through and was  secure mit.  Many managers tend  to premature clo-  sure in  decision-making, They are already too action-oriented. Creativity does not nec-  essarily arise out of the tinkerer in  the  garage, nor  out of turning all tinkerers  loose.  While some  few  may  be innovative,  many others labor in the vineyard. This is true  in all disciplines. ~  Relating to the World at Large  Our leaders also saw themselves as having  an obligation  to society. Wriston pushed  for  what he  thought to  be  the most effective  function of the economic system.   7  MacGregor anticipated environmental con- cerns.  Watson  was concerned about the  impact  of his company on its  surroundings  and Hanley with the toxicological issue. Sulzberger voiced the  concern over  editorial  fairness.  Leaders are  managers of the values of an  organizatiori—but  much  more.  Is  Leadership  Inherited?  Each of  these  leaders had a  strong paternal  model and strove  to  please  that model, even when he only had its  memory  as a guide.  Thomas J. Watson, Jr., was  in business  with his  father. Walter Wriston  turned  to his.. father  for  advice  and  guidance. Jack Hanley  anticipated  being  his  father's partner. PunchTM  Sulzberger knew he  had to carry on  a  family  tradition represented  by  both  his  father  and  his  grandfather. All also had organizational models and  supporters. Our leaders could listen to  these people, though  not always  without  quarrel.  Two were in family businesses. At IBM.  the  father-son rivalry continued in  the busi-  ness unabated. Tom, Jr. was not going to  be  defeated; he would  prove himself to be a  worthy son. At the Times, there  was no -  immediate rivalry between Punch and his  father, there  was an idealized tradition  to be  sustained. Hanley,  MacGregor and Wriston  made their own personal values dominating  forces in their  organizations. “Leadership, as  play, leads to the triumphs of  the human spirit.”  By tact, Leopold  meant skill. His point,  however, was the importance of identifica-  tion with and lifetime apprenticeship to a  master who is one of a ine of masters.  Giving leadership  to an organization  is  as  much a skill as any other, The identification  and apprenticeship starts early, and these became paramount issues  for our  leaders,  Each was concemed  with building an  enduring organization—the figurative  sons  of sons—that subsequently could Tegene-  fate  itself from within.  The of   Affection  All six CEOs changed significant personnel  and made heavy-demands for  performance,  but they were also supportive, compassion-  ate and empathetic.  They were sensitive to  people's self-  esteem and face-saving needs; the lower in the organization,  the greater the concern for  the  person. MacGregor was so subtle,  one  subordinate didn’t know he had been fired.  Jones did personal favors for those in dis-  tress.  All were  acutely aware  of the need for  more competent managers—and five out of  the six  saw themselves as  teachers  of the  younger  generation.  A central  issue  for all was  their involve-  ment in succession.  When it came to that,  there were no clones, Jones, Wriston,  MacGregor, Hanley and Watson chose  men  who were quite different from themselves  and who, in tum,  would choose  different directions,  The leaders knew they  were in the busi- ness of building  enduring corporations. Each  understood whatever he achieved,  in the last  analysis, had to be the product of the be-  havior of his people, All this led to bonding  and strong mutual loyalty.  These men were also in  what Erik  Erickson calls the stage of  generativity.  They loved to mentor and to develop others.  They were talent  scouts and people-  growers. Their comfort with the aggressive  side of themselves and their sense of who and what they loved  allowed  them to enjoy  the rough and tumble of relating to others.  Only the  true  leader, like the parent who  enables his  child to leave home when he  grows up, can leave his company in the 7  hands of others, having assured himself that  his job is done. Not to let go is to manipulate  and exploit in one’s own self-interest. To be  able to endure the pain of letting  go takes  deep and  abiding  affection.  Levinson on Leadership 1,   Strong leaders are necessary for organi-  zations that must undergo significant change.  Not good managers or executives; -  but strong  leaders.  2. Leadership that  builds changing organi-  zations into larger and better social instru-  ments will not achieve its ends by consensus.  ~ Permission, yes. But consensus, no.  3. The leader  must  have a highly developed  capacity for abstraction, for  vision, and the  strength to take  charge. He must pull his  organization  into the future.  4. The leader must serve as an identifica” tion figure—yet he must  also  be attentive  to  detail. He must fight the tendency  to over-  control, but  he cannot hang loose without  creating chaos.  The required  behavior is exemplified by  no less a leader than Winston  Churchill. His  biographer Simon Schama writes: “By sheer force  of  personality, transmitted to the Brit-  ish Parliament and  to the  people through Tadio broadcasts, he tumed  fear  into  for- titude. By telling the truth  he actually suc-  ceeded in making  things  seem better, not  worse.” Schama reduced  his  peculiar  chem-  istry to four  elements:  —his indefatiyability in the face  of  stag- geringly hard work  —his impressive  grasp  of  details  — the passion and  dignity of his  rhetoric  = i Reginald H. Jones of G.E.  —his unswerving moral decency.  5. When one is in  love  with one’s work, then the extraordinary hours  are  like play.  Take Churchill again: he could work joyfully at full capacity for 15 hours or more  each  day. Despite his burdens, a leader  enjoys the  work he is doing and makes of it a kind of  play. We agree with Warren  Bennis that the  leader's  intention  is a playground, an arena  surrounding an  idea. But  we go beyond  that  to affirm  that leadership  is a form of play.  Barbara Tuchman  says: “Man at  play is  surely as significant a figure  as  man at war or  work. In human activity, the  invention of the  ball may  be said to  rank with the  invention of  the wheel.” Leadership, as play, leads to the  triumphs . of the  human spirit.  6. It  is also the enactment of a dramatic  human story. Said  Ben Kingsley of Gandhi fame: “I  want  to  be a great storyteller and have’  people  come  a  long way to hear the stories I  have  to tell  The storyteller has always  been  at the center of the community, and if we  start to  ease him  out, then we're in trouble  politically, as well as socially. If we lose our  sense of  the  theatre, then  we  lose  our identity as a nation.”  The leader has to be a great storyteller. People come a long  way  to  share  in his  stories,  his fantasies. The leader  has  alway's been  at  the center of  the community. We  cannot  do  without him.  October  1985

SUMMARY OF THE CASE   STUDY IN COMMUNICATION:  The content of why an organization  is failing is helpful to demonstrate a  model  for communication problems, however, it is only a model. The content  is  not  important  beyond that.  The   dynamics   of the communication  is   the place of real   information  from   which to learn. Unclear communication and  harbored  resentments greatly impede the  company's  prosperity. Actually, any  aspect of a relationship that is  "undercover" (not  talked about) will grow  bigger and adversely effect  the company.   Reactions not  dealt with  responsibly begin to fester.  When there is a time  lag  between reaction and correction, you're dealing in the past. The results of festering reaction are devastating to  companies and relationships. The festering seeps  out and affects all  your interactions.  Your communications become very   clear as you motice  and correct   your   reactions.  See  what  your company is really saying to all who touch it -- nothing  really goes unnoticed by  your co-workers  or  customers although  there  may be  agreements to not notice  things. MASTERY Mastery in one’s career simply requires that we constantly produce results  beyond and out of the ordinary.   Mastery is a product of consistently going beyond limits.   For most people it starts with technical excellence in a chosen  field and   a commitment to that excellence.   If you are willing to commit yourself  to excellence, to surround yourself with things that represent this and miracles,  your life will change.   (When we speak of miracles, we speak of events or  experiences in the real world which are beyond the ordinary.) It's remarkable how much mediocrity we live with, surrounding ourselves with  daily reminders that the average is acceptable.   Our world suffers from terminal  normality.   Take a moment to assess all of the things around you that promote  your being “average”.   These are the things that keep you powerless to go beyond  a “limit” you arbitrarily set for yourself.   The first step to mastery is the removal  of everything in your environment that represents mediocrity, removing those  things that are limiting.   One way is to surround yourself with friends who ask more of you than you do.   Didn't some of your best teachers, coaches, parents, etc.? Another step on the path to mastery is the removal of resentment.   Develop compassion for yourself so that you can grow from experience.   Rather than comparing yourself and resenting people, remain open and receptive; let  experience be like the planting of a seed within you that, with nourishment, will  grow  into your own individual mastery.  We are all ordinary.   But a master, rather than condemning himself for his “ordinariness”, will embrace it and use it as a foundation for building the extraordinary.   Rather than using it as an excuse for inactivity, he will use it as a  vehicle for correcting, which is essential in the process of attaining mastery. You must be able to correct yourself without invalidating or condemning yourself, to  accept results and improve upon them.   Correct, don't protect.   Correction is essential to power and  mastery.  - Stuart  Emery  Choices International

NAGEMENT  The New Wizard of Corporate Culture  Steve Covey’s   program takes  one year, but executives say the changes are permanent.  hen Stephen R. Covey talks,  executives   listen.   The Utah-based   management consultant is not a spellbinding speak- er. Nevertheless,   he   has   captivated thousands of executives with his theo- ties about how to change a corporate culture. And he has wona   rich congre-  gation of corporate converts, including  Aetna Life & Casualty, Walt Disney, McDonnell   Douglas,   Consolidated Freightways,   Security   Pacific   and  Trammell Crow. “His seminars have  absolutely   changed   my   life,”   says President   J.   McDonald   Williams   of  Trammell Crow Corp. Unlike quick-fix training programs,  offering   solutions   to   crises   or   tech- niques to coax more production out of  workers, Covey emphasizes the long haul. He teaches executives to change  themselves  and  the way they  run  their  companies   in   a   year-long   program,  with monthly sessions to monitor their  progress. It adds up to seven days—  stretched over a year.  It takes   that  much time, he says, to inculcate new  habits.   “We believe that learning is a sequential process, and therefore time  is required to develop your character before you can develop as a manager.”  For   the   past   three   years,   the course, called the Art of Executive Ex- cellence, has  been a hot seller.  Compa-  [nd a)  by Thomas J. Murray  nies pay anywhere   from   $30,000   to $400,000, depending on the number of  executives enrolled. Usually they send  groups:   McDonnell Douglas has   175  managers attending; Aetna 100. Mak-  ing it   a company—rather than an indi-  vidual—effort   means   that   managers  reinforce each other in changing the  corporate culture.  “There are two quick ways to take charge of your own life,” barks Covey  to the fifty managers attending a re-  cent seminar at the Sundance Ski Re- sort in Provo, Utah. Striding back and  forth in front of the suddenly alert ex- ecutives, he goes on to show them how to, first; set a goal and work to accom-  plish it and,   second,   make a promise  and keep it. Using lots of eye contact and humor, the bald-headed, muscular 53-year-old  former professor of organizational be- havior   and   management   at   Brigham  Young University exudes personal be- lievability. “His greatest strengthis his  credibility,” says Michael G. Winston, director of human resourcé develop-  ment at McDonnell Douglas Astronau-  tics Co. “You sense that he practices  what he   preaches   and   lives what he teaches.” The backbone of Covey’s course are seven habits of excellence. In the sem-  inars, the executives practice integrat-  ing the seven habits in their lives, par- ticularly in their current corporate cul-  ture and using them to devise new and  more effective management systems for their companies.  And   corny   as   it   sounds,   Covey preaches   that   “Virtue   pays!”   And, hard as it is to believe,   he convinces  executives that his principles of human relations—integrity, self-reliance, re-  spect for others, keeping promises, in- corporating another’s point of view—  can be applied to   virtually every on- the-job   situation they will ever face.  Carl Hayes, senior vice president at La Quinta Motor Inns,   says: “He brings  us a message we don’t often hear: that strong commitment to a set of princi-  ples can help us to operate in almost any kind  of  environment.”  ovey’s seven habits are proac- tivity (taking the initiative and  responsibility   for   making things happen), creativity, productivi-  ty,   interdependency   (cooperation),  empathy   (seeing   the   other   person's point of view),   synergy (team work) and consistency.   The first three, he  claims, break dependency  habits  that  hold back an executive’s ability to act  for himself.  The next three help him interact ef-  fectively  with other people. keeps him practicing the first six.  Instead   of   “blaming   others   when things go wrong,” he  maintains, a pro-  active executive  exercises his  freedom  to  make his  own choices. Covey says:  focus on your “circle of influence,” the  area over which  you  wield  control, and  avoid your “circle of concern,” the sur-  rounding  areas that  affect  you  but  are  controlled by  others. These could be a  closed-minded  boss, a company-wide  system that doesn't  work or govern-  ment  regulations that straitjacket your operations.   Instead   of  railing   against  misfortune, he says,   use   your re-  sourcefulness  to  improve your lot from  your own  end. “Since you  can't do any-  thing   about   that   outer circle,   it’s a  waste  of  valuable  time and energy to  get involved,”   he asserts.  Covey’s formulation  of  proactivity is  one of his more  original contributions  to management training  folklore. The other   habits   are   commonly   found   in  most training programs, Creativity, as  Covey defines  it,  is  to  begin a task with  the end  in mind—that is, knowing  what  PHOTOGRAPH  SY DOUG MARTIN  JULY 1986  one wants to accomplish and having a  plan to attain the goal. Productivity is leveraging the use of time. Covey rec-  ommends   that executives   set  priori-  ties  by categorizing their  tasks as “im-  portant   and   urgent,”   “important   but not urgent,”   “urgent but   not impor- tant,” or  “not important  or urgent.”  In- terdependency is   creating   coopera-  tion. In dealing with superiors, peers,  subordinates,   suppliers and custom- ers, Covey advises  executives to seek  benefits for both   sides,   using a “win-  win” approach to negotiations. mpathy, Covey says,   means  E getting  “inside  another per-  son’s   shoes.”   This   requires  careful listening.   But, he adds, it  pays  off in building trust and credibility with  employees.  Covey defines  synergy as the  skill to knit the individual talents of a group of  employees ina team effort  to achieve a  larger end result than  could  come from  separate efforts. “It is consensus  deci- sion   making,   and   that   is   the   highest form of decision making,” says Covey. The final  habit is consistency. The effective   manager,   says   Covey,   re- fuses to allow backsliding. To maintain output, however, he says, executives  must   renew themselves physically,  mentally,   emotionally and   spiritually.  He recommends: exercise daily, read  prescribed books   monthly and   medi- tate regularly.  But   what   sets   Covey’s   program  apart from others is the commitment  he asks of each company client. To be- gin with, he expects a group of manag- ers—not just a few—to participate at the same time. And then, of course, it is usually a year-long effort.  Moreover, each executive involves  peers,   superiors   and   subordinates in the program by asking them to make anonymous assessments of the execu-  tive’s weaknesses and strengths dur-  ing the  year-long course. These evalu-  ations measure his progress,   as seen  by fellow workers. And at the monthly  sessions, Covey uses the assessments to advise him on ways to improve his

performance. An Aetna general man-  ager regards this as “the most mean-  ingful part of the entire program.”  On top of that, Covey requires each  executive to teach what he has learned  to fellow managers within 48 hours af- ter each session.   “Teaching not only  reinforces   what   is   learned,   it   also  spreads the concept through a compa-  ny almost immediately,” says Covey. e   also   favors   performance agreements between manag- ers   and   their   subordinates.  One of the biggest flaws in companies today, he claims, is their failure to de-  vise workable accountability systems.  Antagonistic   relations   with   supervi-  sors   have   drained   trust   out of many workers, he says. He argues for jointly formulated   performance   contracts,  setting   out   the   employee’s goal,   re-  sources available, and rewards await-  ing him.   “Treat your employees   the  way   you   want your customers   to   be  treated,” he says.  Covey also asks executives to prac- tice their new habits on their families.  “When did you last congratulate some-  one—your son or a subordinate—for  doing something right?” he asks a sem- inar audience,   producing a   stir of dis-  comfort. Covey believes it is inherent-  ly wrong to wear two faces,   one for home and another for the office. Graduates   of   the   Covey   course boast about how they have put his prin- ciples into practice. For example, Me-  direc Inc., a Salt Lake City-based hos-  pital supply firm,   told the suppliers of equipment   that   it   rents   to   hospitals that they were charging too little, says  Vice President Charles R.   Harrison.  Medirec discovered that its contracts  with its suppliers gave it a large price  and   service   advantage   at   their   ex- pense. Instead of taking the profits and  saying,   “Tough luck,” reports Harri-  son, top management renegotiated so that both sides came out ahead. Even- tually, they would have found out and  could   have   gone   into   competition  ”   against us, he says. This way, Medirec gave up some of its short-term gain in  favor of its long-term self-interest.  After   taking   Covey's   course,   the field managers at Aetna’s Personal Fi-  nancial Security division   convinced  management to cede to them control over the annual staff training sessions, which   had   become   ineffective.   And Ralph J. D’Amato, Minneapolis branch manager, says this had created “tre- mendous frustration” for branch man-  agers.  The problem was that the division management dictated the material to be used, even though it rarely worked. Using   Covey’s   proactivity   habit, branch managers made a presentation  of   their   ideas   to   top   management,  which, to their surprise, were accept- ed. By working out a solution from the place they controlled, adds D’Amato, the field  managers  helped to improve productivity for the first time in years.  Another Aetna general manager re-  ports   that   in   preparing   a   significant change ina   planning program, he broke  with tradition and allowed employees from   four   separate   departments   to come up with the final evaluation and recommendation. “What emerged was synergistic   problem-solving and true team building,” he says.  Despite   the popularity of Covey’s  program, one question remains: How much does it.depend on the personal magnetism of Steve Covey? While he is backed up by a 35-person staff and also   uses   such   other   high-powered  consultants   as   Tom   Peters,   Peter Drucker,   John   Naisbitt   and   Roger Fisher at his seminars,   it is Covey’s  singular power to convince executives  of the rightness of long-term reliance on principles that “stands him head and shoulders above the rest,” says Mc-  Donnell   Douglas’   Winston. CHOICES:   MBLTM 8)   Integrity and Leadership,   Self-Directed Program  Handling   the   Reactions There are tools at your disposal to take care of the child inside of you. Pick the most recent experience that you had with. another person and you left yourself, you "lost it," you got little, whatever phrase  you use to describe it.  Remember how you felt.   Remember what the other person said. Remember what your strongest compulsions were. Visualize the child that's inside of you.   See the little girl or boy.  You may not see a   picture, you may see a color or an energy of  some kind.   Whatever comes up.   There is no right way to have a  kid inside of you.  Remember to keep breathing.  Now, you be there for that child.   Whatever that means right this minute.   Hold him or her.   Sit next to him/her while you drive or  while you're in your office -- wherever this incident you're  remembering   occurred.  Let the child start to talk, cry, pout, laugh, whatever he/she needs to do right  now.   Let the child sit or stand or do  whatever he/she needs right now.   Is he holding himself, is he having a physical  tantrum, is he crying?  ..Give yourself some  time  here...  Visualize you  creating the context  for that child. Beliefs Create Perceived Reality  Typically, most decisions are made for the sake of survival. We try to make sense of the world around us and fit in with an acceptable level of comfort and safety. 4.   Wi   The Triune Brain  Paul MacLean, Chief Scientist at the National Institute of Mental Health, developed the  Triune Brain Theory. Like an archaeologist, he went on a dig, but he explored the brain. According to MacLean, the brain has three parts - the reptilian brain, the limbic brain, and the neo-cortex. The triune brain consists of: *   The reptilian brain - where the instincts for survival are based.   It makes you feel safe. If the reptilian is about our basic instinct, when do you think this part of the  brain is used? Does it sometimes affect decisions that determine results?  *   The limbic brain - the home of emotional expression, and memory. It is where our  emotion bonds with our memory. That is why it is so difficult to make “simple”  changes.  *   The neo-cortex - the center of intellect and reasoning. This part of the brain wants to solve problems. Can you think of times when you use this part of the brain? In studying the brain, MacLean discovered something fascinating. In fact, he  revolutionized how people looked at information retention and application. MacLean  discovered that the whole brain had to be engaged for successful learning and application  to happen.  This workshop will engage your whole brain, particularly the limbic region, because the limbic is where emotions and long-term memory reside. Effective ways to use information  are learned more quickly this way. To do this, well involve the physical and other senses and engage the whole brain, so you embrace the learning and are able to act upon it immediately. Radical Choices and Emotional Literacy  Individuals all have an inherent emotional intelligence (EQ). Emotional Literacy is  the ability and commitment to be self-aware, and, as a result, fo make decisions  and behave in alignment with an individual's objectives and vision. People who achieve this ability can accomplish business and personal relationship goals with  ease and unimagined success. Radical Choices teaches people to apply this  skill to their everyday decisions and behaviors through our emotional literacy  learning process.  Studies now substantiate that an individual's success is more dependent upon “Emotional IQ" than intellectual intelligence. Emotional literacy is a transferable skill. Radical Choices has developed a learning technology that facilitates the learning of emotional literacy. Training programs designed and delivered within the context of emotional literacy provide deeper, longer-term learning and  facilitate real behavior change. What Is Emotional Literacy?  Throughout our lives, there are many events that we want to leave behind, so  we often cloud them up or create pleasant illusions to cover up the pain. When  we do this we then forget in our conscious minds what happened.   However, when experiences are interpreted and changed and the feelings are diluted  and dulled, the experience doesn't go away. They build up power and begin to  control our behavior, albeit unconsciously.  We develop our patterns of clouding over painful emotions, patterns of  interpretation and protection, in our childhood.   Because of this, many of us  have no idea what and when we're feeling.   We are really reacting fo a  situation according to the patterns we developed as children.   We “act ouf."  Acting out is when we feel something like sadness or anger or happiness and either don't realize it, don't understand why, or won't allow ourselves to experience the feelings all the way. Instead they explode or leak out in other

ways.   For instance, a child who is jealous of a new sibling is not usually allowed to feel that--instead they may stab the baby with crayons.   Similarly, feelings of jealousy on the job may not be experienced, but acted out through backbiting  or sabotage.  Emotional literacy is the ability to be self aware, to understand what we are feeling and finally to choose our behavior. With this self-awareness, we can behave in ways that produce specific, desired results in the workplace. Radical  Choices methodologies specifically teach emotional literacy tools that help people to become conscious of their own experiences, feelings, and resistance to change so that they are not compelled to continue old behavioral patterns  that unconsciously sabotage their relationships with managers, employees,  customers, friends or family. It includes developing the skills to recognize the  unspoken messages from others, so that individuals can align themselves and  adadress real needs and issues. The direct results include the development of  authentic, healthy relationships based upon trust and relevant information.  These results can translate into motivated, empowered employees and loyal  customers.  Radical Choices and Business Results  A disadvantage of not feeling everything is that we misinterpret what is going on. This is deadly in our relationships and our businesses. Someone we are dealing with may feel angry, and if we are not able to experience anger we  may think he or she are sad or not notice, and then act on that faulty information. This kind of misinterpreting seriously damages business and personal  relationships.  Knowing the emotional underpinning of the decisions that we make and the  emotional content of interactions with our co-workers and clients can provide a  new dimension of comprehension to almost every situation in the workplace. ETP Instructor's Manual   2  Extended Teaching Program  (Personal Responsibility Training)  Instructor's Notes:  The ETP is an educational curriculum in the teachings of  PERSONAL RESPONSIBILITY. It is not therapy or a  substitute for therapy. The instructor's role is to teach the  information introduced in the Choices Weekend on a   deeper,  more  personal level.   The participants are responsible for  their own learning and how they choose to use the  information.  The instructor sets the context of personal responsibility by  being with the truth of their own and each participant's experience while at the same time teaching the content of each session. They do not process anyone unless that particular experience will demonstrate a point in the  teaching.  As the material is taught, and participants begin their  journey, they will be in and out of their old belief systems or illusions regularly.   When a   participant is in their illusion, the instructor stays with the content they share until they are about to have a monster fight, or the participant is clearly  incongruent. The instructor then STOPS the interaction and uses the content to teach about what is true in the situation, ALWAYS using humor and without judgement. If there are any judgements, the instructor demonstrates a way to include  not judging the judgements.  Revised 4/23/91

ETP Instructor's Manual   3  It is not the instructor's responsibility to see that the participants use the information in a positive, supportive  way, but rather to see that the truth about their choice is  clear. This sets the context of unconditional love as well by  demonstrating acceptance that everyone is responsible for their own life.   This is a crucial part of the transformation  process.  The intention is to allow the participants to be 100% responsible for the learning they receive from the program. The TA is there to support the instructor during the session to  stay centered and clear. They will also be available to the participants for support during the intervals between sessions. Tell the participants that this  session is about Vision and Power and that tonight (Wed) through Friday afternoon is preparation for a vision quest  Friday night through Saturday.  Ik   Teach about perturbation and change»  e   When   we take in and receive new information, there is multiple data, multiple beliefs about the same  situation, conflicting   information. The old belief system mixed with the present reality.   The brain cannot tolerate it. And there is strong agitation and  perturbation.  ¢   The brain is a dissipating structure. It is an open system and with enough perturbation it shifts to a  higher order, which means it can contain a bigger  picture and can hold more paradox and ambiguity.  ¢ Perturbation that YOU create from within in order to grow creates lasting change. GRADUATE TRAINING OUTLINE   2  GRADUATE TRAINING  Purpose:   To provide follow up support for graduates of the Choices Weekend. Specifically, it is to provide a place where participants can continue the growth  initiated in the workshops, get answers to any questions they have, and have a consistent place to get support  on issues they are working on in  their daily  lives. Participants   set specific goals they want to achieve by using the Choices concepts.  Format:  The Graduate Training is a 6-week program for graduates of the Choices Weekend.   The participants meet for three hours once a week in  a residential setting. The cost is $375  per  person. There is a 12-person  maximum and 8 person minimum for each  group.  A graduate training group should be scheduled after every Weekend.  ENROLLMENT   GUIDELINES  Announce the date of the next Graduate Training at the end of a Choices  Weekend with maps, times, and instructor.  Send out information and begin calling potential participants at least one month in  advance.  Recruit someone to barter to hold the sessions at their house and to provide all beverages for half the cost of the Graduate Training.   This person should keep an  accurate record of expenses of the workshop.  Gold Cards -   a maximum of two Gold Cards may be used per Graduate Training.  *jf a person uses the card as a gift they pay 1/2 the Graduate Training cost  *if the person uses the card for themselves, they pay 1/4 the Graduate  Training cost Copyright © 1990  by  QED

Your Story  For over 25 years, Judith Orloff has dedicated her life to helping people transform  their perspectives, allowing them to see through judgements, assumptions and the  brilliantly constructed walls we build around ourselves. Doing so empowers us to  make clearer decisions and create new possibilities for ourselves. She has worked with individuals, corporations, universities, and families, and her work continues to create meaning for participants long after the programs are complete. Using her Six Principles of Emotional Literacy, Judith has developed a   core learning methodology so fundamental that it has been used successfully in a diverse range of applications: strategic learning initiatives for Fortune 500 companies, aligning executive teams, healing family and individual trauma, and personal transformation.  Radical Choices is the next stage in the evolution of Judith’s teaching. As we move  through a rapidly-changing world of technology and interconnectivity, our company seeks to address the needs and concerns of today’s world through today’s medium:  smartphones and tablets. Social Movements  Environmentalism had it’s origins in the 1970’s with the first Earth Day being held  on April 22, 1970.  2nd-wave feminist movement in the US took a prominent role within society, he  Supreme Court's 1973 decision of Roe v. Wade that constitutionalized the right to an abortion brought the women's rights movement into the national political spotlight.  The wage gap failed to close but progress was made in lessening the gap.  The gay movement made a huge step forward in the 1970s with the election of  political figures such as Harvey Milk to public office and the advocating of anti-gay discrimination legislation passed and not passed during the decade. Many  celebrities, including Freddie Mercury and Andy Warhol, also “came out" during this  decade, bringing gay culture further into the limelight. The Black Nationalist movement grew out of frustrations with the “non-violent” strategies of earlier Civil Rights Activists. With the assassinations of both Martin Luther King, Jr. and Senator Bobby Kennedy, many blacks were compelled to reject ideas of negotiation and instead embrace isolation. The feminist movement also splintered from a larger push for Civil Rights in the 1970s.  John Dewey  The overriding theme of Dewey's works was his profound belief in democracy, be it in politics, education or communication and journalism. As Dewey himself stated in 1888, while still at the University of Michigan, "Democracy and the one, ultimate, ethical ideal of humanity are to my mind synonymous." The ideas of democracy and social reform are continually discussed in Dewey's writings on education. Dewey makes a   strong case for the importance of education

not only as   a   place to gain content knowledge, but also as a place to learn how to live. In his eyes, the purpose of education should not revolve around the acquisition of a pre-determined set of skills, but rather the realization of one's full potential and the ability to use those skills for the greater good. "education is a regulation of the process of coming to share in the social  consciousness; and that the adjustment of individual activity on the basis of this  social consciousness is the only sure method of social reconstruction". Dewey advocated for an educational structure that strikes a balance between delivering knowledge while also taking into account the interests and experiences of  the student.  "the child and the curriculum are simply two limits which define a   single process.  Just as two points define a straight line, so the present standpoint of the child and  the facts and truths of studies define instruction” Children enter education with 4 innate impulses; To communicate, to construct, to  inquire and to express in finer form.  Tempered Radical  "Tempered radicals" may not sound like the type to start revolutions or topple corrupt governments, but in the corporate world, it is often these quiet change advocates that get the ball rolling and policies changing". It’s being both an insider and an outsider, working to fit into what is currently acceptable and working to change norms of acceptability. It’s about rocking the boat, but not so hard that you fall out of it. So tempered radicalism is in many ways a balancing act that gets expressed in a variety of ways.  Asserting the nonconforming aspects of oneself can pave the way for learning and  change by questioning current practice and expectations and providing an alternative. ... When people act in ways that outwardly express a valued part of their  selves, they make that part of their selves ‘real.’  Another view sees organizations as organic and evolutionary, which means they are changing all the time. If we think of organizations that way, little nudges in the system can change the network of relationships, stimulate learning, and affect how work gets done. It means that small actions actually matter and that people can  provoke change from many places within the organization.  When actions produce   a concrete result, they increase a person’s sense of efficacy, which in turn fuels new efforts and a different perspective on what constitutes an opportunity for making change. Success fuels involvement, and involvement fuels  more action, and so on. The process begins, though, with action rather than analysis.

Proposed   Conceptual   Scheme   for   the   Core   Teachings   of   Radical   Love  The   Radical   Love   teachings   give   us   an   approach   to   our   activity   that   leads   us   into  the   unconditioned   through   our   conditioned   reactive   self.  Activities  Pure   Inseeing   (Just   Own   It)   —   We   notice   our   blaming   others   and/or  circumstances   for   our   experience   and   switch   to   owning   our   experience.   We   start  describing   our   experience   in   terms   of   what   “I   am   feeling/thinking”   rather   than  speculating   about   what   “others”   are   doing   to   me.   This   taking   of   responsibility   for  our   experience   empowers   us   and   frees   us   from   a   victim   mentality.   As   we   look  closer   at   our   experience   we   start   to   notice   that   our   thoughts   and   feelings   shift  about   and   have   no   real   substance   to   them.   We   start   to   become   as   free   and   open   as  the   nondual   space   in   which   these   thoughts/feelings   are   arising   in   awareness.  Pure   Listening   (Just   Get   It)   -   We   notice   how   we   react   to   what   others   present   us.  We   notice   our   tendency   to   afÏrm   or   negate   what   is   being   offered.   We   then   shift   to  just   getting   what   is   being   shared   without   needing   to   identify   with   or   reject   it.   We  notice   any   pressure   we   feel   to   respond   and   allow   ourselves   to   be   with   those  feelings   without   acting   on   them.   We   become   the   open   space   of   awareness   neither  resisting   nor   grasping   at   whatever   is   arising.  Pure   Speaking   (Just   Share   It)   —   We   notice   how   we   attempt   to   obscure   and   shade  the   truth   in   what   we   say   and   don’t   say.   We   become   aware   of   our   discomfort   with  sharing   the   truth   in   a   direct   and   clear   way.   We   shift   to   speaking   the   truth   rather  than   trying   to   manipulate   the   people   with   whom   we   are   in   communication.   We  find   that   we   can   share   without   imagining   any   need   for   separation   between  ourselves   and   others.   This   allows   us   to   speak   with   integrity   from   the   open   space  free  of  any   personal   agenda.  Pure  Choosing  (Just  Choose  It)  —  We  notice   our   tendency   to  talk  ourselves   into  our   choices   and   our   dependence   on   reasons   to   justify   them.   We   notice   our  tendency   to   indecision   and   our   discomfort   with   decisions   based   on   picking   one  viewpoint  over   another.  We  acknowledge   the   competing   reasons   and   viewpoints  that   arise   when   we   are   faced   with   a   decision,   but   we   don’t   try   to   reach   a  conclusion   through   reasoning.   Instead,   we   release   our   reasons   and   make   our  decision   from   the   open   space   of   nondual   wisdom.   We   can   then   move   beyond   the  choice   point   without   the   burden   of   the   limited   viewpoint   that’s   involved   in   a  justification.  Pure   Doing   (Just   Do   It)   —   We   notice   how   we   disempower   ourselves   and   others  when   we   fail   to   keep   our   word.   We   acknowledge   any   discomfort   or   aversion   that  we   experience   in   doing   what   is   necessary   to   keep   our   word,   but   we   keep   it  anyway.   If   we   really   can’t   keep   our   word   then   we   immediately   acknowledge   that  fact   openly   and   share   it   with   those   affected.   This   allows   us   to   cooperate   effectively  with   others   and   builds   trust.   We   also   find   that   when   acting   to   fulfill   our
commitments   we   are   acting   from   an   open   space   without   any   need   to   like   or  dislike   the   activity.

Objections  How  do  you  feel  when  you  hear  an  objection?  How   do   you   feel   when   a   prospect   raises   an   objection?  How   do   you   know   it's   a   real   objection?  Reaction:   What   is   it?  Reactions   are   a   cover-up.   They   protect   our   true   feelings   and  experience.   But,   reactions   are   gold   mines!  A   reaction   is   a   wonderful   opportunity   for   freedom.   It's   a   key   to  something   you   do   that   keeps   you   from   being   the   present   moment,   so   you  can   have   what   you   want.   If   you   stay   open   to   learning   while   in  reaction,   you   can   choose   a   different   behavior   right   in   the   middle   of  it.   This   changes   the   pattern.  How   can   you   tell   if   you   are   "in   reaction"?  A   reaction   does   not   have   to   look   a   certain   way.   In   fact,   it   will   not.  Since   it   is   a   learned   behavior   based   on   our   individual   interpretations  of   how   we   were   supposed   to   be   in   our   families,   a   reaction   manifests  itself   differently   for   everyone.   But   here   are   some   unmistakable  clues.  You  may  be  "in  reaction":  %*   when   your   body   feels   tight   and   anxious,   not   present;  *   whenever   you   think   that   what   you   feel   is   about   someone   else;  *   when   your   mind   will   not   shut   up;  *   when   your   thoughts   relate   to   the   past   or   the   future,   not   the  present;  *   when   you   are   hiding   or   numb,   felling   foggy   or   confused;  *   whenever   there   is   a   judgment   (good   or   bad);  *   whenever   you   feel   compelled   to   act   or   not   act;  %*   whenever   you   have   accumulated   good   evidence   and   can   prove   beyond   a  shadow   of   a   doubt   that   you   are   right;  %*   when   events   appear   to   be   coming   at   you   —   you   feel   like   a   victim,   a  victimizer,   and   a   judge   all   at   the   same   time.

Reactions   are   Goldmines  Areaction   is   a   creative   cover-up   learned   to   obfuscate   and   convolute   our  unadulterated   experience.   It   is   an   acceptable   response   we   learned   while   very   young.  Now,   when   we   begin   to   feel   those   feelings,   we   automatically   experience   the   same  cover   up,   even   though   there   is   no   story.  How  Do  You  Know   What  Is  A  Reaction  and  What  Is   a  Feeling?  You   know   you   are   in   a   reaction   when   there   is   a   value   judgment   on   what   you   are  feeling   (for   example,   greed,   or   fear,   or   lust,   or   need   or   yearning).  Here   are   some   clues   that   you   are   “in   reaction”:  Your   body   feels   tight   and   anxious.  Events   appear   to   be   coming   at   you   from   outside   -   you   may   feel   like   a   victim  and   a   judge   all   at   the   same   time.  You   usually   think   what   you   feel   is   about   or   because   of   someone   else.  You   feel   compelled   to   act   or   not   act.  You   think   other   people   are   doing   something   to   you   or   you   to   them.  You   think   you   can   hurt,   help,   or   change   someone’s   experience   including   your  own.  Your   thoughts   relate   to   the   past   or   the   future,   not   the   present. Archetypes   are   likewise   supposed   to   have   been   present   in   folklore   and  literature   for   thousands   of   years,   including   prehistoric   artwork.   The   use   of   archetypes   to  illuminate   personality   and   literature   was   advanced   by   Carl   Jung   early   in   the   20th   century,   who  suggested   the   existence   of   universal   countless   forms   that   channel   experiences   and   emotions,  resulting   in   recognizable   and   typical   patterns   of   behavior   with   certain   probable   outcomes.  Archetypes   are   cited   as   important   to   both   ancient   mythology   and   modern   narratives.  Jung   outlined   five   main   archetypes:  +   The   Self,   the   regulating   center   of   the   psyche   and   facilitator   of   individuation,  +   The   Shadow,   the   opposite   of   the   ego   image,   often   containing   qualities   with   which   the   ego  does   not   identify,   but   which   it   possesses   nonetheless,  +   The   Anima,   the   feminine   image   in   a   man's   psyche,   or  *   The   Animus,   the   masculine   image   in   a   woman's   psyche,  +   The   Persona,   the   image   we   present   to   the   world,   usually   protecting   the   Ego   from   negative  images   (like   a   mask),   and   considered   another   of   'the   sub-personalities,   the   complexes'.’”!  Although   archetypes   can   take   on   innumerable   forms,   there   are   a   few   particularly   notable,  recurring   archetypal   images!*!“"""°"4,  °   The   Child   ¢   The   Damsel   in   distress  *   The   Hero   *   The   Trickster   or   Fox  ¢   The   Martyr   ¢   The   Devil   or   Satan  ¢   The   Great   Mother   ¢   The   Scarecrow  ¢   The   Wise   old   man   or   Sage   *   The   Mentor  *   The   Wise   Old   Woman/Man,   archetypes   *   The   Warrior  of   the   collective   unconscious  Jung   also   outlined   what   he   called   archetypes   of   transformation,   which   are   situations,   places,  ways,   and   means   that   symbolize   the   transformation   in   question.   These   archetypes   exist   primarily  as   energy   and   are   useful   in   organizational   development,   personal   and   organizational   change  management,   and   extensively   used   in   branding.

2.   The Reactive Self  A reaction is when you respond to the present situation from the past.  When we are “in reaction,” our responses are coming from automatic pilot, from our past, from all the ways we learned to act in childhood when our feelings and thoughts were not  okay with the people around us.  So, what is so important about our Reactive Self? We have an old response to something—  so what? We think we are feeling one thing and are really feeling something else—what  difference does it make? We blame somebody or something for what we are feeling—is  this so unusual?  No, most of us blame someone or something for what we are feeling. Many of us are not  aware of what we are feeling, and most of us respond to what happens in the present the way we did ten, twenty or thirty years ago. There’s nothing “wrong” or “bad” with any of it.  Yet, this behavior keeps us at a disadvantage.. We end up perpetuating old patterns that prevent us from achieving our present day goals. Dissolving our Reactive Selves always involves telling ourselves something we don’t want  to hear.  2.1.   The Reactive Self - How to Recognize It  There are several ways, then, you can tell when you are in reaction:  « When your body language is rigid (you cover your eyes, or face, or fold your arms)  ¢ When your comments are irrelevant to what is being discussed * When your affect is numb, foggy, confused or angry * When you make judgments rather than thought out feedback and evaluation.  + Whenever you are compelled to act or not act  * When you act as if you are in a courtroom, presenting good evidence and prove beyond a  shadow of a doubt that you are right about your point of view.  * When you  want  to argue,  find  fault, want to make  everything  okay. 3.   Personal   Responsibility  To some, the word “responsibility” may connote “doing the right thing” or bearing the “purden” of responsibility.  In the context of DLT, to be personally responsible is defined as “response-ability.” Being  Personally Responsible means, literally, being able to respond. It means people choose the behavior that will get their desired results, rather than the behavior dictated by their feelings.   This also means acknowledging oneself as the source of their feelings and results. Thus, the leader can consciously choose how to respond to any situation instead  of being stuck with patterned responses from the past.  Now, how can you be personally responsible?  « Assuming positive intent on the part of others.   Even if you can prove the opposite.  Being   in the present rather than in the past  Acting in a way that promotes getting the results we desire * Choosing not to defend, blame, justify, or judge  3.1. 4.   Reactions as Pitfalls:   Judgment,   Interpretation, Projection  4.1.   Judgment When you make a judgment, it is always about you, not the other person. Our judgments stem from something inside ourselves. How many of us judge ourselves? Judgments always attribute negative or positive motivation. When we judge we give up  our power to deal with Life situations. Judging substitutes for action, because once we  judge, we distance our self from the situation.  Then our possibility for awakened action in that moment is gone.  4.2. Interpretation  When we interpret, we are only in relationship with our own mind, not with the other  person. When that occurs, we continue to condition our next response.  We interpret other people’s behavior. How many have ever assumed you knew why someone said or did something? How many have discovered later that your assumption  was wrong?  When we interpret, our experience is the way we believe things are, instead of what is  true.  4.3.   Projection  When we are having an experience we don’t like, we act as if the other person is causing  the experience. This is called projection.  When we assume a motive behind something, we're projecting. This can be positive or negative. If we do this with customers, it causes a disconnect and we can't get to the real  problem.  Projection is   a destructive form of behavior because it’s based on denial. It’s taking what  we won't tolerate about ourselves, and putting it out on to the other person. Or taking  what we admire in another and seeing them as special or better than.  Any time we have an experience that doesn’t fit our picture of who we are, we attribute our emotion to another person. If it is   a negative feeling we do it to distance ourselves.   If  it is a positive emotion, we lose ourselves as well.   Whether positive or negative, we are unable to experience our natural emotions.  Page 6 of 11

6. A  IC   y  Authenticity is sharing your natural self. Everyone can tell if someone is being real. They may not consciously know why, but everyone feels it if someone is pretending. Authenticity attracts others who are also authentic. It’s hard-wired into our brains as a  survival mechanism.  We have been told repeatedly by society and shown by our family upbringing that we are supposed to hide certain emotions and not show our full humanness.   We have been  taught that it is better to repress, sublimate and ignore feelings that are “negative.” The  definition of which are “negative” vary according to your family’s beliefs and history. When we hide or repress our emotions, we eventually end up hiding them from ourselves. When that occurs, people around us pick up that which is not said and respond to our conflict with a conflict of their own...We are incongruent when we show one face on the outside and another to ourselves. When this occurs, our work and family suffer. We usually become ill or medicate ourselves. Our relationships and our results suffer.  6.1.   You Always Communicate Your Intention  When a   person's heart and mind are integrated, his communication is very clear. You  don't ever have to think about what he’s saying.   You don't ever have to figure out the message when this integration is present.   You don't ever have to hear different voices  when he’s talking. You just hear what he's saying and the message goes right into your  body.  There is no incongruity between what they're saying and what they're feeling; what their minds are saying and what their hearts are saying.   When this occurs in a leader success is  the only thing possible.  Page 8 of 11

7.   Integrity  Our definition of integrity comes from a professor at MIT, Michael   Jenson.   It doesn’t  have an ethical or moral connotation or religious or philosophical basis. It is simple  and elegant: You honor your word. We know we cannot always keep our word. We can always honor our word.  There are times when reality changes and we are unable to keep our word. We let the  person know as ahead of time as we can. We ask them what they need so that they are whole. The times we don’t honor our word add fire to our un-experienced anxiety. 8.   Six   Principles  8.1.   Insight  Knowing yourself and knowing others. Insight lets us know where our beliefs, values and points of view come from and how we view them. We see where in our lives we were  conditioned to think, believe and feel the way we do. Insight is the preparation for  Personal  Responsibility.  8.2.   Personal Responsibility  Owning yourself.   Knowing that we are the source and authority of our experience, and  recognizing how we Create our results ~ tangible and intangible. Making amends for  blame and judgment by dissolving ‘right vs. wrong’, ‘better vs. worse’ thinking in favor of a  more balanced view and assuming that others have a   positive intent. Handling damaged  relationships.  8.3.   Authenticity  Difference between reactive sharing and sharing your natural self. Everyone can tell if someone is being real. They may not consciously know why, but everyone feels it if  someone is pretending. Authenticity attracts others who are also authentic. It’s hard-wired into our brains as a survival mechanism. Taking risks. Taking a stand. Being true. 8.4.   Integrity  What do you stand for and how you honor your word. You are your word. You walk your talk. You don’t make promises you do not intend to keep. You tell the truth.   Of course,  your truth is not absolute and can change as you evolve.  8.5.   Clear Mind The fullness of clarity. The state of being that is without bias or preconceptions. Having openness to what is occurring in the present moment. Brings the ability to live in Paradox.  Living in Paradox allows the brain to become an open system developing new neural  pathways and alternative problem solving skills.  8.6.   Awakened Action  Knowing what action to take to benefit yourself and others - being connected. Brings an  ability to build collaboration and unity. Understands differing perspectives and how they are part of   a whole.   No need to argue about who is right anymore.  Page 10 of 11

1.4. The Simple Ugly: Pictures &  How They  Affect Our Lives  Learning  to  become aware  of  true intentions is a skill directly related to achieving clarity and  harmonious relationships.  We all developed  pictures  of how life is  supposed  to be: about relationships, childhood,  parenting, making  money, getting ahead, being happy, etc. Our pictures  create expectations,  demands for how we should act, how others  should  act toward us. Other people have other  pictures. Pictures are not reality, and yet  they engender very  powerful feelings and behaviors.  For example, we fall in love  with someone who fits our pictures, and we are so attached to  those pictures that  we ignore the  reality  of the  relationship. We are addicted to our picture of  reality and gather people who agree about our pictures about someone  else,  positive or  negative. Being “stuck in our pictures” is just  that - it is like  glue that attaches itself to us  psychically and often runs the  show.  It  is not logical, possible or reasonable  that we do not  have what  we  want. If there is  something that  we  want that we do not have,  it is because a part of us wants  something else. Our results reflect our deepest, full intention.  Intention is amoral and  it attaches to the  strongest part of our will - the part we  don’t see.  We  have it the way our conditioning  demands.  1.5. Our Personal Greek Tragedy: Our Fatal  Flaw  What we are afraid of is that  which we cannot  see  about our self. Ina Greek Tragedy  the hero  has a fatal  flaw. We  can all see it as we read or watch  the play.  Yet, we  cannot  do  anything to  save our  hero.  He  has to see it for himself.  1.6. peeee2. Day Two: Clarity  2.1.  Day One Debrief  Share  anything that came up last night or yesterday that  was not addressed. Share  eulogies/obituaries.  2.2.  Disruptive Learning Technology Demo: Individual  Judith will work with an individual in front of the room to demonstrate and teach under  the  hood of DLT.  2.3:  Disruptive  Learning Technology Core  Perspective  In order to have Clarity,  we have  to  know  what's true in the moment. Truth is  always relative  and changes with each  moment.  —~ Disruptive Learning TechnologyTM Core Perspective:  °  The essential you is no different from the essential me. There is only one. Everything in  the  universe arises from that essence.  All of our thoughts,  feelings,  sensations, interpretations,  opinions,  come  from us  Blame is a choice  to give our essential power to  someone else  to be responsible for.  We  each have  unique  gifts, talents and skills. No other is exactly  like us  in our  conditioning.  Believing we  can  hide ourselves from others is just  another  illusion.  Our  suffering is  held  in  place by strong  beliefs and  opinions that  can  be in opposition to  another  or our  true nature. The Way of Transformation  The man who, being really on the Way, falls upon hard times in the world will not, as a consequence, turn to that friend who offers him  refuge and comfort and encourages his old self to survive. Rather, he  will seek out someone who will faithfully and inexorably help him to risk himself, so that he may endure the suffering and pass  courageously through it, thus making of it a “raft that leads to the far  shore.”  Only to the extent that man exposes himself over and over again to annihilation, can that which is indestructible arise within him. In this  lies the dignity of daring. Thus, the aim of practice is not to develop an attitude, which allows a man to acquire a state of harmony and peace wherein nothing can ever trouble him. On the contrary,  practice should teach him to let himself be assaulted, perturbed, moved, insulted, broken and battered — that is to say, it should enable  him to dare to let go his futile hankering after harmony, surcease from pain, and a comfortable life in order that he may discover, in doing battle with the forces that oppose him, that which awaits him beyond  the world of opposites.  The first necessity is that we should have the courage to face life, and  to encounter all that is most perilous in the world.   When this is  possible, meditation itself becomes the means by which we accept and welcome the demons which arise from the unconscious — a process very different from the practice of concentration on some  object as a protection against such forces. Only if we venture repeatedly through zones of annihilation, can we firm and stable. The more a man learns whole-heartedly to confront the world that threatens him with isolation, the more are the depths of the Ground of Being revealed and the possibilities of new life and Becoming  opened.  From the Book,   The Way of Transformation, by Karlfried Gras  von Durkheim 18 RADICAL  LOVE

MISTAKES  In   1943, Wernher von Braun was working on a rocket that the Germans hoped  would destroy London and end the war.   Producing this new rocket required new metals, new fuels, new guidance systems, new everything.   Von Braun's superiors were  impatient to move the project to completion.   They were angered by the many changes  he had sent to the factories responsible for manufacturing the rocket.   "You are  supposed to be the ultimate brain in this operation...do you know offhand how many last-minute changes you've made in your rocket plans...since you started two years  ago?"   They waved a   piece of paper before Von Braun.   "Make a guess, Professor.   How  many changes have you sent to the factories?"   And there the ridiculous figure was:  65,121.   It was accurate.   Von Braun acknowledged his 65,121   mistakes.   He then  estimated he would make 5,000 more before the rocket was ready.   "It takes sixty-five thousand errors before you're qualified to make a rocket," he said.   "Russia has made  maybe thirty thousand of them by now.   America hasn't made any." In the second half of World War Il, Germany, alone, pounded her enemies with  ballistic missiles; no other country had them.   And when the war was over, Wernher  Von Braun became the “ultimate brain" in America's space program.   Only a few years--  and many mistakes--later, America put a man on the moon.  adapted from SPACE  (pp.62-62)  by James R. Michener "Mistakes are sins only when not admitted."  R. B. Instead of giving up, we sat down and used our experiences to redesign  our core processes.   The traditional delivery system, with all of its weaknesses, eventually became the  source of inspiration for the next advance, and we call it ArchistructionTM.   ArchistructionTM is a new  style; it is   a way of being together that takes most functions inhouse to achieve integration. Conflict resolution without litigation. Following a core process that allows us to blend multiple disciplines into a cohesive whole. V - Validate  Validate  the  statement and the  other person. This does not mean you have to agree  with them. You are  letting them  know that  you've  heard  them and understand their  concern.   Remember, if  you were  that  person  with their life experiences and their  thoughts and feelings, you would respond exactly as they do.  O - Open  Open the space by including yourself in what the other person is describing. ‘I've felt  that way myself” Or share what arises for you. By doing this, you are giving the other person time to realize that he or she is not alone. You   are giving yourself the  opportunity to connect with yourself and the other person.  R - Return  Return to the original situation. Complete what was started. Relate to your  experience, knowledge, or expertise, if applicable. Then   let the other person discover  the  answer  to his or her  own  dilemma.

Emotions  We know from quantum physics that emotions are simply waves of energy. Sometimes, the wave passes through us as if we are transparent, other times, they  stick to us and we react to them and attract the same emotion over and over again. They stick to us until we make certain distinctions about others and  ourselves.  Emotions are pure energy and exist both inside and outside of us simultaneously.  When an external stimulus occurs that resonates with an emotional state inside of  us, we respond based on how well we  know ourselves.  What happens to those emotions? Do they stay inside us?   All emotions eventually  move through us as long as we are willing to experience them   fully. When we do  not, we wall this un experienced anxiety. Week 5   - Authenticity  There is a clear distinction between authentic sharing and reactive sharing. We   all know when someone is pretending, although we might not know how to deal with it. Although most of our families did not actively teach us this, we learned how to be by how they responded to us.   We knew how  to take care of their feelings. Some of us learned how not to make  waves, some of us became adroit at manipulation, others blew up.  We learned different ways of being, none of them right or wrong.  Lots of our adaptive behaviors are a result of our unexperienced anxiety. When   authentic sharing occurs, we are given nothing to think about.Why is that?  Who do we think we are?  Do we think we can be fake and people won’t know? Sounds True presents The End of Your World—An Interview with Adyashanti  More and more people are “waking up” spiritually. And for most of them, the question  becomes: now what? “Information about life after awakening is usually not made public,” explains Adyashanti. “It’s most often shared only between teachers and their  students.” The End of Your World is his response to a growing need for direction on the spiritual path—and his personal welcome to “a new world, a state of oneness.” In this interview conducted by Sounds True Publisher Tami Simon and excerpted from the  book, Adya tells us more about the enigmatic experience of spiritual awakening. Tami Simon: Let’s return to your metaphor of awakening being compared to a rocket ship achieving lift-off. How do people know if their rocket ship of being has actually  taken off? | could imagine some people being deluded about this. Maybe they have  read lots of books about spiritual awakening, so they make the leap in their mind that awakening has occurred, but perhaps in reality they are simply sputtering on the ground. How do we know for sure that we have attained liftoff?  Adyashanii: It’s not an easy question to answer. The only way | can answer it is to  reiterate what the  nature of awakening is.  The moment of awakening is very similar to when you wake up from a dream at night.  You feel that you have awakened from one world to another, from one context to a  totally different context. On a feeling level, that is the feeling of awakening. This whole  separate self that you thought was real, and even the world that you thought was objective, or other, all of   a sudden seems as if it’s not as real as you thought.  {'m not saying it is or isn’t a dream; I’m saying that it’s almost like   a dream. Upon awakening, the experience is that life is like a dream that’s happening within what you  are—within vast, infinite space. Awakening is not experiencing vast, infinite space, feeling spacious or expanded or blissful or whatever. These feelings may be by- products of awakening, but they  are not the awakening itself.  Awakening, quite apart from its by-products,   is   a change of perspective. Everything we  thought was realis seen fo not be real at all; it’s more like a dream that's happening fithi   infini   emptiness. What is actually real is the infinite expanse of  emptiness. Tami Simon: When you describe your own life story, you say that the rocket ship of your being achieved liftoff at a specific time and date—when you were twenty-five years old. Adyashanti: I’ve seen that, too. I’ve met people for whom awakening almost happened as if in retrospect, like it snuck up on them. Tami Simon: Not to kill the metaphor here, but is it possible to say that the rocket ship  requires a certain kind of fuel, and if so, what kind of fuel?  Adyashanti: | wish | could say what the fuel is. | don’t know that it’s really possible to say  what the fuel is, because it’s not limited to something personal. Awakening does not  happen just to people who really want it. Awakening does not happen just to people who are sincerely looking for it. It happens to some people completely out of the blue. I’ve  met awakened people who were not on a   spiritual path at all. In fact, I've met people who were in denial of spirituality, and then boom—out of nowhere—awakening hits them. We couldn’t call such people sincere, and we couldn’t say they were pursuing  spiritual realization or even had an obvious yearning for it. That’s true, but the problem is,  anytime we say “this” is necessary or “that” is necessary, there will always be examples  to the contrary. Awakening is a mystery. There is no direct cause and effect, really. It  would be nice if there were, but there really isn’t a direct cause and effect. Tami Simon: You often talk about thoughts and feelings like they are two sides of the  same coin. Isn't it possible to have feelings that don’t have any thoughts associated with them? Adyashanti: There is what | would call pure feeling or pure emotion, as anybody who  has experienced a great moment of beauty or awe knows. If we look carefully, we will see that the vast majority of emotions that human beings experience are derived from what we are telling ourselves at the moment.
