Adyashanti: On the level of mind, there is the pure perception of infinity, or what  Buddhists call emptiness—the perception of vast, vast, vast, vast vastness. It is being perceived not through the mind in terms of thought, but we could say that section of the  body, the mind area, is literally where we are taking in the vastness of infinity, the vastness of space, the pure light of being, the almost blinding light of being. That is being seen on the level of mind, not on the level of thinking. Perceiving in this way is a different capacity than just thinking; it is the mind as a sensing instrument sensing  infinity. At least in my life, | can certainly look and see that there were moments where| did not  have certain capacities yet. And only after ten years did | think, “Oh. . . now   | get it. Now | understand. Now it has sunk in.” How was   | going to force it ten years before? Could | have forced it? It doesn’t  appear  as though | could have.  This may not be the empowering spiritual teaching you are looking for, but everything has its time; everything has its place. Everything happens in its time. You’re not in control. This isn’t something we want to hear, though, is it? It isn’t something our mind wants. Mostly we want to hear things that  empower our sense of control. And we radically push away anything that does not  empower our sense of control.  | say this to people all the time. When you start to accept what you see as true—not  what | say, but your experience— that’s when everything starts to change.  Many times students come to me and say, “I can't do anything about this, this part of my  delusional apparatus, this part of my personality.” They'll ask, “What do | do? What do |  do?” Often | say, “Well, let’s go back. You just told me there’s nothing you can do. Is that  true? What if you took it in instead of trying to push it away?” Often, when they take this in—not just conceptually, not as a teaching that can be  dismissed, but really allowing it into the body—then this realization of what it is like to  live without resistance starts to change everything. Even if it’s part of your experience, year after year, decade after decade—  even if you keep experiencing the same thing over and over—the impulse is to avoid it,  to not let it in, to push it away. can find a way beyond this,” no transformation is going to happen. Bottoming out is  nothing more than coming out of denial. There’s nothing | can do, and look where | am. But it played a role because it got me to an end of that role. | danced that dance until it was extinguished. But |   failed. | failed at meditating well; | failed at tiguring out the truth.  Everything | ever used to succeed spiritually failed. But at the moment of failure, that’s  when everything opens up.  We know that, right? This isn’t sacred knowledge. Almost everybody knows this; we've experienced it in our lives. We’ve seen moments like this. But it’s not something we  want to know, because it’s not convenient. Tami Simon: | loved your teaching on the cul-de-sacs that people can get into after an initial experience of awakening. | am curious if you would comment on a cul-de-sac that  1 see fairly often, which is when people decide to take on some kind of special mission to save the world after they have an initial awakening experience. There was   a   certain sense of missionary zeal about it, which can be alluring and empowering. There’s something wonderful in that  inspiration when it comes from   a   true place.  There was   a   lot of energy for it, especially in the first couple of years that | was teaching. I’ve found that it can be part and parcel of awakening, because one senses that all this suffering is unnecessary; one really can wake up from this. A sense of  mission can come from that place.  After a few years of feeling that missionary zeal myself, | noticed it started to ebb. At first  it was like | was a new puppy in the house, jumping up and down at your legs all the  time, wanting attention and wanting you to do something. The first couple of years of my  teaching | felt empowered with what works and what helps people, and | wanted to  share it with people. But after two or three years, that energy waned. | started to feel  more like an old dog that was curled up at the side of its master’s easy chair, lying there  and letting the world go by.  At this point in my life, the sense of missionary zeal is pretty much gone. There is no  sense that something needs to happen. | see the potential in everybody, but there’s no  sense of hurry about it.  | see it as a process of maturing. It’s   a phase that many of us go through. | think the key is—do we go through it? Do we keep going? Or, at some point, does that missionary  zeal provide the platform for the ego’s reformation? If that starts happening—if the ego uses awakening as a new and improved missionary platform—that can lead to all kinds  of  distortions.  For example, we might start seeing ourselves as the savior of humanity or our teachings as the greatest teachings ever. As far as | can see, if things go that way, we start to get delusional. Often, when this happens, it’s because someone’s ego has grasped on to some powerful experience he or she has had. If there’s latent energy there, and that energy starts flowing into the ego, it can lead to some of the deepest delusions possible.

We’ve seen this from time to time in disastrous cult-like behavior. This can happen when there is a lot of energy flowing into the ego and deluding it. Before you know it, you think  you are the savior of humanity.  Whereas in truth, none of us is the savior of humanity. The greatest avatar who has ever  walked the Earth, if such embodiments even exist, is like a grain of sand on a vast  beach. As human beings, we are all just doing our little part. It’s the totality; it’s the One itself that we are but expressions of. If any of us start to think we are playing a bigger part than we are—if we see ourselves as anything but a small part of an infinite mosaic  —it seems to me we're starting to become inflated and deluding ourselves. Adyashanti: Traditionally, there were some safeguards used by spiritual traditions to prevent the ego using realization in this way, but if we look back in the history of  Spirituality, we see the safeguards didn’t work that well. In truth, it never happened like it was supposed to. Teachers can keep an eye on their students, but once somebody breaks out of that role, there’s not that much keeping an  eye on each other. | mean, we've seen that in almost every tradition. There are people  who get inflated or go off on some strange tangent. | do think it’s perfectly appropriate that we try, if not to change people, then to reflect back to them—especially if we see somebody really half-cocked. Not that they'll listen!  | wish | had a good antidote to what you are describing. It can be a   really  difficult thing to do. All the power is in the students’ hands. And it’s good for people to know that. I’ve always experienced that when people give me too much power or authority, | start to feel like I’m living in a surreal bubble. Inherent in people giving other  people power is a projection, right? When somebody gives me too much power, they've

projected that | am something different from them. And|   find that a surreal environment  to be in. That's why | avoid it as much as | can, because it has a sense of unreality to it. Other people, quite obviously, are more attracted to power than | am. They find it alluring to be the positive projection of others. It’s enticing to them. | couldn’t say exactly  why; it’s just never been comfortable for me, personally.  Tami Simon: At the age of twenty-five, when you experienced what you call your “first  awakening,” you mentioned that you heard a voice that said, “Keep going, keep going.”  What is that voice? Would you call it your conscience, or the still, small voice within?  Adyashanti: You can call it either one of those. Tami Simon: It seems that if we each have that type of inner voice, then that inner voice would keep us from co-opting our realizations into a personal power play. You heard that voice that said your realization was not complete, but does everybody possess an  inner voice like that?  Adyashanti: In one sense, | would say yes. In an ultimate sense, we are all the same, so we all have access to the same capacities. At the relative level, however, the question is  whether everybody hears their inner voice. Apparently, not everyone does.  What is this inner voice of wisdom? It is what | am pointing to when   | talk about sincerity. It is the intelligence within us that keeps us on track, keeps us in alignment. In one sense, | think almost everybody has experienced this still, small voice. The example | often give is when you are dating some man or some woman and it ends badly. Something inside you says, “Don’t do that again.” But then we meet someone new, and we don’t listen to the voice. We are attracted; this person is sexy, and we just  want to be with him or her. In the end, we find that the still, small voice was correct. We shouldn't have kept dating that person. In the end, it all collapses, and in the end, this  still, small voice wins.  So this still, small voice is not mystical. It is something that | think a vast majority of people have heard at times. But we're so good at dismissing it. We want that still, small  voice to justify itself—to tell us why. One of the good indications that the voice within us is authentic and sincere is that it will never justify itself. If you ask it, “Why?” you'll get silence. If you ask it to explain itself, it won't. The still, small voice doesn’t need to do  that—and it doesn’t.  If you are talking to the ego and you ask, “Why?” it will talk back to you. If you ask the  ego, “Does this mean everything will be okay?” it will give you assurances. The still,  smail voice, though, has an inherent sort of insecurity about it. It offers no guarantees.  The voice is a gift. Either we listen or we don’t.

Why| listened, and why others don’t, | don’t know. | couldn’t say why. I’m just glad that  the voice was there in my case and that I could hear it. It was persistent. Adyashanti: | think it’s all of that. It is a guide. It is a protector. It is the flow of existence. By the way, this intelligent flow of existence doesn’t always show up as a   voice. Many of us aren't sensitive enough to feel that, and so the flow appears as a voice. But at this point, for me, it’s much more like following a natural flow. As the Taoists would  say, follow the flow of the Tao.  So it has different aspects to it. It’s a flow. It’s a voice. It’s a protector voice. It’s your counselor. It’s your conscience, but not the conscience society taught us. It is a different  conscience than that. Because the conscience that society taught us is our superego—  and  that conscience always  contains judgments. This is  not  the superego. This is  something else. This comes froma   totally different state of being. More from Adyashanti »  Adyashanti (whose name means “primordial peace”) dares all seekers of peace and freedom to take the possibility of liberation in this life seriously. He began teaching in  1996, at the request of his Zen teacher with whom he had been studying for fourteen  years. Since then, many spiritual seekers have awakened to their true nature while  spending time with Adyashanti.  The author of The End of Your World, Emptiness Dancing, The Impact of Awakening, and My Secret Is Silence, Adyashanti offers spontaneous and direct nondual teachings  that have been compared to those of the early Zen masters and Advaita Vedanta sages. However, Adya says, “If you filter my words through any tradition or ‘-ism,’ you will miss altogether what | am saying. The liberating truth is not static; it is alive. It cannot be put  into concepts and be understood by the mind. The truth lies beyond all forms of conceptual fundamentalism. What you are is the beyond—awake and present, here and  now already. | am simply helping you to realize that.”  Anative of Northern California, Adyashanti lives with his wife, Mukti, and teaches extensively in the San Francisco Bay Area, offering satsangs, weekend intensives, and silent retreats. He also travels to teach in other areas of the United States and Canada.

Adyashanti: The gut is just another way in which we sense the world. You hear this when people say, “I have a gut feeling.” Sensing with the gut is a certain type of intuitive capacity; it is an instinctual way of knowing. We feel things through that place in the body: our gut is an intuitive sense organ. Of course, we can feel things that are duplications of the mind—fearful thoughts, angry thoughts, conflicting thoughts, contracting thoughts—but the gut also responds as a pure sense organ to what's  happening.  When thought isn’t constricting who we are, people have these kinds of intuitive experiences. Say you walk up to the edge of a cliff. You look down, and you see a huge expanse. There may be fear when you look down, but if you are sensitive, you might notice another response, which is that your consciousness may actually fill the expanse. When we look at huge expanses, often we breathe in, right? In the breathing in, we’re feeling our consciousness open to that environment. We breathe into our lungs, into our heart center, into our gut. Our whole being, our whole body, is in tune with the  environment. This kind of opening of the heart—when the lungs go “aah” as  consciousness expands—isn’t happening because we’re thinking. This is happening because consciousness is interacting with the environment. This is what | mean by pure  sensation or pure feeling. And yes, it happens through gut sensations as well. It’s very  powerful  and it’s very,  very beautiful.  It’s literally the experience of intimacy. It is our being experiencing itself with an  incredible intimacy. I’m not saying it’s wrong to comment on it, but as soon as we say  something, as soon as we turn to our friend, something changes. For most people, that experience happens for a split second, and then they turn to somebody and say, “Isn’t it  beautiful?” And that’s not a wrong thing to say. | say it to people, too, sometimes. But at  that moment, if you’re sensitive, you notice that your whole internal environment starts  to change, and you start to experience what you just said. Then you are moving into a virtual experience. It’s slightly different from that moment of awe, that moment where the  entire body is participating in perception. APPLYING ACCELERATED LEARNING TO COURSE DESIGN  Setting the Context  Set THE Context  a ie \  Sa   N   .  fj   \   permission  h ‘eliminole:   for  \ fear ) | mistokes  \ /  Nn  The context in which learning occurs determines its level of success. A con-  text is an environment. It is also   a model, and a way of being. It is the most  important initial aspect for learning. In childhood, the way a parent interacts  with a child determines, to a large degree, the behavior of the child. In a  classroom, an instructor’s behavior will model the way the learner will respond to openness, connection, humor, spontaneity and flexibility. When  an instructor teaches with this context, it is imprinted and transferred to the  learner. Those very qualities will make learning fast, easy and permanent. There are many elements in a   positive context for learning, including the physical environment and the emotional attitudes of the instructor and the students.   The physical space needs to be bright, well-lit and alive with nat-  ural plants, color, artwork, etc. The emotional space is even more powerful in terms of setting context. Whereas it is possible to learn in a bare, stark  room, it is not possible for any true learning to occur when fear is present.  3

Some of the criteria for a context without fear include demonstrating equali-  ty among instructors and learners, permission to make mistakes, and valuing  all participation, even that which can be deemed disruptive.   Equality with- out fear creates a quality environment where learning can occur.  Establishing and maintaining an optimum learning context is a key role for  all program designers and instructors. To see how this works in a learning  situation, think about our society’s existing views about accounting and  accounting education.   For many it is seen as black and white, dull, difficult  and shrouded in mystery.   It has traditionally been taught using mostly linear  left brain methods.   In The Accounting Game, we have replaced some of the  black and white accounting content with color—~green, blue, yellow, and  red, etc.   Next we’ve added props such as cameras to teach concepts like the balance sheet and income statement, and eye glasses that see only green to teach the cash method of accounting.   All of these are tools which make the content of accounting clearer and more user friendly; however, we go one giant step further by literally pouring that content into a lemonade stand,  thereby creating an environment of a child operating a summer lemonade  business.   In addition, we have designed interactive role plays with partici-  pants who actually play our mom and the grocer!   The lemonade stand allows Accounting Game instructors to set and hold a kid’s easy, playful  context for the entire day-long program.  In general, students will come to class with all their individual histories (school, family, culture, etc.) about learning.   They will have made decisions about themselves and the learning process based on these experiences. Successfully designed courses will circumvent the students’ past history and  reframe it with new learning.   To do that, the course must go beyond the  neo-cortex to the limbic and reptilian brains and reprogram the learning  experience, so that the context of learning changes from one of fear to one  of fun and joy—like watching   a   child’s natural curiosity take hold when  learning something new.  The child’s lemonade stand successfully accomplishes this for The Accounting Game.   The idea of accounting being child’s play and that it is fun, easy, and creative establishes a whole new model (context) for the  learner. Positive suggestions such as “My success is absolutely assured”  e%,,.   throughout the day also helps establish and reinforce a new and posi-  LL sy Hf “tive context for the learner. Positive suggestion provides continual  *   APPLYING ACCELERATED LEARNING TO COURSE DESIGN

reinforcement of successful new  learning. When learners  have had this new  and visceral connection with the information, it is grounded and new  possi-  bilities  exist immediately. The opportunity now  exists that Accounting Game graduates will return to their companies not only having learned the  content of accounting, but they will also return with  new attitudes  and  behaviors when  dealing  with financial decisions and issues.  At Educational  Discoveries, we believe that the skill to establish and main-  tain the context is the most powerful tool available to the designer  and train- er.  It  is certainly as important in our minds to all of the content  being taught  in a program.  Elements of  Setting The  Context  Enrollment  Enrollment is the process by which people  become  participants in a  program. A traditional enrollment  process includes  introducing the  instructor and participants, and discussing  what’s going to be learned  and why.  For example, a college  professor walks into a lecture hall,  announces the title of the course  and his/her  name,  and  then begins  lecturing on the subject. The professor has “enrolled” the  students: as  participants  in the course, students are expected for the most part to  sit,  listen, and  take  notes. Here’s another example: after a brief  intro- duction of his/her  background in  marketing, the instructor  asks  each  person to stand up, say their name, their company, and share some  personal experience in sales.   The participants have been enrolled, and  can  expect that  their personal  sales experiences will provide part  of the  content of the course. More  importantly,  in  addition to begin-  ning  the  program, enrollment starts the process of creating the context  for learning.  Every course has an enrollment, but let’s examine one in the context of accelerated learning. In The Accounting Game seminar, the instruc-  tor starts with these questions,  How many people here today have had formal training in account-  ing? ... Please raise your hands ... thank you.   ” oie,  =  Ne APPLYING ACCELERATED LEARNING TO COURSE DESIGN  5

How many of you do not have formal training but learned accounting on  the job? ... thank you.  How many of you do not have any background at all in accounting? ... Whether you had training,  leamed on  the job, or don’t have  any back- ground whatsoever in accounting, how many of you have experienced  some confusion about  this subject? ... thank you.  If you will notice, almost everybody has experienced some confusion  about accounting.  By starting with asking general questions, the instructor immediately  gets people involved in a physical way by having them raise their hands. Note that the questions  draw out not only those who are famil-  iar with the topic, but also those who are not.   And the last question  brings everyone together to agree that their understanding of the sub- ject can use improvement. The instructor’s hand is  also  raised. Right from the start, the instructor and all the participants are treated as equals. The more  participatory the enrollment  process  is, the more it  sets  a context  for learning.  These enrollment questions set the context of inclusion, participation,  and equality.   Following the initial questions, the instructor then  shares something of his or her background.   A personal story connects participants with the instructor. If the personal story relates to the  subject matter, it creates credibility for the instructor and the seminar.  Next, the “Big Why” must be answered, along with the “How” and “What” of the program.   Part of the enrollment process includes stat- ing the purpose, method, and desired results:   Why is this subject  important? Why should these participants attend?   How is the subject  relevant to their lives?   Generally what will be the activities and the desired outcome of the course?   Just because the subject is important to the instructor doesn’t mean that its importance is self-evident.  A   sense of anticipation and excitement can be created in the begin- ning.   In fact, throughout the program participants need to stay con- nected to the Big Why to stay interested and excited.   The initial  oes   enrollment may end as the lesson begins, but participants  +   APPLYING   ACCELERATED   LEARNING TO COURSE   DESIGN  Mes

must be re-enrolled again and again as the demand on the learners increases in intensity.   By providing the theory and reason for why the information being taught is both personally valuable and necessary  for the success of the student, the analytical brain is satisfied and  ready to cooperate.   In addition, handing out an agenda also satisfies  the left brain.  The participants’ personal introductions can also occur in the enroll- ment.   They give their name and talk about what they do in their com- pany, and their reason for attending.   Then they are asked to add something personal.   Besides providing the instructor with informa- tion on the group’s knowledge level and expectations, this sharing of  personal information establishes intimacy and safety among partici-  pants.   An effective enrollment process goes deeper into the brain than just the neocortex (intellectual).   It penetrates into the limbic (emotional intimacy) and reptilian (safety) parts of the brain, the seats  of instinct and feelings.  Enrollment can be done in many ways.   When effective, it sets the  context for learning, creates some common shared experience for par-  ticipants (common ground), and prepares them for the next level of learning and intensity (gradient).   It breaks the ice, gets people’s minds off other concerns in their lives, and creates an environment  that gets them fully engaged in the present learning experience.  Common  Ground  Common ground refers to both the information learned and the expe- riences shared by participants in a classroom.   As people experience new learning they begin to share a sense of belonging to the group. For example, witnessing an event together, or working in small teams  on the same project in a course give those who witness and those who  have worked on the project common experiences.   This commonality forms the basis for group awareness.   That awareness enhances inter- action and collaboration, and increases the opportunity for new learn-  ing.   Once common ground has been established, the gradient (inten-  sity) of the program can be increased.  APPLYING ACCELERATED LEARNING TO COURSE DESIGN 7

In The Accounting Game  people  learn about a financial statement  called the balance sheet. The course does not start out by calling it a  balance sheet; instead it is referred to as a scorecard.   The assumption is that everyone has had some experience of a scorecard. Starting  with the familiar allows us to advance to the unknown quickly in a  non-threatening  manner. Because the scorecard  is a common  concept that everyone can identify with, it becomes “common ground.” Using the scorecard the instructor and participants work through some exercises together. From these exercises, new  concepts  and terminol- ogy are  developed. These new  concepts  in turn become  part of the  shared language and common ground.   Once the scorecard and its  concepts become common ground it is then labeled a balance sheet.  In this way a foundation of knowledge (common ground) has been  built step by step assuring that no one has been lost along the way. Each new segment covered successfully by the participants becomes new common ground to build the next level of complexity and learn-  ing.  What if our assumption is incorrect and some participants have no  experience of a scorecard?   We would have to find something else to create common ground.   This is an important concern when designing  learning experiences using metaphor or themes.   For example, with a  culturally diverse group, a metaphor like Dumbo the Elephant may have fun associations from childhood for some, but for others it may conjure up passionate associations like racism.   Personal stories, myths and analogies can create connection and bonding with learners.  The course designer and instructor must be able to establish common  ground  that is universal  for all participants.  Gradient  Any mischievous youngster who’s ever caught a frog and decided to  cook it has learned a lesson about gradient.   This lesson is simple—if the water is too hot, the frog will jump out.   To cook a live frog, start in cold water and warm it up slowly.   The frog won’t notice the  oa   APPLYING ACCELERATED LEARNING TO COURSE DESIGN  8

—>  increase, and will stay in the pot. The same is true in class: start with  low intensity and warm it up slowly. Otherwise the student’s  atten-  tion, like the frog, will jump out.  Ina learning  environment, gradient  refers to the level of intensity and  commitment  required to participate in a given exercise or learning  experience. Attending a lecture on the presidential  election is low  gradient when  compared to developing a group  presentation of the  same topic. Listening to the thermodynamics of dissipative structures  is high gradient  compared to watching a demonstration on making  paper airplanes. A learning  segment has higher  gradient if the content  is  more  complex, or if the personal  interaction required  is more  involved or intimate. Also, when participants are ready for more  complex content or more interaction, one can say that they are  at a  higher gradient.   In general, the higher the gradient the greater the  learning. Ideally, the gradient of the material  should be high and should keep  pace with the gradient of the participants.   If the gradient is suddenly  too high, participants  feel  discomfort or fear. They will give puzzled  looks, ask rapid-fire questions, show resistance to an exercise or les- son,  and possibly act with hostility.   Learning stops. The  frog  jumps  out of the pot.   If the gradient is kept too low, participants can become  bored, and learning  stops.  The best  situation  is to gradually increase the gradient in  activities as  the course progresses.   For example, a morning session could begin  with a short lecture, then written exercises, followed by a class discus-  sion.   Then increase the interaction among participants by having  them do collaborative exercises, presentations, and mock debates or  improvisations.   This sequence is an example of activities of increas-  ing gradient.   At each transition establish enrollment and common ground, and increase the gradient so that participants feel challenged  but not threatened.   Doing this will keep the frog from jumping out of  the  pot  and  dramatically increase  the quality  of  learning.  APPLYING ACCELERATED LEARNING TO COURSE DESIGN  9   ‘Training

Creating the Learning Experience THE  LEARNING LYXPERIENCE  When most people hear the word “experience,” they start thinking about what it means. When this happens, an intellectual understanding of the con- cept of experience occurs. That is very important in the learning process.  However, for whole-being learning to occur, a person also needs to have a  physical experience of the information. As Deming has taught us, theory plus experience equals knowledge. Without both, quality learning cannot  occur. For example, understanding the theory involved in riding a bike is not  the same as actually knowing how to ride it, as anyone who has ever learned  to ride  a bike can  remember.  As is true in the principles of holographic photography, all parts of the whole contain the imprint and information of the whole. This is true in our bodies, wherein each cell contains a genetic blueprint of the whole organ-  ism. So, when we physically have an experience of information being pre-  sented, we will know that information in a very different way than if we just understand it. It is imprinted and becomes part of us.  Oya  APPLYING ACCELERATED LEARNING TO COURSE DESIGN   -   :  1   em  ‘Training

The steps for creating a whole-being learning experience are: Clarify objectives and select key content points. One of the main hindrances to learning  is being bogged down in details. Most people get so focused on  the myriad of content, that they lose  sight of the context, or big  picture. Be  specific and precise, trusting yourself to teach the relevant content areas that will cover the important aspects  of the material.  Visualize the end result again. Remember your vision and the pur- pose of the learning  experience, and  stay in the big picture. Use  a  metaphor/analogy/theme in order to  evoke the desired emo-  tions. The emotional framework evoked in the learning experience  makes the learning physical. Be aware of which emotions the  theme  will evoke  for  optimum impact.  Find humor in the content and make the process fun. Humor con-  nects  the intellectual  with the physical. It also  bypasses  resistance and  all other barriers to learning, allowing the learner to retrieve child-  hood learning capabilities, and to see old information with new eyes. Simplify and dramatize. Simplify, dramatize, simplify. Use music, color, graphics and all of the tools and techniques of accelerated  learning to enhance  the whole-being learning  experience. Ne Using metaphor to communicate the  content of a course is to see the content as  a set of concepts, processes,  or relationships, and placing it  in an entirely different setting. In The  Accounting Game, the financial  world of accounting is placed inside a child’s summer vacation pro-  ject—running a lemonade stand. The lemonade stand establishes and  maintains a unique  learning  environment  for this material.  A basic accounting class may have  negative connotations to many people:   accounting  is  boring, difficult, and full of arithmetic. By  using the metaphor of the lemonade stand, we created a context of  accounting that is different  from  people’s  expectations—accounting  is fun,  easy and creative. After participants experience a balance sheet in a fun, creative way  in The Accounting Game, the possibility that  they will return  to work  with a positive and confident attitude  about  reading and using  their company’s balance sheet is  increased.   The  Accounting Game is set in the world of kids, a special  learning  con- text that is safe for  participants to take risks and make  mistakes.  Participants take on childhood nicknames, so mistakes are made by  the participants’  aliases,  not the participants  themselves. It’s natural  and healthy for kids to  be successful  in learning, and to make lots of  mistakes.  A metaphor that  has a story line or story  sequences  can give addition-  al meaning to a   lesson.   In the street-side lemonade business of eight-  year-olds, the arithmetic  for the scorecard is simple and practical.  The special  accounting  language of the balance sheet has a simple  business-like meaning, and is no longer arcane or arbitrary.   For example, in The Accounting Game, “notes payable” is developed by a  role-play dialogue with Mom, who loaned us five dollars.   The entry, “notes payable,” on a corporate financial balance sheet is now no longer just a number. It involves trying to get approval from some- one, and has the weight of an obligation.   The simple arithmetic cal-  culations in a conventional course do not make those linkages.   An  “accounts receivable” is   a kid who bought lemonade on credit  because her mom has not yet paid her weekly allowance.   The story- line helps make concepts palpable, simple, and more easily grasped.  APPLYING ACCELERATED LEARNING TO COURSE DESIGN 13

How does a course  designer take a program and develop a metaphor?  First determine what skills are to be learned, and what process would  best develop those skills. Does the content suggest a theme or a  metaphor?   With another person or team, creatively brainstorm differ- ent ideas and options.  Search for a  metaphor by reviewing:  * Popular movies,  plays,  television shows.  * Genres like westerns, outer space, fairy tales, fables, game  shows, sports  events.  *   Major events like elections or holidays. * Geographical settings.  ¢ Settings in  industry like cruise lines, movie-making,  the courtroom.  The  possibilities are only  limited  by the imagination.   Once a list of  possibilities is made, consider  how each metaphor will support the  skills and concepts the course  is  designed to develop.  An effective metaphor  can provide the course  designer with a contin- ual source of inspiration  for props,  characters,  and linkages. The lemonade stand easily suggested lemons and  sugar as props  to  demonstrate raw  materials as part of inventory. But how does one  illustrate the difference between a balance sheet as a snapshot of the  business at a given point in time and an income statement as a record  of certain  transactions  over a period of time?   In the world  of chil-  dren, we found some toys: a toy camera to illustrate the “snapshot” nature of balance sheets, and a toy  movie camera to demonstrate  that the information of the income statement is  over a period of time. A  possible area of confusion  between concepts  was simplified and  dra-  matized by using  props to simplify the  concepts.  Another key to an effective metaphor is its emotional impact. Memory and  retention  are optimized  when  there is emotional connec- tion  with the learning material.   Metaphors  then offer the  course  designer  three  simultaneous  and very powerful tools:  1)   the ability to establish and maintain a learning context.  2)   the ability to simplify and dramatize learning concepts.  3)   the ability to create emotional connection with the  content to deepen learning. ‘Training   14  APPLYING ACCELERATED LEARNING TO COURSE DESIGN

Ritual  At all major sporting events, the national anthem is  played to signify  to the crowd that the event is ready to begin.   The national anthem has common ground for everyone there.   It evokes emotion and creates a communal feeling among all the fans.   Creating beginnings and end- ings, and connecting the participants to each other are the essence of a  ritual.  In program design a ritual is a formal procedure, that when repeated, connects to deep parts of the brain, especially the reptilian brain.   The  reptilian brain is where instinctual survival behavior patterns reside.  Ritual and habits are also in the realm of the reptilian brain.   Long  ago, the school day began when the teacher rang the school bell.  Children near and far would hear the bell, and run to gather at the  school house.   The bell would ring every school day, and that repeti- tion conducted in exactly the same way and time became   a   ritual and habit.   These are subjects of the reptilian brain.   When the reptilian brain is stimulated in a way that creates safety and doesn’t threaten survival, more of the whole brain is engaged, and learning becomes  easier.  Breathing and heart rates are also controlled by the reptilian brain. Repeated activities in class that involve heart and breathing rates, that are conducted with everyone, and that are repeated in the same form also become rituals.   For example, in The Accounting Game after a  long or difficult section, or beginning a new section, the presenter  leads the whole class into taking a deep breath together. Physiologic- ally, this increases oxygen to the brain, releases muscular tension, and  generally relaxes the body.   Repeated throughout the day, this becomes   a   ritual, and is another method of engaging the whole brain.  Rituals have the practical application of organizing transitions.   In  beginning a section or closing one, the presenter can lead the class in  physical stretching or in the “letting go” ritual. They draw the class  together. Rituals like these reduce participant anxiety, and evoke feel- ings that subtly bonds participants.   Rituals calm the reptilian brain. For these reasons rituals are an essential part of whole-being   * *%  course design.  APPLYING ACCELERATED LEARNING TO COURSE DESIGN   od 15   ‘Training

In addition to being   a   ritual, ringing the school bell had a practical  purpose:   the children must come together. Rituals often seem to go beyond the practical into the symbolic.   During the deep breath in The Accounting Game participants expand their chests to take in the air, and relax their bodies to exhale.   They take a pause after reaching a plateau in their learning, and relax just before continuing the ascent.  They take in a bigger picture, and share the action together. Since the reptilian brain is concerned with safety issues, perhaps rituals evoke a  sense of significance and meaning that go beyond any practical pur-  pose. Whole Being Program Design  by Educational Discoveries  This program design model was derived from examining the process in the development of  many successful programs.   Designing a course requires creativity.   Though this model is in a linear format, the actual process is holistic and much more dynamic.   Several steps can happen  concurrently; many of the creative parts can be spontaneous. Your Left and Right Brain  For some time it has been known that the brain is divided into two sides, left and right.   It has also been known that if damage is done to the left side of the brain, the right side of the body tends to become paralyzed, and correspondingly, that if damage is done to the right side of the brain, the left side of the body tends to become para- lyzed.   In other words, each side of your brain controls the opposite side of your body. The recent research of Professor Robert Ornstein of the University of California has thrown more light on the different activities handled by each side of the brain. Starting with the realization that the two halves of the brain are biologically similar  and can more realistically be thought of as two identical brains working in harmony,  rather than as one brain divided into two, Professor Ornstein decided to find out if each of our separate brains handles different intellectual activities in addition to the  different  physical  activities.  Placing special caps for measuring brain waves on some of his   students, he asked  them to do different kinds of mental tasks.   They were asked to add lists of numbers, write formal letters and essays, arrange colored blocks, analyze logically, and think "day dreamy” thoughts.   All the time these activities were being performed, Professor Ornstein was measuring the brain waves coming from the two halves of each person's  brain.  His findings were both surprising and significant.   In general the left brain handles the following mental activities:   mathematics, language, linear and sequential informa-  tion, logic, analysis, writing, reading, and other similar activities.  The right side of the brain handles very different activities:   imagination, color, graph- ics, music, rhythm, daydreaming, holistic thinking and other similar activities. Ornstein also found that people who had been trained to use one side of their brain more or less exclusively were relatively unable to use the other side, both in general  and those special situations where the activities specifically related to the other side were particularly needed.  Even more significant, he found that when the "weaker" of the two brains was stimu-  lated and encouraged to work in cooperation with the stronger side, the end result was  a great increase in overall ability and effectiveness. Mindmaps are easy to read.   The title, main theme or central idea is located  in the middle of the page.   Main points radiate from the center, beginning at one o’clock and continuing clockwise.   Elaborations, clarifications, and other details branch off the main limbs from the center outward.   The originals use different colors to keep these points separate from each other. THE CHANGE PROCESS:  CHOOSING THE PATH TO EMPOWERMENT  CONSCIOUS CHOICE FOR  CHANGE  Change  begins with a commitment to attain a vision, along with a decision  to take action, which is motivated by  a desire to grow.  RESISTANCE  Whatever the degree of change, it  will always be matched by an equal  expression of  limiting  beliefs which  are   the   true barriers to success.  Resistance occurs because  change is  perceived as a threat  to an individ-  ual's core belief system.  The core belief system  is founded  in  the individual's adaptation to   the  original  family system and  is modi-  fied by and includes adaptation to his chosen  role  in  society and its estab-  lished beliefs. This adaptation  creates  the personality.  The   protection of the core  belief system,   based   on   the  personality’s fight   for survival,  is   the primary   reason for  failure.  The   original decision to adapt  was  precipitated by fear; e.g.  fear  of  loss,  fear of abandonment,  fear  of  pain.  In  the  past, in  order  to cope  with the  fear, a belief  was formed  about  how  to be in a family in order to survive.  A pattern of behavior was developed  that created an illusion of connected-  ness, stability and safety.   These  beliefs and the behavior patterns that  followed were believed to   be   the  safest choice possible at  that time.  Now, when the fear is re-activated by  the  threat of change, and that fear  is  not experienced through avoidance  or  denial,  we  automatically revert to the  habitual pattern of behavior and  recreate the familiar comfort of our  protective  illusion.   Choices calls this  behavior a “reaction”, and recognizes  the result as impotence - not living to  our full potential.  MISDIRECTION  When illusions are  acted  upon  as if  they were  real,  they  represent a way  of rationalizing not taking  risks.   In  most people the possibility  for  creat-  ing   or   responding   to   change   and  growth stops  here.  CRISIS  Operating   in a continued   state of  illusion erodes  self-esteem,  limits the  ability to  perform,  and  results  in a  state of dispiritedness.  The   self,   seeking a return   to  integrity, impels  the   individual to  create  a crisis,  e.g.   an  accident, a  Copyright © 1990  by Choices International

loss,   or a   failure.   The   crisis   creates  an opportunity to consciously choose  change again.  CREATION  If we choose to experience   the fear,  and risk   a   new way of being, the op-  portunity   for   true   freedom   and   un- limited potential   is present.   Choices guides people through the fear to ex- perience this state of empowerment.  THE CHAOS   OF CREATION  The decision to risk going beyond old beliefs   to   new behaviors   results   in   a re-experience   of the   denied   feelings  present at   the time of the original  choice to adapt.  GUIDED   SUPPORT  At   this   point,   during   the   chaos   of  creation,   two  possible  actions are: a  return   to   the   familiar   comfort   of  illusion,   or to   breakthrough to   free- dom and goal actualization.   Choices  supports   the   choice   to   breakthrough by   providing the information, the  tools, and the support necessary to:  * Understand  feelings as data * Welcome the learning  expe-  rience  * Gain the clarity to choose a  new  outcome.  *   Be personally   responsible  PERSONAL   RESPONSIBILITY  The   core   of the   Choices’   work   is   to teach each individual to acknowledge  themselves   as   the   source   of all   re- sults.   This   choice to be personally responsible creates breakthrough. BREAKTHROUGH  Breakthrough   occurs   when   core  feelings are re-experienced in the ab- sence of judgement.   Information that had been repressed is now available, clarity   occurs,   old barriers   dissolve,  and the peace   of freedom is   experi-  enced. The  Model  for Change  Step 1. You decide  to change and to leave the status quo. The decision needs a clear vision and  strong intention  to carry  it through. It does not  matter  whether the change is prompted by an inner  desire or an external situation.  Step 2. Your inner resistance to the change hits! You desire  to  go back to where  you were. In  order for resistance  to exist, there must be an equal  balance of order and chaos.  Step 3. The balance of order and chaoscreates immense  agitation. Orderand chaos  are  neither negative nor positive  and both  are necessary for the possibility of change.  Step  4. If the agitation gets strong  enough, you  move to a choice point—you will go one way or the other.  Step  5.  Choosing to  go for the  past does  not work. If the past was  workable there would be no need  to  change in  the first place. Choosing the past results in illusion, a self-deception. You either deceive  yourself into  thinking that the change was not  necessary,  or that you have already  achieved it. Self-deception eventually erodes your self-  esteem.  Step  6.  When you choose illusion you often  cannot see what  you are doing. You create a crisis in  order to wake  yourself up to the change you need  to make. The  crisis can be ignored, which leads eventually to demise; or, it car  shake you up to recommit to  the intention to change, and mean it.  Step 7.  The other option  is to risk the unknown and do  something  new; to stay with your intention to change. This  choice throws us into the chaos of creation.  ‘Chaos’ because you are pulled  in  opposite directions—you are in  paradox, maintaining two  seemingly opposite  experiences at once. ‘Creation,’ because  when  you are in the  unknown,  you  have the space to choose new  behaviors. You must  be  able to simultaneously  contain  the  past  and  create the future by staying with your decision to change.  Step 8. Chaos  is  extremely  uncomfortable and leads  to another choice  point. At this  point, help or support is  critical! It is easy to  lose sight of your  vision and fool  yourself about where  you are without the  support of people  who know your intention and vision and help you stay on track.  Step  9. If you get  through  to  this point you  reach the next step—responsibility. You see yourself as the source of  your  experience and  are able toreceive and  use new   information. You change the way  you  see—the  same  data means  something  different than it  did before. You are able to see new solutions  to  old problems. Step 10. You are  at a critical  point. You are close to having  what  you  want, yet  you  could stop just short of the goal  because things are  not  as you  pictured  they  would  be.  It may  not feel or  look as you expected or you  may  not  even  recognize it. At this  point, you  need  to  remember what  your  intention  was  and  stay congruent, using everything  you  have  learned  so far. It is  okay that  things don't look and  feel  as  expected. If you continue  to risk the  unknown,  you will break through to achieve your vision.

MISTAKES  In 1943, Wernher von Braun was working on a   rocket that the Germans  hoped would destroy London and end the war. Producing this new rocket  required new metals, new fuels, new guidance systems, new everything.   Von Braun’s superiors were impatient to move the project to completion. They  were angered by the many changes he had sent to the factories responsible for manufacturing the rocket.   “You are supposed to be the ultimate brain in this  operation...do you know off-hand how many last-minute changes you’ve made in your rocket plans...since you started two years ago?”   They waved a piece of  paper before Von Braun.   “Make a guess, Professor. How many changes have you sent to the factories?”   And there the ridiculous figure was:   65,121.   It was  accurate.   Von Braun acknowledged his 65,121 mistakes.   He then estimated he would make 5,000 more before the rocket was ready.   “It takes sixty-five thou- sand errors before the rocket,” he said.   “Russia has made maybe thirty thou- sand of them by now.   America hasn’t made any.”  In the second half of World War II, Germany, alone, pounded her enemies with ballistic missiles; no other country had them.   And when the war was over,  Wernher Von Braun became the “ultimate brain” in America’s space program. Only a few years—and many mistakes—later, America put a man on the moon. High CE individuals tend  to be empathetic and people  oriented. They generally  find theoretical approaches to  be unhelpful and  prefer to treat each  situation as a unique  case. They learn best from specific examples in which  they can  become involved.  Indivuals who empasize Concrete Experience tend to  be oriented  more towards peers and  less towards authority in their approach  to  learning, and benefit most  from  feedback and discussion with fellow CE learners.  ABSTRACT CONCEPTUALIZATION (AC) THINKING  A high  score on Abstract  Conceptualization indicates an analytical, conceptual approach to  learning that relies heavily on logical  thinking and rational evaluation. High AC individuals tend  to be oriented  more  towards things  and symbols and less  toward other  people. They learn best in  authority-directed,  impersonal learning situations that emphasize theory  and systematic analysis.  They are frustrated by and benefit little from unstructured “discovery” learning  approaches like  exercises and simulations.  ACTIVE EXPERIMENTATION  (AE) DOING  A high  score on Active Experimentation indicates an active, “doing” orientation to learning that  relies  heavily on  experimentation. High AE individuals learn best  when  they engage in such  things as projects, homework,  or small group  discussions. They  dislike passive  learning situa-  tions such as lectures.   These individuals tend  to be extroverts.  REFLECTIVE OBSERVATION  (RO)  WATCHING A high score  on Reflective  Observation  indicates a  tentative,  impartial,  and reflective approach  to  learning.   High RO individuals  rely heavily on  careful  observation  in making  judgements,  and  prefer learning situations  such as lectures that allow them  to take the role of impartial  observers.  These  individuals tend to be introverts.  APPLYING ACCELERATED LEARNING  TO  COURSE DESIGN

STAGES OF  LEARNING  CONCRETE EXPERIENCE (CE)  This stage of the learning cycle emphasizes personal involvement  with people in everyday  situations. In this stage, you would tend to rely  more on your feelings than on a systematic ap-  proach to problems and situations.   In a learning  situation,  you would rely more on your ability to  be  open-minded and adaptable  to  change.  REFLECTIVE OBSERVATION (RO)  In this stage of the learning cycle, people un-  derstand  ideas and situations from different  points  of view. In a learning  situation you  would rely on  patience, objectivity, and careful judgment but  would not necessarily take  any  action. You would  rely on your own thoughts  and feelings to form  opinions.  ABSTRACT  CONCEPTUALIZATION  (AC)  In this  stage, learning involves using logic and  ideas,  rather than feelings, to  understand problems  or situations. Typically, you  would rely on sys-  tematic  planning and develop theories and ideas to  solve  problems.  ACTIVE EXPERIMENTATION  (AE)  Learning in  this stage takes an active  form— experimenting  with influencing or  changing  situa-  tions. You would  have a practical appproach and a  concern   with   what really  works, as opposed  to  watching a situation. You value getting  things  done and  seeing the results of your influence and inge-  nuity. LEARNING-STYLE  TYPES  ACCOMMODATOR (Combines leaming steps of Concrete Experience and  Active Experimentation)  People with this learning  style perceive information  concretely and process it  actively.  They have the ability to learn primarily from “hands-on” experience. This person's  greatest strength lies  in doing  things. If this  is  your  style, you probably enjoy carrying  out plans and involving yourself in new and challenging  experiences. You tend  to be  more of a risk-taker than people with the other three learning styles. Your tendency  may be to act  on “gut” feelings,  solving problems in a trial-and-error  manner, and  relying  heavily on other people for information rather than on yourown analytic abiliy.  The Accommodator is at ease with people but is sometimes seen as impatient and  “pushy.”  This learning  style is important for effectiveness in action-oriented careers  such as marketing or sales.  DIVERGER (Combines  learning steps of  Concrete  Experience and Reflective  Observation)  People   with this  learning   style  perceive information concretely and process it  reflectively. They are best at viewing concrete  situations from  many  different points  of view.   Their approach to situations is to observe  rather than take  action. This  person's  greatest strength lies in imaginative  ability. If this is  your  style,  you may  enjoy situations that call  for generating a wide range of ideas, as in a  brainstorming  session. Research  shows that you are interested in people and  tend to be imaginative  and emotional. You probably  have broad cultural interests and like to  gather  information. This imaginative ability and sensitivity to feelings is needed  for  effectiveness in the arts,  entertainment, and service careers.  fr  ASSIMILATOR (Combines  learning steps of  Abstract  Conceptualization and  Reflective Observation)  People  with this learning  style perceive  information abstractly and process it reflec-  tively. They are  best  at understanding a wide range of information and putting it into  concise,  logical form. This person's  greatest strength lies in the ability to  create  theoretical  models. For this  person  it  is more  important that the theory be logically  sound  and precise;  in a situation where  a  theory  or  plan  does  not fit the "facts," the  Assimilator  would be likely to disregard  or  re-examine the facts. If this  is your  learning style, you probably are less  focused  on  people  and  more interested  in abstract  ideas  and  concepts. This learning style  is  important for effectiveness in  planning  departments,  accounting,  information  and  science  careers.  es  CONVERGER (Combines  learning steps of  Abstract  Conceptualization and  Active Experimentation)  People with this learning style perceive information abstractly and process it actively.  This person's  greatest strength lies  in the practical application  of ideas and theories.  If this  is  your  preferred learning style,  you  have  the ability to solve  problems  and  make  decisions  based on  finding solutions  to  questions  or  problems. You  would  rather deal  with technical  tasks and  problems  than  with social  and  interpersonal issues.   These  learning  skills  are  important  to be  effective in  specialist  and  technology  careers  APPLYING ACCELERATED LEARNING TO COURSE DESIGN  a

Theory  of  Dissipative Structures  Condensed from The Aquarian  Conspiracy by Marilyn Ferguson  Darwin’s theory of evolution by chance  mutation  and survival of the fittest has  proven  hopelessly inadequate to account for a great many  observations in  biology.  Just as inadequacies  in Newton’s  physics led  Einstein to formulate a shocking  new  theory, so  a larger  paradigm is  emerging to broaden  our understanding of evolution.  The new  paradigm attributes evolution to periodic leaps by small groups. This  changing view is significant for at least two reasons: (1) It requires a mechanism  for biological change  more powerful than chance  mutation, and (2) it opens us up to the possibility  of rapid evolution  in our own time, when the equilibrium  of the  species is punctuated by stress. Stress in modern society  is experienced at the fron- tiers of our psychological rather  than our geographical limits. Pioneering becomes  an increasingly  psychospiritual venture since our physical frontiers are all but  exhausted, short of space exploration.  Given what  we are learning  about the  nature of profound  change,  transformation of  the human  species seems less  and less  improbable.  Biochemist Albert  Szent-Gyorgyi, discoverer of Vitamin C and a Nobel laureate,  proposed that a drive toward greater order  may be  a fundamental principle of  nature. He  calls this characteristic syntropy - the opposite of  entropy. Living mat-  ter  has an inherent drive to perfect itself, he believes.  Evolution  involves true transformation,  re-forming of the basic structure, and not  mere adding  on.  Physicist John  Platt has proposed  that humankind is now  experiencing an evolu- tionary  shockfront and “may emerge very quickly into  coordinated  forms  such as it  has never known  before... implicit in the biological material all along, as surely as  the butterfly  is  implicit  in the caterpillar.”  %  “gs ys  “APPLYING   ACCELERATED LEARNING TO COURSE DESIGN  “A

THE SCIENCE OF TRANSFORMATION  When the puzzles and paradoxes cry out for resolution, a new paradigm is due.  Fortunately,   a deep and powerful new explanation for rapid evolution - biological,  cultural,  personal - is emerging.  The theory of dissipative structures won the 1977 Nobel  prize in chemistry  for a  Belgian physical chemist, Ilya Prigogine. This theory may  prove as important a  breakthrough to science  in general as the theories of Einstein were to physics. It bridges the critical gap between biology and physics  - the missing link between liv-  ing  systems and the apparently lifeless universe in  which they arose.  It explains  “irreversible processes” in nature - the movement  toward higher and  higher orders of life. Prigogine, whose  early interest  was in history and  the human-  ities, felt that science  essentially  ignored  time. As Prigogine  keeps  saying, there  are many aspects of time:  decay,  history,  evolution, the creation of new  forms, new  ideas. Where  in the old universe  was there room  for becoming?  Prigogine’s theory  resolves the fundamental  riddle of how living things have been  running uphill  in a universe that is supposed to be  running  down.  And the theory is immediately  relevant to everyday life - to people.   It  offers a sci-  entific  model of transformation at every  level. It  explains the critical role of stress  in transformation  - and the impetus  toward transformation inherent in nature!  As we  shall see,  the principles revealed by the theory of dissipative structures  are valuable in helping us understand profound change in psychology, learning, health,  sociology, even politics and economics.   The theory has been used by the United States Department of Transportation to predict traffic flow patterns.   Scientists in  many disciplines are employing it within their own specialties.   The applications are infinite.  The essence of the theory is not difficult to understand once we get past some semantic  confusion.   In  describing  nature, physical scientists  often  use ordinary  words in their most literal sense - words for which we also have abstract meanings and strongly loaded emotional  values. To understand Prigogine’s  theory  we need  to withhold traditional value judgment about words like “complexity,” “dissipa- tion,” “coherence,” “instability, “and “equilibrium.”  APPLYING   ACCELERATED   LEARNING TO COURSE DESIGN —

Some forms in nature are open systems, involved in a continuous exchange of ener- gy with the environment.   A seed, an ovum, and   a   living creature are all open sys-  tems. There are also human-made  open systems. Prigogine gives the example of a  town:  It takes in energy from the surrounding  area (power, raw materials), trans-  forms it in factories, and returns energy to the environment.   In closed systems,  on  the other  hand - examples would be a rock, a cup of cold coffee, a log - here is no  internal  transformation of energy.  Prigogine’s term for open systems is dissipative structures. That is,  their  form  or  structure is  maintained by a continuous dissipation  (consumption) of energy. Much  as water moves through a whirlpool and creates it at the same time,  energy moves  through and simultaneously forms the dissipative structure. All living things and  some nonliving systems (for instance, certain chemical  reactions) are dissipative  structures. A dissipative structure might well be described as a flowing wholeness.  It is  highly organized but always  in process.  Now think about  the meaning of the word complex:  braided  together. A complex structure is connected at many  points and  in many  ways. The more complex a dis-  sipative structure, the more  energy is needed to maintain all those connections.  Therefore  it is  more  vulnerable to internal fluctuations. It is said to be “far from  equilibrium.”   (In the physical  sciences,  equilibrium does  not mean healthy  bal-  ance.   It refers to ultimate random dispersal of energy.   This equilibrium is a kind  of death.)  Because these connections can only be sustained  by a flow of energy, the  system is  always in flux.   Notice the paradox; the  more coherent  or intricately connected the  structure, the more unstable it is.   Increased coherence means increased instability! This very instability  is the key to transformation. The  dissipation of energy, as Prigogine demonstrated by his elegant mathematics, creates the potential for sud-  den  reordering.  The continuous movement of energy through the system results in fluctuations; if they are minor, the system damps them and they do not alter its structural integrity.  But if the  fluctuations  reach a critical  size,  they  “perturb” the system. They increase the  number of novel interactions  within  it.   They shake it up. The  ele- ments of the old pattern come into contact with each other in new ways and make new connections.   The parts reorganize into a new whole.   The system escapes into  a  higher  order. The more complex or  coherent a structure, the greater the next level of complexity.  Each transformation  makes the next one likelier. Each new level is even more inte- grated  and connected than the one  before, requiring a  greater flow of energy  for  maintenance, and is therefore still less  stable. To put it another way, flexibility  begets flexibility.   As Prigogine said, at higher levels of complexity, “the nature of  the laws of nature changes.” Life “eats” entropy. It has the potential to create new  forms by allowing a shake-up of old forms.  At first the idea of creating new order by perturbation seems outrageous, like shak-  ing up a box of random words and pouring out a sentence. Yet our  traditional wis-  dom  contains parallel ideas. We know that  stress often  forces sudden new  solu-  tions; that crisis often  alerts  us to opportunity; that  the creative process  requires  chaos  before form emerges; that individuals are often  strengthened by suffering  and conflict; and that societies need a healthy airing of dissent.  Human society offers an example of spontaneous self-organization.   In a fairly  dense society, as individuals become  acquainted with others, each  soon has more  points of contact throughout  the system via friends and friends of friends.   The  greater the instability and mobility of the society, the more interactions  occur. This  means greater potential  for  new  connections, new  organizations, diversification. Much as certain cells or organs in a body  specialize during the course of evolution,  people with common  interests find one  another and refine their specialty  by mutual  stimulation and  exchange of ideas.  Historians have  long noted that a creative  minority can  reorder  a society. “The  his-  torical  analogy  is so obvious,”  Prigogine said. “Fluctuations, the behavior  of a  small group of people,  can completely change the behavior of the  group as a  whole.”  Cultures are  the  most  coherent  and  strangest of dissipative structures,  Prigogine  remarked.   A   critical number of advocates of change can create “a preferential direction” like the inner ordering of a crystal or magnet that organizes the whole. Because of their  size  and density,  modern  societies are subject to large  internal  fluctuations.   These  can  trigger shifts to  a higher,  richer  order.   In Prigogine’s  terms,  they  can  become more pluralistic and diversified. We are transformed through interaction with the environment. * THE BRAIN  AS A DISSIPATIVE STRUCTURE  Aharon Katchalsky, also a physical chemist,  had been studying  dynamic patterns of  brain function for  many years. He was trying to  understand how the brain inte-  grates, what  its rhythms and oscillations mean.  The brain seemed a perfect  example of a dissipative structure.   It is the ultimate in  complexity.  It is characterized by form and flow, interaction with the environment,  abrupt shifts, sensitivity to being perturbed. It demands the lion’s share of the  body’s energy - with  only 2 percent of the body  weight, it consumes 20 percent of  the available  oxygen. The ups and downs of its  energy influx are characteristic of  the unstable dissipative structure.  The theory of dissipative structures might well tie dynamic brain patterns to transi-  tions in the mind.   “The restructuring of an individual personality may take a sud- den form, as in flashes of understanding,  learning a new skill, falling in love, or the  conversion experience of St. Paul.”  Brainwaves reflect  fluctuations of energy. Inward attention generates a larger fluc-  tuation in the brain.   These fluctuations then reach a critical level, large enough  to  provoke the shift into a  higher  level of organization.  Memories,  including  deeply entrenched  patterns of behavior and  thought, are dissi- pative structures.   They are patterns of forms stored in the brain.   Remember that  small  fluctuations in a dissipative structure are suppressed by the existing form;  they have no lasting effect.   But larger fluctuations of energy cannot  be contained in the old  structure. They set off ripples  throughout the  system,  creating  sudden  new connections.   Thus, old patterns are likeliest to change when maximally per-  turbed or shaken - activated in states of consciousness in which there is significant  energy flow.  The old pattern is broken.   A stuck thought pattern, an old paradigm, a compulsive behavior, a knee-jerk response...all of these are dissipative structures, capable of  sudden enlargement.   The new structure is like a larger paradigm.   And the pertur-  bation that provokes the new order in a dissipative structure is analogous to the cri- sis  that  helps  force  the  shift to a new paradigm.  If we try to live as closed systems, we are doomed to regress.   If we enlarge our awareness, admit new information, and take advantage of the brain’s brilliant  capacity to  integrate and  reconcile, we  can leap forward. tgs  “APPLYING ACCELERATED LEARNING TO COURSE DESIGN   a

Taking  on  the  big courses They selected two customer-service-  representative training courses  for con-  version to   the accelerated-learning  format: a six-week one  in private-resi-  dence order taking and a four-week  one  in private-residence  billing. The development team worked ina think-tank environment it called the  Skunk  Works—an office far  removed from the  team  members’ normal  work-  place.   Life in  the  Skunk  Works was  designed  to be  informal, playful, anc  creative,   with  an energetic environ-  ment that  would  stimulate everyone's  imagination. As the team members thought  about  and planned the courses. they wrote their thoughts in words and  pictures  on large sheets of paper. '§ Keep the energy  high.  ; Trust  the learner and the learning  Process. They wanted to give  the rooms  a natural look and   to make   them  learner-centered,  even playfuli—places  where  people  could relax,   be  them-  selves, and enjoy learning. From the start, the  learning  advisors  expected  the  trainees to be proactive  rather than  passive,   to  take charge of their  own learning,   and,  certainly, to master   the   learning   material of the course. Learning  accelerators  Collaboration rather than competi-  tion is important for  accelerated  learn-  ing. Trainees were  encouraged to help  each  other in any way  they could. At  various times throughout the course,  they  formed ad hoc learning groups or reinforced each other’s   training in  pairs. They were  responsible not just  for their own learning,   but   for the  learning of everyone in the   class as  well—everyone was a student and a teacher  simultaneously.  Accelerated-learning  technology is  a powerful ally in meeting  today’s challenge  to do more with less  One important collaborative learn-  ing technique is learner articulation.  To  his   or her   partner,   the   iearner describes, out loud and in detail,  the  material   he or she just   learned. This  articulation of   newly learned facts, ideas, and  procedures (with demon-  strations where possible)  helps speed  the learning and make it  stick. Of course,   different   accelerators work better  for different people. The  environment has  a lot of diversity,  and people  can pick  from a smorgas- bord  of  options  and  choose  learning  methods and  materials that work best  for them.  Evaluations  Training,  courses   that   employ   the  techniques  of  accelerated learning  are  now a   standard part  of Bell Atiantic’s  training program. How do people really learn?   The answers and theories are endless. They include ideas ranging from genetic imprinting to osmosis and  modeling and emotional intelligence.   Brain research is voluminous  as we go into the 21“ century.   A later book in this series   will deal  with the scientific basis of that research and how Educational  Discoveries uses that research to work with corporations to achieve extraordinary results.  How do you learn?   Isn’t that an interesting question?   And, what do  you learn?   Do you learn information from reading , watching videos,  through computers?   Can you learn people skills without people? Can you change behavior without a model of what that behavior should look like?   Feel like?   Are there people you meet in your daily travels that you want to emulate?   Do you?   How does it work?   Can  you remember the words of the   songs of your childhood and not the  ones you listened to last week or even this morning?   And, remember  what we heard about a baby’s first year of life?   They learn more in  that year that in all the years combined afterwards.   So, what does  this have to do with you and this book?   Good question.  “The Accounting Game”   is written to create a specific learning  experience for you as well as teach you the basic skills of Accounting. We call the learning method   accelerative learning.  What do you think that means?   It is a learning methodology that uses all of your senses as well as your emotions and your critical  thinking skills.   If you   can remember your kindergarden or elementary school classrooms, you will see many colored maps, letters and numbers, drawings from each child, etc.   You learned the alphabet by singing,. You learned the multiplication tables by saying them out loud with each other.   You laughed a lot.   You were creative.   It began to change when you entered middle school or high school.   Learning became more lecture, more black and white, more rote.   You studied before tests and probably did well or maybe not. Most of the information you learned in high school you don’t remember now.   That's because it went into your short term memory so that you could pass the tests and move on to the next grade. While in elementary school, much of the information you learned went directly to your long term memory, because it was peppered with music, color, movement, smells, emotional experiences and lots

of play and  fun.. The methodology we  use in this book in many ways  parallels  how you learned in grade school. We do this by accessing  the part of your brain where long term memory lives. Now, the way  to reach  your long term  memory has to include emotion, because  they reside in the same place in your brain ---  The Limbic Brain.  Because of  the way  we humans  learn, we have to discover  something ourselves to really learn it. TAG Book  Forward  Business people and students have over the  years  found the subject of accounting  quite difficult  to master. Many have simply given up in frustration,  others have decided  to  leave accounting  to the “experts.” This book is  for all of you who have  hated accounting,  had difficulty learning it, or ever  thought you didn’t really “get it.”  I think that  most attempts to teach accounting fail  because of over attention  to  details and a failure to present the big picture  framework of how it  all works and fits  together. In this book we promise  not to over burden you with details and to  focus on  what are really the key concepts of accounting that any  business person needs to know.  You will learn the structure and purpose of the  three primary financial  statements-the  balance sheet, the income statement, and the cash flow statement. You will learn how  these fit together and their  interrelationships. You will also learn the basic  language of  business—concepts like cost of goods sold, expenses, bad debts, accrual vs.  cash  methods  of accounting, FIFO and LIFO, capitalizing vs. expensing,  depreciation, and the  difference  between cash and profit.  Our promise  is that you will get all this  information in a fun and easy way that  allows you to participate,  interact and discover all that you need to know. Many people  need to have  understanding and confidence in working with financial concepts, but  are  not  ever going to  be doing accounting details. If that is  you, then  this book is for you. It is  set  up so that you can actually do financial statements as you are learning them. I invite  you to “play the  game” as you are reading  the book.  Understanding all  this information is nice, but what do you do with it?   The final chapter will give  you some tools  for analyzing financial  information and making better  decisions for  your company and your  career. Feel  Ask  Validate  Open  Relate  Feel what the questioner  is  feeling, the emotion that  is the source of the question.  Ask a question to clarify the real  question.  Validate the question  and the questioner. Ask, “Who else has or has had this feeling, experi-  ence, or question?”  Relate what your own experience is, or has been, what you learned and how you did things differently. Relate the question to your discussion or subject  material  and  complete the learning.

WHY  A Game  of Integrity  Game Rules  WHY Trading Company is in the business of trading commodities and finished products.  Competition is  fierce, and WHY outposts  have  been established to expand and create  trade agreements with as many countries and other traders as possible.  The purpose of this game  is  to develop an awareness of the emotions of oneself and  others in an intensive business environment.  The  Players  Individuals have Operating  Styles. Players maintain their integrity by  always behaving  in the game in their  Operating Styles, and by keeping them secret from other players.  Players are members of teams, either Trader Teams or Country Teams.  The  Trader  Teams are  outposts of WHY Trading Company: North WHY, South WHY, East WHY, and West WHY.  Each outpost starts with $3,000,000 in cash as working  capital  from the World  Headquarters of WHY Trading Company. The Country  Teams are agencies  licensed by their  governments to trade:  Beeferino,  Chickenwoo, Wheatzig, and Cornado.  Each  Country Team starts with commodity  cards representing their raw materials stock in metric  tons. The cards are valued at $3,000,000. Country  Team members  must consistently  observe and  demonstrate  their Local Customs, not discuss them,  or  trade with  any violators of them.  The Board  of Trade (BOT) is played  by the instructor and staff.  The BOT enforces  all rules with cash penalties or jail time.  * It  establishes  and  increases the standards for agreement  approval.  * Itissues  Integrity  Cards, and awards Bonus or Audit  Cards.  ¢ Itrelays memos  of governments  to  their  Country  Teams and of the World Headquarters of WHY to WHY Trader Teams.   Teams  must  comply  with these  memos, or forfeit the game. ¢   It opens and closes the trading sessions.  * It  sets the  cash  conversion rates for all commodities  and  products  that  is  used  for final scoring.
