The Trader  Team takes the commodity cards,  and  exchanges them with the Board  of Trade  for  product  cards. The Trader Team uses the product cards to sell to other  Teams. f. The process whereby a Country  Team agrees to buy  finished products (product cards) from  any  Team is essentially the same.  The BOT announces the close of the trading  period. Teams at that point  must  total the cash and  number of cards  they  have. The results are posted.  General Rules  Country  Teams  sell commodity cards to any Trader  Team, but  not  to any  other Country Team.   Country  Teams may not  buy any  commodity  cards. Any team may  buy  or sell product cards  with  any  other  team. All transactions  must be in  cash. No barter,  debt  financing, or option  is  permitted.   Prices are generally  determined by  supply and  demand.  All meetings and negotiations  must  held in the room.  All teams must  purchase minimum  amounts  of  all  finished  products.   Once the mini- mums  are  purchased the Team  can draw a Bonus Card from  the Board  of  Trade.  Audit  Cards are specific  instructions issued  by BOT auditors.   Teams  must comply with these  instructions, or  forfeit the game.  Integrity Cards are  issued  by  BOT auditors when  players  and teams do  not  behave  in integrity with their operating styles or  are  in reaction. A Game  of Integrity  Conformer  You’ve seen people get in trouble when they don’t conform to  the rules. So you’ve  become a champion of the rules: precedence  is important, literal interpretations of  the rules are  the only  valid ones, and written  words are more true  than spoken ones.  What to do:  Police others so that they conform to  the rules. Remind them of what  has been written and established.  Tips on playing your  role: Resist change. Resist what has  not  been permitted  in  writing.  WHY  A Game  of  Integrity  Blamer  You may  have made a few mistakes but you feel like you  have done a pretty good  job overall.   Besides, the problems are really created by other people. You  would have  done a better job if it  wasn’t for  their mistakes and  changes.  What to  do: Blame others  for what has  gone  wrong in the  past and  what is  not  working right now.  Tips on  playing your  role:  When  in  doubt,  blame.   Never  take  responsibility  for  anything.
O)

A Game of  Integrity  The Lone Wolf  You don’t want to have to count on anyone else for your  survival. Your primary  concern is looking out for #1. What to do: Do what will benefit you personally.   Avoid things that don’t.  Tips on playing  your role: Keep  your own  counsel. Be aggressive about protect-  ing what is yours and getting what you deserve.   The end justifies the means.   Don’t  get bogged down in meetings or teamwork.  WHY  A Game  of  Integrity  Confronter  Many problems are not  addressed  because  people  avoid  confronting the  issues. To  succeed in any project, people must be willing to experience the discomfort and to examine the issues honestly and dispassionately.  What to do:  Compassionately, confront the key  issues.   Speak the  truth  without  euphemism, denial, or justification.   Share all information, including emotions, as value-neutral data for decision-making. Way of Being: You are open and compassionate.   You listen for what is really meant, not just what is being said.   You share you feelings freely.
wy

A Game of Integrity  Controller  Things will get out of control unless you personally intervene. You are the only one  that  has  the level of logical  thinking,  organizational ability, and proper sense of pri-  orities to get the results your team needs. What to do: You must play a leading role in  any decision making. Keep people focused on the objectives, and make  sure you are decisive. Tips on playing the role: Interrupt discussions and  change the direction of the  meeting to make sure things are in your control.  WHY  A Game  of Integrity  Avoider  You hate conflict. You avoid  it, even if it means  ignoring  what  you  believe is  going  on:   strong feelings, hidden  agendas, lies, emotional  reactions, etc.  What to  do:   Maneuver  yourself and  others to slide past conflict and  emotional issues. Keep  focused on the content of the discussion or  issue. Tips on playing your  role:   Use  humor,  diplomacy.   Be logical and do  anything  to  avoid  or  deny  the  emotional  issues.

A Game of  Integrity  Victim  It’s not your fault, but circumstances always seem to turn out so you look bad.   If  people  recognized the power  they have over you and were more conscious of being  fair, you would get the recognition you deserve.  What to  do: Play it safe. Spread the risk. Make people agree with you that things  are unfair and you are powerless.   Those that disagree with your point of view are probably part of the power structure. Tips for playing your role: Those in power ought to feel guilty.  WHY  A Game of  Integrity  Coach  You believe that most  people  have untapped capabilities they are not  even  aware  of. When  given the proper environment,  they can  do great  things. Your pleasure is  not to do  their jobs, but to  enable  them to do  theirs better.  What to  do:  Determine for  yourself  what skills you do have.   Demonstrate those  skills and  help others  to gain  them.  Tips on playing  your  role:  Be  patient,  allow  mistakes without  criticism,  encourage  them to demonstrate the skills.
C)

A Game of Integrity XX  Conspirator  You think people and events are shaping up  to threaten you and your job. You never  share what you think or feel. You get pleasure from breaking rules without getting  caught. What to do: Find an ally.   Conspire together to protect yourselves, challenge  authority, and thwart any threat, real or imagined.  Tips on playing your role: Be outwardly cooperative but maintain a secret opposi-  tion.   Use fear and promises of support to enroll allies.   If threatened, make excuses,  feign illness, mumble, claim ignorance or confusion.  WHY  A Game  of Integrity XY  Groveler  The most important thing is business is not what you know, but who you know.  People respond to flattery.   When people feel their slightest whims are worth attend-  ing to, your personal advancement is assured.  What to do:   Be a great follower:   repeat their sentences, praise them for their ideas.  Attend to trivial comforts of your betters, and treat with contempt your inferiors. Tips on playing your role: Act humble.   No one likes a show-off.   Talk softly so others must strain to hear you.

A Game of Integrity   ia  Resister  You choose what you will resist carefully.   You don’t resist everything, but what you do resist, you resist totally.   You secretly gather allies, you drop hints about your  reservations.  What to do: Often the most powerful action is an act of omission.   You are skilled at that.   Not answering any question directly will slow things down. Tips on playing your role: Gather documentation to protect yourself.  WHY  A Game of Integrity   YK  Risk Taker  You are excited by gathering a team to take on a challenge and win.   The more diffi- cult the challenge, the more exciting the win.   For you, it’s always to try something than to wait, or to do more studies. What to do: Help your team stay focused on the objectives and the rewards that come when those objectives are reached.   Share you fears and excitement.  Tips on playing your role: It’s all a game, so the fun and humor are not extraneous, but fundamental to the process.

A Game of Integrity  Complicator  You are not really good at this job, but your family wanted you to do it, and you’ve got to work somewhere. You have made some real boo boos in the past, and you are  afraid your incompetence will be discovered now.  What to do: You work to make things as complicated as possible so people won’t easily see what is really going on.   This is the way to become irreplaceable, because  people have to go to you to figure things out. Tips on playing your role: Bring in as many ideas and methods as possible. Avoid  the simple and go for the complex.   Look like you are trying to find a better way.  WHY  A Game of  Integrity  Whiner  People haven’t listened to you in a long time.   They should.   Get their attention by  telling them in detail what doubts and special conditions they have overlooked.  Repeat yourself in different ways over and over again.   You feel powerless; but if  they start to listen, you feel validated.  What to do: They will hear you  better, if you  speak  louder.  Tips on playing the role: You basic objective is to lay the ground work so that you will not get blamed.

A Game  of  Integrity  Cynic  People operate out of fear, and  are really  only concerned about themselves. They  put  on a facade: the real person is pretty pitiful. When things go wrong,  you feel validated. When things reportedly go right, they are  not telling the whole truth.  What to do: Look for  conspiracies: headquarters wants to eliminate our jobs.  People don’t mean what they say, and they don’t say what they  mean.  Tips on playing the role: Attribute unworthy  motives to others.  WHY  A Game  of Integrity  Connector  Teams and  processes are successful  when  everyone is connected to themselves,  each  other, and to  the mission of the organization.  What to do:  Create  harmonious  relationships.   Share your feelings to others  and be  open to receive their feelings.  Way of  Being:  You are vulnerable. You present  “one face” to the world.   What  you  feel inside is what you show  outside. You are  accepting  of others, and do not judge  them.

Enrollment  Enrollment is the process by which people become  participants in a  program. That “program” can  be a meeting,  a team, a project such as  CPR, or a training session. A typical enrollment includes a greeting,  personal  introductions, and  a discussion of what’s going to be  done  and why.  Enrollment creates  the context for the gathering.  Enrollment also gets people interested in supporting an idea or  action,  or in performing an action. In this  program,  participants  were  asked  their  background and expec- tations. With such questions,  people  responded verbally or raised their hands.  People got involved  in a physical way.  The more multi-  sensory and participatory the interactions are, the more  people buy  into the  process and purpose. Note that  the questions  draw  out not  only those  who had  experience  in the topic, but  also those who didn’t. The last question  in  this  series is intended  to bring  everyone  together.  The presenter models the agreement by raising her  hand. In this way,  the  presenter  and all the participants are treated  as equals. These  questions set the  context of inclusion,  participation, and equality.  TN  a   a  oe  11

Common Ground  Participants enter  programs with a wide variety of abilities and experi-  ence. This is an advantage when the learning activities are group  interactive types. And to be effective for everyone, the course must  begin at  a point where everyone can  be included. We  call this point common ground. Common ground refers to  the content or experi- ences  shared by participants that give each  one a  sense of belonging to  the group. For example, imagine a seminar  on basic accounting with  a diverse audience that included a trainer  from  Saudi Arabia, a dentist  from Denver, and  a chief accountant from a major corporation. The  seminar starts, and everyone is asked  to  get comfortable, relax, close  their eyes, and listen to, “When you  were a child....”.   Everyone had  the common experience of getting comfortable  and closing their  eyes,  and whatever  their  background,  everyone had a childhood.   These  common  experiences when  recalled together  created for the partici- pants  a sense of belonging  with the group. Common ground was  established. The creating of common  ground  continues whenever  possible throughout the  presentation. It’s like coming home, over and  over again. Gravient Any mischievous youngster who’s ever caught a frog and decided to  cook it has learned a lesson  about  gradient. This lesson is simple—if  the water is too  hot,  the frog will jump out. To cook a live frog, start  in cold water and warm it up slowly.  The frog won’t notice the  increase, and will stay in the  pot. The same is true in  class: start with  low intensity and warm  it up slowly. Otherwise the student’s atten-  tion, like the frog, will leave.  Ina learning environment,  gradient refers to  the level of intensity and  commitment  required to participate  in a given exercise or  learning  experience.   Attending a lecture on the presidential election  is low  gradient  when compared to developing a group presentation of the  same topic.   Listening to  the thermodynamics of dissipative structures  is high gradient  compared  to watching a demonstration  on making  paper  airplanes. A learning segment  has higher gradient if the content  is more  complex, or if the  personal interaction required is more  involved or intimate. Also when  participants  are ready for more com-  plex content or more  interaction, one can say  that they  are at a higher  gradient. In general, the higher the  gradient the greater  the learning.  The presenter’s  personal gradient  needs  to match  the level of the  material presented. EMOTIONAL INTELLIGENCE  PROJECT  INTERVIEW WITH  Judith Orloff  Q:   What’s  all this about emotional intelligence? Ten years ago nobody was  talking about it?  A: Well, ten years ago people  were doing it and they weren't talking about it,  because in business  it  was considered, um, dangerous to have  emotions. (OFFSTAGE) A: — Well, emotional intelligence  is not new. It's been around for,  forever. It's just that as our world became more industrialized and  business  became more formal, people felt that  emotions  were dangerous in the workplace.   So the reason  it's so,  um, open,  it's becoming open now is  because the people  that were the, uh, hippies  in the,  in the sixties are running  businesses  today. And I,  I believe,  personally, that  they  always have been emotionally intelligent.   So  now that they're in more powerful positions in,  in  organizations,  I, I believe that people are taking  emotions  more seriously, and yet less seriously at  the same  time. Q:   A hundred years ago---  (OFFSTAGE)  Q: A hundred years ago people valued the strong silent type,  the man of action.  Were these skills important back then?   Or have things changed in our human universe?  A:   A, along time ago, when, uh, John Wayne did "High," -- I think it was John Wayne that did "High  Noon," I'm not sure it was him. But  whoever, Gary  Cooper  did "High  Noon."  A: A,a long time  ago, when I was a kid and I was  watching  "High Noon"  with Gary Cooper,  I,  I  always  thought he  was  sexy and  attractive, 'cause  he  didn't  say  anything.   And the men  at that  time were considered powerful  and  macho when they  didn't  cry,  when they  didn't—   wh-when they  were able  to  brush off death, and brush  off serious issues  by taking  care of people.   And  I  think  even today,  that's still  valued

in, in, in a lot of areas.   It's still valued in,  in situations, particularly in  business, uh,  when there's a crisis to be had, and the person  that  can solve the crisis is  not showing  strong feelings. I think that's still  very important. It doesn't  mean they're not having  them. There's an, an incredible  difference between having a feeling and acting that  feeling out, and who  knows what Gary Cooper was really  feeling? I mean he might  have been terrified. But the way he dealt with  his terror is what was appealing and  attractive. He was able to  do  what he wa-- had to do no matter how he felt. And  from  my  point of view, emotional intelligence includes Gary Cooper at "High  Noon," 'cause it  doesn't--   it means being able to keep your word, being  able to do  what  you  said you were  going to do and create the results you were  going to create,  whether  it's killing your opponent  in  front of the clock in the main street,  or getting  the results  for the organization in terms of the profitability. No matter how  you  feel, and no matter what  you feel,  being able to continue  doing what  you said.  Q: Can you explain  for the laymen  what  emotional intelligence is?  A: — Emotional intelligence is, um...  (OFFSTAGE)  A: My de- My word  for  emotional intelligence is emotional literacy. Uh,  I  don't  usually use  the concept  emotional  intelligence.   But emotional literacy  is one's  ability to  be aware of what's going on inside, and focusing on that, rather  than the  other  person or the situation. So once  I'm  aware of what I'm  experiencing, it seems  to give me more ability to know  how to deal with  whatever is  going on  around  me.  So emotional intelligence or emotional literacy is  that capability to choose how to  respond in  any  situation by  knowing what's  going on inside of me in  that,  in  that  moment.  (OFFSTAGE) Q:   Is there a difference between the way men  and  women deal  with this  question of emotional  intelligence?  A: Um, can I  say  I  love your  question?   I  mean I,  I  love the  question of the, of the  gender  differences  in emotions  and how  men and  women  deal with  emotions. I think that they  deal  with  them  outwardly differently,  but they experience  them the  same  inwardly.   And I  think that I, I am  not sure  whether  there really is  a genetic  difference  in  capability  of expressing emotions, but  every  man I've  ever known  wants  to fix something.   And, uh, and  they  love  to fix things.   I've  never  known a  man that doesn't  want  to  solve a  problem right  away,  and  do  something about  it.

They take action-- even if it's children, even if it's little  kids of three and four  years  old. The little girl tends to want to play with something -- the little  boy wants to take  it apart and  put  it back together, very  quickly. So I, I think that  women have, um, the  ability to express  their emotions very differently than men do, in general. And I  think that's wonderful. I, I just think it's  wonderful. And  I don't think being  emotionally literate  has anything to  do with the way you feel emotions -- it's got to  do with the way you  express them, and it's got to do with the way you deal with  situations. So I think cultural differences apply, whether it's people  from Europe  express them differently.   Ethnic differences  apply.   Um,  Mediterranean  cultures  express  emotions  much more openly than people  from Connecticut in general. So  I,  I  don't think  there's... I, I think  we have to... In,  in  order to be emotionally literate  we have to really be able to accept how everybody  expresses their emotions. Just  everybody expresses them differently.  (OFFSTAGE)  Q:   What are  the myths  or objections that you’ve heard about EI?  A: Well,  in my work, the people I talk to  that, uh, want to work  with our  organization  love EI. And  I haven't met anyone that is of any intelligence that  doesn't think of it as common sense. J haven't met anyone that,  um,  I  speak to  on a  regular  basis, that isn't  afraid that  it  means touchy-feely. I don't think  it means  anything like that. In  fact, I think it's very different than what the general public  might think of. For me it's  being  able to  keep your word, and have  your will take  precedence over what your experience is.   And that's very different than touchy- feely, and it,  in terms of business, people  want it as long as it  doesn't interfere with  getting  results done. And most organizations that want E.I., uh,  don't  want to  hear  all the  details about  it. What they  want  is  results -- results, results,  results.   So  in terms of leadership, for  instance,  uh, every leader  that I've ever  spoken  to in  any company is already emotionally literate, if they're successful. (OFFSTAGE) Q:   Give me some examples.   How does a   sensitivity to EI help in the business  world?  A:   I believe that the fastest change in our culture comes through business,  because people can do things very quickly.   Like we have a program where--   that can affect ten thousand people at a time.   Those ten thousand people go home at night and they're different with their families.   They might not kick their dog.   They might not, um, beat their kid.   They might be more patient with what their family

discussions are about. They might think more. They might take a walk at night and  feel love instead of feeling angry at their boss, because they've learned how to  understand firstly, what's  going on inside of them. They've learned to transform  what  we call negative emotions  into positive experiences and learning. And they've  been able to have  more peripheral vision. When, when a person  gains more  emotional intelligence it seems as if they get smarter. It seems as if their  brain takes  a new  order, like a, like the theory of dissipated structure -- as the brain grows a new  way, once  people go  through  changes. And so we believe that business is  welcoming it as long as it's in the context of their  strategic, uh, initiatives that the  business wants to accomplish.   Our organization  won't  sell emotional intelligence products by themselves  without  having them be deeply enmeshed  in the business  processes and the business  results, because then  people will learn how to retain the  knowledge for a long time.  Q:   What do you  say to a person to soften the blow when they are asked to take a  coarse to heighten their EI?  A: I think  line people are probably the easiest  people  we  have  ever worked with,  to accept  new ideas. I don't think we would  ever go  into an organization calling it,  calling the, what we're doing E.I. We go into an organization saying  we're going to  create a re-engineer of the pro--   we're  going to be re-engineering a process. And in  order to be able to, to lead--- (OFFSTAGE)  A: We go  into organizations, um, talking about  the business results, which  I've said a lot during  this,  this time,  because we  don't  want to go in saying we're  doing  E.I.   We want to go in saying  that the way  we're going to re-engineer a process is by teaching people new  models of leadership.   So  in order  to work in a process  environment,  you have to  be able to communicate  differently  with  your  c-peers than  if you're  working  in a functional  environment. You have to  be able to ask  questions.  You have to  be able  to  take in  new ideas. You have to  be  able to  be synergistic.  You have to be willing to let go of your belief system.   So to shift  that  paradigm  we're going to  teach  people new  skills, and  those skills are, are  in  leadership  or  in  process redesign  or in,  um,  in  something  that  makes  sense  to what their work  is.   We, we  do our very,  very best  to  keep our language synonymous with  what  they  do  on  an  everyday  basis.  Q:   — What would you tell a director of training who is not familiar with the EI  approach?

A: That's  different.   That's a whole  different  story. The-- One-- Some of the  most difficult situations  we encounter is with people that have  high level degrees in  organizational development,  in H.R., in training,  people who are already  successful in  what they're  doing. And that's  where the  rub usually is,  ‘cause those people are  the people that could use the skills and learn  them so quickly. But I'm not  sure why  the  threat is so strong with, with,  with professionals. Uh, that's where we find our  most difficult, um, work to do  is making sure  that we treat them as  the heroes and  not us. Because H.R. has  not  been considered very  valuable  in many  organizations,  and so they don't have that much power.  Many people-- this is a hard one. Let's  stop  for a minute.  (OFFSTAGE)  A: Please don't  use   the piece I just did on  the H.R. Manager, or the H.R.  Professional.   We're going to try it again.  Q: You said there  are certain people  who are more  resistant to this sensitivity?  A: — When we work with, uh, line managers or, uh, people that  have P&L  responsibilities, putting emotional intelligence into the work we do is relatively easy.  The most difficult job we have is making sure that the people that already are the trainers and the H.R. professionals, really understand what our intention is, and how we're going to implement what they need to have done in the organization, using a technology that they might not have learned yet.   Once they're, uh, once they  understand what that technology is, and how it can support what they're doing in an  organization, it's not as difficult. Q:   — What would you say to a CEO who’s been successful for thirty-five years? Does he need to change? A:   A   lot of people in, uh, a board roomof organizations are very successful, and they don't really have a need for emotional intelligence, personally.   What they do have a need for is to have their, um, leader, that they, their direct reports be able to accomplish the goals of the organization.   So what we do when we talk in the board room is we give examples to the CFO, or the CEO. about what's going on in the lower levels of their organization that EI could support.   We don't ask them to change because they're great the way they are.   I mean why would they change if they've gotten where they are?   There, there's no reason to.   Some of the times that changes occurs (sic)   are with, with, or when there is a merger and acquisition, when

two large organizations are merging, and the CEO of one, and the CEO of the other, or the CFO  of one, and  the CEO  of the other, have to take new roles.   That's when EI  in the board room  becomes very, very important. Other than that why bother  when  they're as successful as they are? We  just want them to champion what's  going  on  in  their  organization. We don't ask them  to  change unless they believe  they have a  need to change. People don't change unless  they either,  they see a need  from within,  a crisis occurs, they, they get cancer or they have  a divorce, they lose their job, they,  they  have an epiphany of some  sort. Uh, then they do something for themselves. Or,  they're  told, "You'd better make this change, or something quote bad will happen  to  you." Those are  the only--- I mean why would people  change unless there's a true  need in their  own  mind? They own  it, that it, it's  good for them to  do  it. So that's,  that's the tact we always take.  Q: _ Saying there’s a need  to change and implementing  it aren’t always the same  thing. A: Right. Um, I was at a, a con- at a client meeting, a design  session about two weeks ago,  uh,  and the client said  that she had  heard a talk the night  before,  where a  very famous  person  said, "The farthest  distance  in the world  is between the  mind  and  the heart."   And so I, I love that expression.   I,   I was moved by it.   Um, and I thought  to myseif, "Well, how do you move somebody's mind when they say I want this  change, to their heart where they actually make the change occur?   How do you  make something that's intellectual, emotionally true?   How do you make it heart-  felt?"   And we believe the way you do that is by creating cognitive dissonance.   But I mean everybody has a   point of view about everything.   I mean even my thirteen  year old, if you ask, he knows everything.   He knows where, how everything works  and he know, he has a point of view about why it works, and I'm sure everybody's thirteen year old does.   So in order for me to want, have him want to change, I have  to create confusion in his brain, so his old way is in competition with the new way.  And how do you get a person to want to go the new way when it, when they're so immersed in the status quo?   You have to create something at the end of that rainbow in the new way that means more to them and has more value to them than what they already have.   So, that's how we use emotional intelligence in, in designing training, because people have to have that moment when the, the old way and the new way collide, and it's like a bang in the brain and all of a sudden there's "Okay, maybe I can do this."   And then we create the new way to be more exciting, uh, and more powerful for them, that it has more personal value to them.   So that's  how we do it.   I, I mean otherwise I don't see where an intellectual understanding of  something can do more than a temporary es-   like, it's like a temporary, uh, massage.

It's like a tranquilizer. It  feels good at the moment,  but it doesn't  last. So in order to  make  it last you  have to find the highway from the mind to the  heart, and make that a  quick  highway, you know, a quick ride.  Q: How are organizations using EI successfully, from your  experience?  A: I think that the organizations that us-- that are able to use EI successfully are  those that are aware of what we call, um,  the shadow  side of their  organization or the  dark side of the organization. And they're  able to see what the conflicts are. They're  able  to look them  straight in  the eye. They're able to look at them and see  them  and  say, "Okay, this is  what  is. This is where  we are. And here's  where we want to go."  And to  be able to transform the anxiety the, the fear, the disappointment, the anger,  to use it as a positive force to make  change. And, and those organizations  continually use it, and it's not just words, it's, it's, everybody in the organization  is  excited.   There's buy-in. People can do it the way they  believe is the right way. And  they feel that they're  empowered.   That's just the beginning though,  you know. I  mean  that's only a piece of really what  I  want to say. It got  too heady.  Q: Focus in on  narrower  examples.  (OFFSTAGE)  A: We--   For example, our  company's been working  with a franchise  organization  that, um, from the very top, corporately to, to everyone  in that franchise, to support  them in making a paradigm shift.   Now how do you make that happen when people  are from  different cultures?   They're from  different  points of view. There's  executives and there's mechanics and there's...   I mean how do you do the same kind of work with different kinds of people who have different educations?   So the way this organizations! been able to do it is by being authentic, by being honest, by dealing with all the conflicts -- they're right out front.   And by allowing people to  come to  their own conclusions, rather than....  (OFFSTAGE) Q:   Talk about how this particular company saw the successful coalescing of different people coming together through EI. A:   We have the great mis--   the great fortune and privilege. A:   —   Our organization is privileged, uh, tremendously privileged and honored to work with a franchise organization in America that, um, has people from all different

places,  different points of view, different historical  backgrounds, different  educational  backgrounds. And they accepted  our methodology as a way to  go  through the entire organization, whether it was a franchisee, um, the corporate  person, um, the trainers, everyone in the organization. So they were willing to look  at the issues straight on. They were  looking at the conflicts between the franchisees  and the corporate  people. They were looking at people's differences. They were  able to discuss  it  in an honest way.   And so, so they  were willing to take the anger,  the disappointments, the, um, the-- well, the lack of education,  whatever it might be.  Look at it. Feel it. And transform it. Uh, they  were  able to train  their managers to,  uh, deliver the training to their  own people, so we  not only provided EI to  the  audience  in terms of the top people, but we,  we  transferred the knowledge to them,  to train  their own people.   So now it's in  the organization.   It's still in the process of  being  looked at to, you know, see how much it worked. We, we  don't  have a  longitudinal study or anything like that yet, but we do know that when I see those  people they love me and I love them.   And I don't care who they are in the  organization, but the--   if I've met them once, I feel like I've known them forever.  And so to me it's the beginning of a success.   We can't really report on the true success for a longer time. Q:   How does an organization approach the consultant?   Does it require a smart  executive who says “We’ve got problems here.   I wonder if this approach might  work?”   Who is it that recognized something is amiss? A:   Um, um, I could speak of how we do, how we get some of our opportunities. Um, we do some marketing.   People know about us.   There's word-of-mouth.   But somebody in the organization is yearning for something.   Someone in the organization is anxious, is desperate for something to occur.   They don't want to leave their organization -- they love their company -- but something is not working right.   Those are the people that we talk to, whether it be a training director, an operations manager, uh, a CEO.   It's, it's rarely   a CEO that will approach us and say--   they usually send somebody to find out about us.   So those people talk to many different consultants and many different organizations and they wait to see if they can find somebody who they feel safe with.   And I think the minute they believe what the, what the consultant is saying, or the salesperson is saying, and they see it demonstrated rather than talked about, then the next step gets taken.   But in, and with EI, unless it's demonstrated by the person who's trying to sell it, or trying to talk about it, how can anybody trust it?  Q:   Is  that  because.....?

EMOTIONAL INTELLIGENCE PROJECT INTERVIEW WITH JUDITH ORLOFF  Q: __... come from a background of the linear way — “we  have statistics that  prove this.” Is El different enough from that kind of analysis that it requires  some kind of special sensitivity in people to accept?  JO: We believe that  most  people respond to the unspoken  words  that  people say.   Words are only ten percent of a communication. | mean  we all  know that. Q:   Would  you  say  that emotional intelligence  is  basically a  kind  of  maturity?

JO: Um, |, I, | think that children, from  the  time they're born, have emotional  intelligence, and then they lose it as their parents teach them what the appropriate way to behave is.   And they lose it because they have to to survive in their  families. And | believe  so many people  are accepting  emotional  intelligence today because it's a mem--   they, they  remember  what  it was like when they felt good. They remember  what it was like when  they could  be  who they really  were. And we  just have to learn  how to be who we  are, and not act it out. A lot of people  believe that when you have a feeling,  you should share it.   And that was the eighties.   Uh,   and that was fun.   | mean that was really fun,   but a lot of it was very inappropriate.   Uh, today,  uh, we believe that we want you to have every feeling that's possibly available to humans, whether it be the most deep sadness and despair   that  you have at that moment, to the   most   joyful, wonderful,   exhilarating, uh,  experiences you could possibly imagine.   However, we believe that as being a fair witness to those feelings it's what, is what, is what's relevant in emotional intelligence.   Being able to see what you feel, take a look at it, experience it fully, and share what's appropriate in the situation, and to--   that may take the maturity.   But being emotionally, uh, aware is not--   it doesn't  take the maturity.   It's knowing how to use the data from what you're experiencing in a situation for the highest good, that's what we believe takes  the  most  maturity. And there's a   lot of  talk about  people mistising  emotional  intelligence,   so they can manipulate situations.   We don't see that working very well, um, because once you're truly emotionally aware, it's very difficult to go against what you believe is the right thing to do.   Very difficult. Q:   _   Is it ever possible,   in the corporate world, to find a situation where there’s an ethical conflict if you’re using your emotional intelligence? JO:   Um, in, in corporate America people still believe, even those that tend  to become emotionally literate that they have to be careful.   And that may be true.   And sometimes it,   it does interfere with what you believe is right.   And  so what we have discovered that one-one of the benefits or non-benefits of  growing emotionally in an organization is many people leave.   If you become emotionally intelligent you might choose to do something else than stay in  the, in the job you're in, because it might not be meaningful enough.   We hope and we, we, we ask organizations to consider this very carefully, to allow people to share what's really true for them, and to make jobs more meaningful for people, because most people don't want to leave their jobs   -- they want to be able to grow in their organizations, and they want to be heard.   They want to be seen and heard and add value.   We've never met

anyone that doesn't want to make a difference, ever, once  they tell the truth about it. Everyone | know  wants to make a difference, and  that goes from  the very bottom to the very top in organizations. The question  is  how does  my wanting to make a difference interfere with your wanting to make a  difference,  and does that  wanting to make a difference interfere with revenue and needs? And how to bring that  all together in a way that works.  | think when we can do  that, we won't  be  losing top talent. So we  have a,   uh, uh, an education process that is just beginning in corporate America. It's just  beginning. We've only seen the tip of  the iceberg. JO: One of the  most valuable  aspects of  being emotionally intelligent is  you-- it's uh-- Is once you understand what's going on inside of  you,  you  could stop yourself in the middle  of anything, just by will, and  shift it to  something that's  going to be of more value to you  and  the  people around you,  and  that skill is being able to come into the present moment and leave  the  past that you're reacting to, and come right here, right now, wherever you  are, and deal with the situation as it needs to  be dealt with,   not as you used  to deal with it. And we think  that that, that skill in itself,  will create more  productivity, more, more love, even though  that may not be ready to say that  for  the workplace, but certainly more loving feelings and  more generosity of  spirit and  more courage. Q: Do we need to think  about  developing  our  emotional intelligence on  a  Monday, a Wednesday,  Friday? Once a month?   How do we  approach  this  new idea  of  getting smarter? TTT Wkbk 05.28.98  Right Brain/  Left  Brain  For some time it has been known that the  brain is divided into  two sides, left and  right. It has also been known that if  damage  is done to the left side of the brain,  the right side of the body tends to become  paralyzed and, correspondingly, that if  damage is done to the right side of the  brain,  the  left side of the body tends to become paralyzed. In other words, each  side of your brain  controls the opposite  side of  your body.  The recent research of  Professor Robert Ornstein  of the University of California has  thrown more light on the  different activities handled by each side of the brain. Starting  with the realization that  the two halves of the  brain are biologically similar and can  more realistically be thought of as two identical  brains working in  harmony, rather  than as one brain divided  into  two, Professor Ornstein decided to  find out if each of our separate brains handles different intellectual  activities in addition to  the different  physical  activities.  His findings  were both  surprising and significant. In general  the  left  brain handles  the  following mental activities:   mathematics, language, linear and  sequential information,  logic,  analysis, writing, reading, and  other  similar  activities.  The right side of the  brain  handles very different activities: imagination, color,  graphics,  music,  rhythm, daydreaming,  holistic  thinking and other  similar  activities.  Ornstein also found that people who had been trained  to use one  side of  their  brain  more  or less exclusively  were  relatively unable to use the  other side, both  in  general  and in those  special  situations where  the  activities  specifically related  to the  other  side  were particularly needed.  Even  more significant,  he  found that when  the  “weaker”  of the two brains  was  stimulated  and  encouraged  to work in cooperation  with the stronger  side, the end  result  was a great increase in overall  ability and effectiveness.  Tony  Buzan,  Make  The Most of Your Mind  © Educational Discoveries,  Inc. 3 05.28.98

TIT Wkbk 05.28.98  Triune Brain  The development of the Triune Brain Model  in 1952 has provided great insight into  our behavior, ability to learn, and emotional IQ. Dr. Paul MacLean,  chief of the  Laboratory for Brain Evolution and Behavior at the National Institute  for  Mental  Health in Bethesda, Maryland, created  the Triune Brain  Model,  which delineates three  functional brain regions.  MacLean has identified three major layers or “brains,” which were established  successively in response to evolutionary need. They are the reptilian system,  the limbic system,  and the neocortex. Each layer is  geared toward more  or less separate functions,  but  all three  layers interact substantially.  A preliminary way  of  looking at this is to  compare the three  layers with three  brothers living under one roof. The oldest  brother, the reptilian system, is in charge  of maintenance. This includes providing  food and  waste  disposal and  attending to  general security and comfort. Most of his  behaviors are automatic and ritualistic, and  he strongly resists change. He does not use  language, though in some  ways he can  respond  to  it.  The second brother, representing  the limbic system, feels deeply. He  monitors  emotion and plays a significant role in  remembering  new  information and organizing  events. He is concerned to  some  extent with self-defense through fight  or  flight. He  also  tries  to  ©  Educational Discoveries,  Inc. Po 05.28.98

TTT Wkbk 05.28.98  maintain balance between the oldest and the youngest by keeping the oldest brother  from totally dominating the family and by serving as a conscience.  The youngest and largest of the brothers is the neocortex. He is creative, can use  language, compose music, and engage in very complex analysis. He is capable of formal operational or abstract thought, can anticipate and plan for the future,  and is, in general, very intelligent.  Each brother is involved to some extent in the behavior and decisions of the other. They can be supportive of each other. They can also be in conflict. The oldest brothers  are most likely to dominate when threat is perceived, because then the top priority is  safety and survival. Working together, however, they can successfully deal with quite  extraordinary challenges.  © Educational Discoveries, Inc.   6   05.28.98

TIT Wkbk 05.28.98  Our Ancestral Brain — The Reptilian Complex  The reptilian brain consists largely of the brain stem, the mid-brain, and the reticular activating system. Its purpose is closely related to actual physical survival and overall maintenance of the body. Digestion, reproduction, circulation, breathing, and the execution of the “fight or flight” response in stress are all primarily located in this system. It plays a crucial role in establishing home territory, aggression, reproduction, social dominance, and social hierarchy. Self-preservation, activities of hunting,  foraging, hoarding and mating are also centered here. These reptilian behaviors are  evident in human beings: Territoriality  We defend our property both in the physical and abstract sense of ownership, as  my country,” “my room,” and “my  »  evidenced by the terms “my house,” “my family,  chair.” Note the way that students will pick a seat on the first day of class and automatically sit in that seat for the remainder of the term.  Nesting  Behaviors  These are often revealed in the way we fix up the house, decorate it, prepare it for our  personal use, and so on. It is, for instance, the place in which we rear our young, so we  attach importance to having enough space , storage and supplies, appropriate colors,  etc.  © Educational Discoveries, Inc.   7   05.28.98

TIT Wkbk 05.28.98  Maintaining Social Hierarchies  Despite ostensible commitment to democratic processes, most organizations are based  on what have been called “dominance hierarchies.” The dominance derives from such  factors as perceived biological,  intellectual, social or  physical superiority.  “Preening” or Ritualistic Display  We do what makes us “stand out” and attract attention, characterized by the sense of  “look at me,  I  am unique.”  Flocking Behavior  Flocking is closely linked to social conformity and is found everywhere. In schools we  can observe it in groups of students socializing together, perhaps being identified by common hairstyles, clothing, acceptable behaviors determined by “in group” standards,  and so forth.  © Educational Discoveries, Inc.   §   05.28.98

TTT Wkbk 05.28.98  The Guardian at the Gate — The Limbic  System  The limbic system is the second and next oldest brain to evolve. It is thought to have developed between 200 to 300 million years ago. It governs the primary centers of  emotion - the formation of long term memory, short term memory, conditioned reflexes and attention, as well as metabolism, the immune system and the hormonal system.   The limbic system is also involved in primal activities related to food and sex, particularly having to do with our sense of smell and bonding needs, and activities  related to expression and mediation of emotions and feelings, including emotions linked to family attachment and bringing up our young.   These protective, loving feelings become increasingly complex as the limbic system and the neocortex or “third  brain” link up. The limbic system functions as the regulator of emotions and is also essential to  memory.   According to MacLean, subjectively, “something doesn’t exist unless it’s tied up with emotion.”   He contends that memory is impossible without emotion of some  kind, that emotion energizes memory. Personally, we can recognize our facility at  remembering events that are emotionally charged. D.A. Rappaport has provided  research to indicate that emotions may very well be the medium through which memory patterns are organized. Memory of cognitive material can be heightened when structured within an emotional context or in such a way as to elicit an emotional  response.  Greater flexibility of thinking and feeling abilities becomes available through processes that involve the emotions in the learning experience. Emotional repertoire can be  © Educational Discoveries, Inc.   G   05.28.98

TIT Wkbk 05.28.98  expanded through creative stories and assignments that focus on the subtle emotions.  Games or  activities that play with emotional context encourage experiences within various  emotional contexts. Providing students with the opportunity to express and  understand emotions is one of the greatest tools for expanding emotional and  intellectual IQ.  The language of expression used by both the limbic and reptilian brain systems is  emotive and not linguistic. Current research suggests that the limbic brain regulates  much more of our thinking and behavior than we have realized in the past. The experience of feeling positive about learning is, in itself, a stimulus to encourage  excitement  about  the learning process. When sensory input has a positive  emotional  reference point, the brain triggers the release of a pleasing opiate type of chemical that  creates a state of heightened awareness  and well-being.  Within this state, learning becomes  pleasurable  and is accomplished with greater ease. Physiologically, this can explain the  benefits of using  music  to  develop an optimum  learning state and assist in  memory enhancement.  In the cycle of interaction between the inner and outer worlds, the limbic system represents  an  essential link between mind and body. We receive as many as a million sensory impressions each minute,  but only a select few reach our  conscious  attention in the  neocortex. The  limbic system acts as  a switchboard,  reading the  sensations from the body and  deciding which to send on to  the  neocortex  for expanded awareness  and  action. Through this editing process, the limbic system has a significant role in  directing our conscious thought.  © Educational Discoveries,  Ine. 10 05.28.98

TTT Wkbk 05.28.98  Our “Thinking” Brain — The Neocortex  Finally, over the limbic brain lies the neocortex, or “thinking cap,” the convoluted mass of gray matter that evolved with such rapidity in just the last million years to produce homo sapiens. We share the neocortex with higher mammals such as chimpanzees, dolphins, and whales. The neocortex constitutes 80% of the total brain matter in the human brain, as well as most of the brain’s thinking cortex. It is the outer portion of our brain and is approximately the size of a newspaper page crumpled together. It is divided anatomically into two hemispheres, which are loosely referred to as the left and right hemispheres. The neocortex makes language, including speech and writing, possible; in that sense, it is different from the other two “brains.” Because the neocortex contains about 70% of the brain’s approximately 100 billion neurons, it controls high level thought processes such as logic, creative thought, language processing and the integration of sensory information. It renders logical and formal operational thinking possible and allows us to see ahead and plan for the future. In addition, taking place in these cerebral hemispheres are all the processes concerning vision, hearing, body sensation, intentional motor control, purposeful behavior, and non-verbal ideation. The neocortex includes the frontal lobes of the brain and is also responsible for altruism, compassion, pattern recognition and high level  physical/mental coordination.  The prefrontal cortex is that region of the neocortex inside our foreheads. Even though  the removal of the prefrontal cortex results in no apparent change in IQ as we now measure it, it  © Educational Discoveries, Inc.   rf7   05.28.98

TTT Wkbk 05.28.98  appears to be largely responsible for a wide range of abilities that neuro-psychologists call “adaptive behaviors.” These include planning, analysis, sequencing, and learning from errors, as well as the inhibition of inappropriate responses and the capacity for abstraction. Thus, increased compassion and empathy become possible because we can  acquire the cognitive capacity   to “put ourselves in another’s shoes.” pacity  The creative thought process incorporates the limbic brain with the right and left regions of the neocortex, joining the spark of the “Aha!” illumination with the cognitive and intuitive intelligence of the neocortex. When we strengthen the neural  pathways between brain centers, future  communications ability strengthens. Brain-  center bridging activities have been observed to develop pathways to greater intelligence and thinking   potential and even reduce the time required for the brain to  make future connections. Using the creative arts to facilitate cognitive instruction  provides an opportunity for information to bridge between the logic and intuitive  areas of the neocortex.  Under stressful situations, thought processing tends to downshift into the survival- oriented reptilian brain functions or the emotional limbic system. When behavior is limited to these areas alone, significant input from the logical and abstract neocortex and the frontal lobes may be eliminated. Thinking becomes highly limited when access  to these brain  regions is blocked, and  the  integration  of the  abilities  and functions of  the whole  brain  cannot occur.  © Educational Discoveries,  Inc.   0. 2 05.28.98

TTT Wkbk 05.28.98  Setting the Context  The context in which learning occurs determines its level of success.   A context is an  environment. It is also a model, and a way of being. It is the most important initial  aspect for learning.  In childhood, the way a parent interacts with a child determines, to a large degree, the  behavior of the child. In a classroom, an instructor’s behavior will model the way the  learner will respond to openness, connection, humor, spontaneity and flexibility.  When an instructor teaches with this context, it is imprinted and transferred to the  learner.  Those  very qualities will make learning fast,  easy  and permanent.  There are many elements in a positive context for learning, including the physical  environment and the emotional attitudes of the instructor and the students.   The physical space needs to be bright, well-lit and alive with natural plants, color, artwork, etc. The emotional space is even more powerful  in terms of setting  context. Whereas  it is possible to learn in a bare, stark room, it is not possible for any true learning to  occur  when fear is present.  Some of the criteria  for a context  without fear include demonstrating equality  among instructors and learners,  permission to  make mistakes, and valuing  all participation,  even that which can be deemed disruptive.   Equality without fear creates a quality  environment  where learning  can  occur  © Educational Discoveries, Inc.   rfIG   05.28.98

TIT Wkbk 05.28.98  Space  Space as a form in presentations is the physical and emotional environment where the presenter and listeners interact. Physical aspects include the temperature, lighting, visuals like color and signage, sound and music, and the seating  arrangement for the  listeners in the presentation. The emotional space of the room from the perspective of the  presenter  includes his or her appearance, the manner in  which questions are received and responded to, the use of humor, the mode of directions, either command  or share,  and the openness or closeness of the space.  Educational Discoveries, Inc. r 6 05.28.98

TTT Wkbk 05.28.98  Enrollment  Enrollment is the process by which people become participants in a program. A typical enrollment includes introducing the instructor and participants, and discussing what’s going to be done and why. Enrollment creates the context for learning. Enrollment  also gets people interested in doing what you are doing or supporting your idea or  action.  By starting with questions that addresses the common experience of the participants,  the instructor immediately gets people involved in a physical way. The more multi-  sensory and participatory the course activities are, the more learning happens. Note that the questions draw out not only those who are familiar with the topic, but also those who are not. And the last question brings everyone together to agree that their  understanding of the subject can   use improvement. The instructor’s hand is also  raised, In that way the instructor and all the participants are treated as equals. These  questions set the context of inclusion, participation, and equality.  © Educational Discoveries, Inc.   (   7   05.28.98

TIT Wkbk 05.28.98  Common  Ground  Participants enter programs with a wide variety of abilities and experience. This is an  advantage when the learning activities are group interactive types. And to be effective  for everyone, the course must begin at a point where everyone can be included. We call this point “common ground.” Common ground refers to the content or experiences  shared by participants that give each one a sense of belonging to the group. For  example, imagine a seminar on basic accounting with a diverse audience that includes a  trainer from Saudi Arabia, a dentist from Denver, and a chief accountant from a major corporation. The seminar starts, and everyone is asked  to get comfortable,  relax,  close  their eyes,  and listen to, “When  you were a child...” Everyone has the common  experience of getting comfortable and closing their eyes, and whatever their background, everyone had a childhood. These common experiences, when recalled,  together creates for the  participants a sense of belonging with the  group. Common  ground is established.  © Educational Discoveries, Inc. TIT Wkbk 05.28.98  Gradient  Any mischievous youngster who’s ever caught a frog and decided to cook it has  learned a lesson about gradient. This lesson is simple-if the water is too hot, the frog  will jump out. To cook   a   live frog, start it in cold water and warm it up slowly. The frog won’t notice the increase, and will stay in the pot. The same is true in class: start with low intensity and warm it up slowly. Otherwise the student’s attention, like the  frog, will leave.  In a learning environment, gradient refers to the level of intensity and commitment required to participate in a given exercise or learning experience. Attending a lecture on the presidential election is low gradient when compared to watching a demonstration on making paper airplanes. A learning segment has higher gradient if  the content is more complex or if the personal interaction required is more involved or  intimate. Also, when participants are ready for more complex content or more interaction, one can say that they are at a higher gradient. In general, the higher the gradient the greater  the learning.  The presenter’s personal gradient needs to match the level of the material presented.  What emotions, personal information, and interactions with the participants are  appropriate, and when?  © Educational Discoveries, Inc.   7   G   05.28.98

TIT Wkbk 05.28.98  Ritual  At all major sporting events, the national anthem is played to signify to the crowd that the event is ready to begin. The national anthem has common ground for everyone there.   It evokes emotion and creates a communal feeling among all the fans. Creating beginnings and endings, and connecting the participants to each other is the essence of  rituals. In program design, a ritual is a formal procedure that, when repeated, connects  to deep parts of the brain, especially the reptilian brain. The reptilian brain is where instinctual survival behavior patterns reside. Rituals and habits are in the realm of the  reptilian brain.  © Educational Discoveries, Inc.   20   05.28.98

TIT Wkbk 05.28.98  Discovery  People learn at a deeper level and remember more when they have the opportunity to  discover the information instead of just being told. Design and delivery that includes  discovery asks more and tells less. Asking “fill-in-the-blanks” type questions increases  participation and stimulates creativity. Through participation in exercises designed to evoke emotional experiences, people invariably discover things about themselves and  the experience creates new behaviors. Discovery makes information more relevant,  personal and memorable.  © Educational Discoveries, Inc.   a   05.28.98

TTT Wkbk 05.28.98  Reaction  What Is It?  Reaction is a loss of personal power. It is an unconscious or past response to a  present situation. Because we develop unconscious patterns of behavior, we often  do not recognize when the outside situation changes. We keep doing things we  did for survival and protection, even when they are not appropriate in the  present.  Reaction is the way we learned to survive in our families. We developed them  initially to cover up those feelings which were unacceptable to express.   The way we act to cover those feelings becomes the reaction. When we live in our  reactions now, we are creating our lives and our relationships from the past,  rather than from the present.  Reaction is also a wonderful  opportunity  for freedom. If  you stay open  to  learning while in reaction, you can choose a different behavior right in the middle of it. That choice changes the pattern.  You can expect to have the opportunity to experience reaction  and change a pattern often during the Train-The-Trainer.  © Educational Discoveries, Inc.   2s   05.28.98

TIT Wkbk 05.28.98  How can you tell if you are “In Reaction”?  A reaction does not have to look a certain way. In fact, it will not. Since it is a learned  behavior based on  our individual interpretations  of how we  were supposed to be in our  families, a reaction manifests itself differently for everyone.   But here are some  unmistakable clues that you may be “in reaction”:  when your body feels tight and anxious, not present  whenever you think that what you feel is about someone else  when your mind will not shut up  when your thoughts relate to the past or the future, not the present  when you are hiding or numb, felling foggy or confused whenever there is a judgment (good or bad) whenever you feel compelled to act or not act  whenever you have accumulated. good evidence and can prove beyond a shadow of a doubt that you are right  when events appear to be coming at you ~ you feel like a  victim, a victimizer, and a judge all at the same time  Good Afternoon  Ladies  and  Gentlemen  © Educational Discoveries, Inc.   24   05.28.98

TIT Wkbk 05.28.98  How to Handle  Questions  Questions  from the audience create an opportunity to enroll the whole room,  deepen connection, and reinforce learning. They keep  the space alive with  participation.  When people ask a question, think of  it as if they were  doing you a favor. Use  the F.A.V.O.R. method.  Feel Feel your feelings. This is your clue  to what the  questioner is  feeling. Put yourself in  their place. Determine the emotion that is  the source of the  question. Notice if you have any judgments  about  the question.  A- Ask or   Acknowledge the  emotion in a non-threatening way  by  exaggeration, Acknowledge — humor, or  direct recognition. Ask a question  to clarify the  real  question and confirm that you have received the same emotion that  has been sent.  V - Validate Validate the question and  the questioner. This does not mean you  have to agree with them. You are letting  them know that you’ve  heard them and understand their  concern without judgment.  Typical responses are “I Understand,” “I know what  you mean,”  “T’ve felt  that way  myself.”  O- Open Open the space by  including the  other  people in the  room. Ask,  “Who else  bas or has had  this  feeling,  experience, or  question?” You  are giving the  questioner  time to  realize that he/she is not  alone.  The questioner is also  being given  time to reexamine  the question and  its  deeper implications.  R - Return Return  to  the  questioner. Relate  your experience,  knowledge,  or expertise. The Model for Change  eee  10  10 Keys to   Navigating   Through Change Step   |   - Decision to Change  The Decision to Change can come from   a   voluntary internal decision, but is often forced from external sources. Either way, this is the point at which you recognize  the need to change and leave the status quo. It is not necessary to like it, however,  the decision will be easier if there is a clear Vision, strong Intention, and Support to carry it through. If the decision has been thrust upon you, it will help to spend the  time necessary to accept and align internally with the Decision to Change.  Step 2 - Resistance—Order & Chaos  Resistance is the natural response to any Decision to Change. It contains the  balance of Order—-the desire to stay with what you know, and Chaos—the need and desire to move forward to the unknown.  The interaction of Order and Chaos creates agitation and often is uncomfortable. The  temptation is strong here to deny or try to overcome one or the other. Neither  should be viewed as “good” or “bad.” Embracing the initial paradox of Resistance  gives the necessary strength and clarity to accomplish the change. educational   discoveries   inc

The Model for Change  |  Step 3 - Choice Point  After staying in the discomfort of Order and Chaos, eventually something has to give-you move to a Choice Point. This is your first critical moment of choice since your Decision to Change. How you have dealt with Resistance has a great influence on the choice here. You   will either proactively move forward on your intended path of change or reactively move toward illusion. The   illusory path is both tricky and com- pelling. Usually on the reactive path you will claim that you are moving toward  change, while upholding an internal commitment to the past.  Step 4 - Reactive Change-Sea of Illusion  Ilusion is both powerful and tricky-you think and act as if you are on the right path  to change, but it’s deceptive-you are really stuck in the past.   You know the past does not work. If the past was workable, there would be no need to change in the  first place. Supporting someone else in this place is always very difficult, because  they are telling themselves either that the change wasn’t necessary or that they  have already achieved it. Living in self-deception eventually erodes your self-esteem  and ultimately leads to a Crisis. educational   discoveries   inc

The Model for Change  12  Step 5 - Crisis  Crisis is the inevitable result of consistently choosing Illusion, because you cannot see what you are doing. Crisis can be viewed as nature’s wake-up call to get back on  track. It is a great opportunity to jump immediately to the path of proactive  change-to recommit to the change and mean it this time. Crisis also represents danger, for to continue in denial and Illusion will cause further escalated levels of decay.  Step 6 - Proactive Change—Chaos of Creation  This is the decision to risk the unknown and do something new-—to stay with your intention to change.   The Chaos of Creation is usually intense and emotional because  although you've decided what you are going to do, you still do not know how you  will do it. Chaos happens because you get pulled in many directions while looking for new success patterns. Creation happens when you are committed to making new  decisions and choosing new behaviors.  The major distinction between Chaos of Creation and Illusion is that in Chaos, people seek true Support, they take Support when given, and they are always seeking new information. In Illusion, people   will be defensive and feel threatened. All change involves willingness to risk, however, Chaos of Creation is not to be viewed as “risky.” Even though lots of people are risking here, they are self-aware, have a clear objec-  tive, and lots of Support, so that mistakes and corrections can happen quickly. educational   discoveries   inc

The Model for Change  Step 7 - Choice   Point   Two-Intention and Support  Chaos of Creation is extremely uncomfortable. To stay in the discomfort requires a very clear Vision, strong Intention, and Support.While in Chaos, it is very easy to lose sight of your Vision. Having people who know your Intention and Vision will help you stay on track through difficult times. Inevitably, this discomfort creates a temptation  to return to the tried and true—the past—the Sea of Illusion. After   living in the Chaos  of Creation for what usually seems like a long time, another Choice Point emerges. This is the point at which you choose either to return to the past (Illusion) or to move closer to your Vision by choosing Freedom.  Step 8 - Freedom and Personal Responsibility  Seeing yourself as the source of your experience is the most powerful position available to you, because you give up excuses and blame for why things worked out  or didn’t work out.   This represents a new paradigm for most people, because you  literally change the way you see things.   The same situation or data means something different to you than it did before. You see the past differently-you see it more as  the result of your knowledge and choices then. You don’t judge yourself for how  you were, or are, nor do you throw up your arms or shrug your shoulders as if the  mistakes didn’t matter.   You are more committed to correcting mistakes than judging  yourself or others for them. Compassion for yourself and others is essential here. Without it, there is no safety to be vulnerable and to talk honestly. Now, new  solutions to old problems can happen easily.  13  educational   discoveries   inc

The Model for Change  14  Step 9 - Breakthrough  This is the last critical point before achieving your Vision. You   are ninety-eight per  cent of the way to your dream, and all of a sudden, you realize that it doesn’t feel, look, or seem like what you thought it would. In other words, it doesn’t fit your pictures of what you thought it would be like. You may want to give up or abandon the entire effort. There   is usually some final Illusion you are holding onto about yourself or your Vision.   What   is critical here is to remember your decision and  Intention and stay Congruent using everything you have learned so far. It is inevitable  and okay that things don’t look and feel as expected. If you continue to risk the  unknown, you will have continued Breakthroughs and will get closer and more connected to your Vision.  Step   10 -   Purpose,   Vision, Mission, and Objectives  As you grow in this process, often the Vision you   began the process with will evolve  and become   clearer. You may even realize that what had been your Vision might be  your Mission, or even one of your Objectives along the path to your Vision.   Also, the  closer you live to your Vision, you will experience inevitably your Purpose. As you  follow your proactive path to change, you will sense your Purpose permeating  everything you do. You   will experience that your Vision is the picture of your Purpose  brought to life.  educational   discoveries   inc

Introduction  Whenever people make a change  in how  they behave, they go through a process that  follows a path to a new  vision of themselves.  That process  is a challenging one  no matter  what the change is and no matter who’s making it.   Whatever the setting and whoev- er the person, knowledge of the change process is essential to managing the stress and chaos that change brings.   When we make a change we rewire  our  point  of view and how  we  experience a given  situation.  That rewiring confuses our  operating  pat-  tern, and takes us out of our comfort zone.  Successful  change has a pattern.   We  call  that  pattern the Model for Change© and it has 10  steps.

The Model  for Change©  Program Overview  Audience  This two-day program is designed for managers (defined as those who manage others) of teams or organizations that are changing due to the decisions of management and/or  external  factors.  Why this Program is Different  Change  is inevitable.  When individuals understand the internal process of change, they  can  manage and communicate more effectively, and support others so they see change as  an opportunity instead of fearing it. Most other  change processes focus on  the  external  aspects of change.  Program Foundations  1.   Effective managers are able to demonstrate leadership and support others who are in the process of change  up, down and across the  organization.  2.   Employees who understand their internal process of change are more effective at their  jobs, because they are more successful in aligning themselves to the changes around  them.  3.   When employees in changing environments are successful in aligning themselves to change, their team or organization is more effective in achieving its goals.  Learning Objectives  Through participating in this training, managers will:  1.   Take personal responsibility for aligning their vision and intention with the  organization’s change.  2.   Consciously choose the environment they want to create, and provide leadership for  others.  3.   Clarify their own intention, vision and choices within the changing environment.  4.   Recognize where they and others are in the change process.  5.   Effectively manage, communicate and support the organization’s desired change. Model for Change Improvisation Activity  Content:  The Model for Change is a map of the change process that individuals experience. This  model has 8 steps, which participants can use like a roadmap. The model gives participants a common language and understanding, which they can use to predict their own behavior and the behavior of others in change up, down and across the organization.  e   #1 Decision to Change: A decision to change is made. In order to create  successful change two elements are critical to the process: vision and intention. e   #2 Resistance: Resistance occurs when a decision to change has been made. Frequently, the decision to change and the resistance are equally balanced. This  creates agitation. ©   #3 Choice Point: This occurs when the agitation is strong enough. The old way  of operating is experienced simultaneously with new ways of operating and new  information. This precedes any change in behavior or new learning. Individuals  are at a choice point to either choose the past or choose to go forward into the  unknown.  e   #4 Illusion: Being in illusion is choosing the past. This can be comfortable and familiar, and it always involves faulty thinking.  e   #5 Creating a Crisis: If individuals choose the status quo, they eventually create a crisis. Choosing the past does not work—that’s why they made a   decision to change. Crisis does not occur suddenly. Prior to any crisis there are many  opportunities to choose the change. If the old behaviors are continued, there are  a  a   EDUCATIONAL DISCOVERIES  PART OF   THE   PROVANT   BOUUTION  ©2001   5   10.12.01

many signs that the situation is eroding. The purpose of   the crisis is to wake individuals up, so they can be responsible and make the  changes they  have  committed to.  e   #6 The Chaos of Creation: If individuals choose the unknown, they  move  into  the chaos of creation. Chaos  is being open to new information while feeling  uncomfortable and unsure. People learn and experience new  information that was hidden and protected by their old patterns. At the  same time  they know and  experience the familiar ways. They are now “in paradox”—experiencing two  seeming  opposites  simultaneously.  Paradox allows for conscious  choice of new  thinking and behavior. In creation people choose a new reality by the focus of  their will. Another choice point occurs. Individuals can continue with their new choices or retreat again into old patterns. The support of peers and/or outside  helpers is now critical.  e #7 Responsibility: People are  the source of their experience. Individuals change  the way they see. They change how they operate.  e   #8 Breakthrough: As people continue, often another choice point occurs.  Individuals often stop just short of the goal. Things are  not  as they  pictured  they  would be. They hesitate. If people stay on course, they  apply  everything  they  have  learned to break through into integrity and unimpaired ability. They are true to  their vision and intention. The decision needs a clear  vigion, strong intention and support to carry it through.  Your inner resistance to the change hits!   You desire to go back to what you know.   In order for resistance to occur, there must be an equal balance of order and chaos.   Order repre-  serits the familiar-what was; chaos represents the new-the unknown.  The interaction of order and chaos creates immense agitation. Order and chaos are nei-  ther wrong nor right and both are necessary for the change to occur. If the agitation gets strong enough, something   has to give.   You move to a choice  point—you will go one way or the other.  Choosing the past does not work.   If the past was workable there would   be no need to change in the first place.   Choosing the past results in illusion, a self-deception. You either deceive yourself into thinking that the change was not necessary, or that you have already  achieved it.   Self-deception eventually erodes your self-esteem.  When you choose illusion consistently, you often cannot see what you are doing.   You cre- ate a crisis which can wake you up to the change you need to make.   The crisis can be  ignored, which leads eventually to demise; or, it can shake you up enough to recommit to  the change, and mean it this time.  The other option is to risk the unknown and do something new; to stay with your intention to change.   This choice throws us into the chaos of creation.   ‘Chaos’ because you are pulled in opposite directions—you are in paradox, maintaining two seemingly opposite expe-  riences at once.   ‘Creation? because when you are in the unknown, you have the space to  choose new behaviors.   You need to learn to be able to simultaneously acknowledge the  past and create the future by staying with your decision to change. At this point, you need to remember  your decision  and  intention  and stay congruent,  using  everything  you  have  learned  go far. NONDUALITY IN ACTION  ii  Using Nonduality To Ameliorate Early Childhood Trauma: An Autoethnography  Nonduality in Action —  A Universal Healing Method  Judith Orloff  Abstract  The subject of this   autoethnographic study is twofold. The first part of this study explores  how early childhood trauma, whether emotional, physical ,   or sexual ,   can define the course of a  person’s future, leading to both physical and psychiatric disease. The second part expl ores a gap  in a foundational core therapeutic model that could be used universally with all modalities of  therapy, and potentially educational and social services training that could allow the healing of  the traumatized. Through the use of a relational mod el based on nonduality, a Buddhist non -  conceptual model of healing suffering, much of early childhood trauma caused by abusive  behavior of parents could be ameliorated.  This study is focused on a woman in the second half of the 20 th   century, with postpart um  depression and psychosis leading to a misdiagnosis which resulted in labels and inpatient  psychiatric hospitalization. This autoethnography is the story of how a survivor of early  childhood trauma achieved resilience and success   and applied nonduality i n a coaching,  therapeutic ,   and consultative practice.  Key Words: NONDUALITY, POSTPARTUM DEPRESSION, PSYCHOSIS, EARLY  CHILDHOOD   TRAUMA , RESILIENCY   COACHING, RELATIONAL THERAPY
