NONDUALITY IN ACTION   1  CHAPTER ONE: INTRODUCTION TO THE   STUDY  For the benefit of all is the only way I know to save my own life.   (Orloff, 2012, p.9)  In this study I investigate how early childhood trauma can define the course of a  person’s future, particularly women in the second half of the 20 th   century. T his study is  called for because there is a need for a foundational model that could be used universally  in conjunction with all models of therapy. Also needed is educational training that allows  for the healing of traumatized persons in a relational model   that could ameliorate much of  the early childhood trauma most of us experience. This introduction will explore trauma  within the theoretical framework of nonduality (Fenner, 2007 ) . Nonduality has been the  theoretical framework of my life for the past 12 ye ars as well as an integrated system of  thinking about the world, human experience ,   and early childhood trauma. Nonduality is  that which ,   while “fully accepting our finite and conditioned existence, we rest in a level  of consciousness that can’t be damaged   or degraded by the presence of any thought,  feeling ,   or sensation”   (p.2).  I have chosen autoethnography as my research approach because through this  lens I can share my healing process while looking at the larger ,   greater ,   socially relevant  issues of heal ing. It is my hope that it will inspire others to see themselves as okay just  the way they are. I believe it is from that perspective that transformation can occur.  This dissertation is the culmination of my search for liberation and freedom from  the   pain and lack of wellbeing brought on by a severely traumatic childhood. For much  of my life I believed I was the cause of my pain and that I deserved the negative

NONDUALITY IN ACTION   2  treatment from my parents. When I left home at 19   and moved to New York City, I   began  a spiritual journey that ultimately led me to Fielding Graduate University. Beginning  doctoral studies was a challenge in itself. During my studies I often asked myself ,   “ What  are you doing?” My answer and mantra each time has been a variant of kn owing I am  doing this work to save my own life through the healing and   sharing of nonduality,   for  the benefit of all , a   Buddhist non - conceptual practice. I call this nonduality in action.  It is my contention that nonduality   is one essential pathway to reve aling,  clarifying, and miti gating early childhood trauma.   Ira Glovinsky   stated the following   in a  person al communication:  I see trauma as not being reversible because they are real events that happened to  us. I am not sure you can make someth ing that ha ppened, not happen.   I do think  that therapy can help to manage the remnants of trauma, but I don’t see how you  can take the   trauma away . (August 2018)  Even so,   I   hope   this autoethnographical study has the opportunity to show how   it is  possible to   heal every day   and ,   while doing so ,   allow the brain to create new pathways  that take precedence over the old trauma - infused ones.  Background of the Study  Much of my life has   been a   continued   search to understand why my childhood  was so brutal and violent. Was I evil ,   as   my father   suggested   when   he was about to  physically   hurt me?   Of course   not. Was I “making him hurt me? ” ,   as my mother told  me? Of course not. Was I   just a “big mouth child” who deserved to be st opped?  Again, of course not. Well then, what could it be? I certainly believed he meant what he  said. I searched and searched to discover what I did to cause his behavior as my mother

NONDUALITY IN ACTION   3  told me.   I became an edu cator and psychotherapist with the outward reason to heal  others, but my deepest desire was to find the reason my family was so physically and  psychologically violent toward me.  I later discovered that my family’s behavior had many aspects to it, dependi ng  how it was viewed, such as   my father’s   myriad illnesses, including a heart condition,  diabetes, arthritis, possibly high cholesterol — and more that I do not know about — that  necessitated   my father   taking medication that changed his personality. They inclu ded  Seconal, Prednisone, opioids ,   and other heart and various pain medications. There was a  distanced relationship between my parents that was attributed to my father’s gambling  and relationships with other women (one of whom I met while living in New York ).  Both my parents used insults and name calling toward me when they were agitated.  Some of the names, such as “harlot,” verged on sexual aggression. I will elaborate   further  in my review of literature   in   C hapter   2   and   C hapter   4   of   my autoethnography.  Fo r the past   45   years I have been exploring therapeutic approaches to mitigate  early   childhood trauma. Childhood messages stay subliminally hidden, unknowingly  creating deeply reactive responses to situations that may unconsciously be reminiscent to  the pers on or group of what their childhood conditions were. Survival strategies learned  as children take center stage for the moment. The amygdala memories are expressed   as  an either/or way of thinking. These encapsulated and inaccess ible memories take over,  and   as   Jacobs (200 9 )   has discussed, one goes into   a “trance state.” A trauma survivor  cannot see what is occurring at that moment, but rather these experiences take the  survivor   unconsciously   back to the traumatic event as if it were happening in the present  moment. Working individually or with a group of children and adults, I have been able

NONDUALITY IN ACTION   4  to teach a process of self - awareness   that allows people to have countless choices rather  than succumb to a survival - based, either/or, trance approach of viewing the wor ld  (Jacobs ,   2009 ;   Orloff & Doubleday, 1991 ). Nonduality is the therapeutic modality I  discovered in 2009 while participating in two, year -   long programs and   6   years of  nonduality training with Peter Fenner, PhD. ,   a nonduality teacher from Australia ,   and  other spiritual teachers who use nonduality   as their modality.  Nonduality  Nonduality   is a Buddhist non - conceptua l   ( without feelings, thoughts ,   or   mental   concepts )  p rocess of   healing   suffering   that encompasses   the core essence of Buddhist, Hindu,  Jewish ,   and other religious practices. The roots of   n ondual awareness, as experienced on  the journey toward enlightenment, stretch deep into many ideologies throughout the  course of human history. These include Hindu Vedanta, most schools of Buddhism and  Taoism, mystical   Christianity, Judaism and Islam   ( Pren dergast, Fenne r   & Krystal,  (2003).   Non - dual awareness is experienced as the sense of a dissolved separate self and a  fresh sense of connectedness and oneness that encompasses the extraordinary and the  ordinary as one and the same without the need to contra st and compare.   ( Wilber, Engler  &   Brown, (1986),   Wilber , Engler & Brown   (1986)   asserted that oneness attributed to  nonduality   can be viewed as a complete integration of formlessness and form that  embraces all levels   of consciousness so that an individual can   enjoy all levels and let go  of attachment to   “ existence , ”   no matter how it   shows up.   In   essence ,   nonduality   as a  realization of who and what we are is a process where one comes to experience oneself  and others as   pure awareness   (Fenner, 2007). It sounds so esoteric, but it is really so

NONDUALITY IN ACTION   5  practical. Nonduality as a state of consciousness has the power to relieve and heal fears  of death in illness, fear of being alone in relationships ,   and fear of insanity.  In a prac tical sense,   n ondual practices can reeducate the brain to relax and,  through this relaxation, be an aid to the mind, allowing negative thoughts and feelings to  lose their power (Fenner, 2007). Blackstone (2006) described   nonduality   as the  experience of one ness with all that is.   She   stated the “essence of an individual’s being is  the same as, unified with, or dissolved in the essence of the cosmos” (p.26). When  Blackstone discusse d   “oneness , ”   she me ant   oneness with the entire universe . I take that  to mean   an experience of merging with what one is experiencing at that moment .  When I   was 28 years old and had taken LSD ,   I was on a cross - country trip with my  boyfriend and we were staying in a log cabin on the Klamath River in Oregon. The cabin  was rustic ,   with   a deer head hanging in the living room. We took the LSD and after a  while the wood in the cabin seemed to move and the deer head seemed to cry out to me. I  felt so ashamed that someone hung a deer head on the wall and couldn’t stand how I felt.  I went o utside toward the river. It was a very short walk, perhaps 50 to 75 yards.  What happened next created a new paradigm for me.   (See Michael Pollan’s book ,  h ttps://www.amazon.com/Change - Your Mind  ConsciousnessTranscendence/dp/1594204225 .   I   experienced the earth   breathing.   And, I  was walking on its body. Could I break the heart of the earth? Could I hurt the earth by  walking on it? Was I the earth? Was I   the broken heart I projected on the earth?   These  were the thoughts and questions I had at that moment of “oneness.”  It is a natural tendency   as we evolve emotionally and spiritually   to begin a radical inquiry  into the question of “who am I? ” Although I   have come to   live with   the illusion that I am

NONDUALITY IN ACTION   6  separate many times during a day, I have had enough moments of   n ondual experience s   to  trust the realization that I am not separat e and in fact nothing is.   Watching small children  begin their life in what I   obs erve,   and experience is   n onduality, in the sense that within an  hour or two they are experiencing what appears to be many emotions and states of being  without pretense, and then seeing them b egin to shift to a separate self,   used to be  exciting for me. No w, I recognize the possibility of teaching   that separateness is not  possible, but being unique is how we make our differences in the world.   This realization  can be used to look at the trauma of early chil dhood with a clear eye and   o pen   heart  simultaneousl y.   These were the thoughts and questions I had at that moment of  “oneness.” From that moment I recognized that the earth was alive. I know that may not  sound as profound as I experienced it, but that realization shifted how I treated all life.  The acid   wore off in a few hours, but my consciousness of that experience did not and  grew to include all sentient beings. Yet, I had not given up the experience of a separate  self until my work with nonduality.   I have had that experience   of oneness more and more  t hrough my work with nonduality   without drugs , and it has fortified my resolve and  mission to do this work at Fielding Graduate Universit y.  By exploring   nonduality   as a healing model that can reach across time and  culture, this study complements that whic h has come before me and fills a gap that will  encourage other scholars and professionals in their work with early childhood trauma.  We all deserve to be free to live a life of love.  Purpose of the Study  Without understanding emptiness, or   nonduality, it is not possible to cut the root of  human problems. NONDUALITY IN ACTION   7  My purpose is to bring to light   and to the mainstream   this   healing   process so that  individuals and groups can find a way to heal themselves   from   trauma - based childhood  hurts and wounds. Many different therapy models are working diligently to understand  and release trauma. Some of the pitfalls, in my opinion, are that man y of us do not wish  to risk projecting our hurt on our families and the external environment. We have learned  to be excessively   cautious   in how we speak of our experience.   S., S. H. (2010)   posit ed   the  dangers of political correctness are the dynamics that   underlie it   (p.17).   I use the term  political correctness   to mean   descriptive language, policies, or measures that are intended  to prevent offense or disadvantage to members of specific groups in society.   S., S. H.  (2010 )   clai med   there is a resultant self - destruction of the core processes in an  organization (p.48).  I experience that political correctness makes difficult and intimate conversations  awkward and abstract, and our resultant confusion allows for miscommunication and  easily creates a disabled cu lture, just as a family’s miscommunication can create a  disabled family. The limited language “allowed”   makes it very difficult to share an  experience of an individual’s reality. In so doing, the world is redefined (p.19 7).   Also, I  experience deep separation with those who have felt the everyday racist undertones of  our culture. I remember being in Paris in 1960 and hearing and   observing   how the  French   W hite people characterized and treated the Algerians in their midst .   I di d   n o t see  myself as part of that dynamic at the time. That is no longer true. The argument that, for  me, allows me to be silenced is that I will never know what it is like to be a person of  color in our   society,   and I will never be able to understand what   that pain is. However

NONDUALITY IN ACTION   8  true that may be, the resultant experience is separateness and continued trauma.   The  language and communication methods we presently use as efforts to create a bridge are  still complex and not clear at this time.  D eeply relevant to   my   a utoethnographical study is Jung’s work relating to a  shadow self. Jung (2001) asserted that o ver the course of our individual development the  repressed characteristics of ourselves coalesce to form the shadow, which he called the  “dark” side of our be ing. Our lack of self - awareness allows us to see negativity in others  rather than in ourselves.  Jung’s work has informed me during my tenure as a therapist and a student. His  work on the shadow self of each of us is another way of discussin g our projections on  others, our extreme judgments of others and, for this study   in particular, how trauma  occurs in a family through attempts to change a child’s experience from what is to what  the parent wants it to be. I will use the idea of the shadow   peripherally   as this study is  focused on   nonduality   as a healing modality, and not Jung’s work.  In   this autoethnography ,   I   explore my personal journey of healing   my   suffering,  from the time   stretching between   the 1950s and   ‘ 60s to today, with the intent   and  objective of offering practical ideas and curricula to mitigate early childhood trauma in  present time. My journey recovering from postpartum psychosis highlight s   how  nonduality   transformed my suffering through continually resolving the trauma that le d  me to a mental hospital at age   26 . This study also focus es   on issues particular to women,  such as post - partum depression and psychosis, and how that was misdiagnosed and  treated as mental illness, rather than hormonal imbalance.

NONDUALITY IN ACTION   9  To this   day ,   I do   n o t know whether   if I had been treated for post - partum  depression rather than an   a djustment   d isorder,   an emotional response to a stressful event,  my life would not have included as much suffering and also as much growth. It is a state  of   subjective distress and emotional disturbance, which arises during the course of  adapting to stresses of significant life changes, stressful life events, serious physical  illness, or possibility of serious illness ( Patra & Sarkar (2013) .   O’Hara ( 2009 ) d ec lared  post - partum psychosis as   a disabling disorder occurring once in every 1 , 000 deliveries,  and one where intensive treatment, usually   on an inpatient basis, occurs.   Patra and Sarkar  (2013) discussed adjustment disorder as a common diagnosis in psyc h iatr ic settings  which carry a significant rate of morbidity. When I research the term   morbidity , one of  the symptoms is a preoccupation with death and other gloomy emotional responses to  stressful situations.   When I feel frightened at times, this symptom is pe rfectly descriptive  of my experience.  Another   issue   illustrate s   how being a single mother during that time, with the  politics and laws that dealt with child support and maintenance, made it almost  impossible for me to pursue a career that brought my uniqu e gifts and talents to the public  arena. To this day, I find it extremely difficult to share the responsibilities of childrearing  and the day - to day household maintenance with my partner. I   can see how   my  experiences of early childhood abuse by my father   continues in my response to everyday  circumstances   with my sons and partners, other men in my life. At times, I want to gain  their approval and find myself attempting to speak in a way that I know will please them.  At other times, with no apparent reaso n, I am resentful and angry at them. When I  inquire why I might feel that way, I recognize I am experiencing a trance state in which I

NONDUALITY IN ACTION   10  am not really in the present, and not seeing them as who they are. Rather ,   I am back with  my father and I am behaving l ike my mother. I know this is a reaction ,   and I know at the  moment   I did not have the capacity to shift my behavior.  I believe that having a memory and an experience of the trauma - related events  allow for a more resilient response to present day sit uations.   In a personal communication  from Ira Glovinsky   ( July 2019 )   he stated ,   “ Here is where we have to be careful. You can  get a resilient response from a resilient person, but a person who is not resilient will not  respond the same way. Resilience is an   important variable in recovery. There is still so  much we don’t know. What some of the neuroscience research is showing   is   that each of  us has a ceiling in areas of our functioning . ” The definition of resilience is one’s ability  to recover quickly from d ifficulties. I do not know what causes one person to be resilient  in a particular situation and not another. I can sa y this is still being explored.  Brewin, Huntley, and Whalley (2012)   suggested that a child’s awareness and  memory of the events may be necessary for symptoms of trauma to be examined and  alleviated. The question of the correlation between traumatic events in early childhood  and resilience in adulthood   has been   investiga ted (Masten, Best ,   & Garmezy, 1990).  Although I have suffered from anxiety much of my teen and adult life, I am an example  of a resilient survivor of trauma. Many of these transformative shifts have occurred  through the experience of   nonduality .  My au toethnographic   study   seeks   to discover how   nonduality   can provide a  foundation for healing that other healing modalities will be able to work with. The  ethical stance that I am taking is crucial for the autonomy and integrity of a researcher  while   dealing   with a   secularly cleansed   model of healing.

NONDUALITY IN ACTION   11  Autoethnographers challenge canonical ways of d oing research and representing  themselves and others through a political and socially responsible, socially ju st ,   and  socially conscious lens (Ellis, Adams , &   Bochner,   2011). The self - reflection and  exploration of my unadulterated truth has been a strenuous, emotional ,   and intellectual  challenge each day. When I am able to both show and tell an event with cultural and  social meaning that extends to others, I   feel no resistance to this work; rather, it becomes  a labor of love for want of a more academic turn of phrase.  Many of us have encountered early childhood trauma, from the benign to the  severe. Some children can escape most of the negative long - term re sults of external  trauma, from something as simple as a clock ticking all night long in an infant’s bedroom  ( Blackstone,   2007 , 2008 a , 200 8b ).   Others suffer greatly from any kind of continued  negativity,   w hether parents or caregivers are   conscious of the ef fect or not   (Eliot, 2000).  Although w e are each unique,   we are also all human with the shared capability to  experience human emotions   (Gazzaniga, 2008, 2009 p.7) . It is common knowledge that  at times we wish to forget uncomfortable experiences. So, we often   obfuscate them   or  create pleasant illusions to cover up the memory and pain. When our feelings and  memories are diluted and dulled, the experiences do not d isappear from our bodies (Van  der Kolk ,   201 5) .  As we know from our instantaneous, hair - trigger reaction to situations that seem  innocuous, our reactions do not seem appropriate for what is happening in the moment.  A serious disadvantage of not experienc ing our feelings in d ifficult situations is that we  often misinterpret what is occurring in the present based on what occurred in our past  personal childhood conditioning (Orloff - Falk & Doubleday,   1991 ). In speaking with

NONDUALITY IN ACTION   12  Glovinsky (2018), he asserted that   one’s “internal working model” begins to get laid  down very early in development, and then we develop cognitive biases that drive our  thinking in the direction of these models (I. Glovinsky ,   personal communication, August  30, 2018).  Our internal working   models become solidified with memories that seem to prove  our points of view. Two siblings present at the same event have different interpretations  of the event. Is either one inaccurate?   These early childhood memories, whether  repressed or malignantly ex perienced, continue to impact us throughout adolescence and  adulthood. The quality of care during the child’s first   2   years corresponds with the  development of adolescent troubles and can became a “vicious cycle” ( Van der Kolk,  201 5 , p.327). Van der Kolk   (201 5 )   also considered an informal discussion he had with  Alan Sroufe, a researcher working with him ,   who believes that resilience in adulthood  could be predicted by the love or lack of love that mothers or caretakers felt toward their  children by age   2   (V an der Kolk ,   201 5 , pp.160 - 161).  In my exploration of the literature ,   I discovered there are more anxiety - related  disorders in girls compared to boys .   It may be that girls have more difficulty regulating  negative emotions, and this   difficulty   to regulate e motions   is more predictive of anxiety  in girls than boys ( Bender,   Harris,   Reinholdt - Dunne, Esbjorn,   & Pons ,   2015 ). This has  been true for me, personally,   since I was a small child unable to have a voice when my  parents were in conflict   situations. They had conflicts with each other, with me, or with a  server in a restaurant who did not trim the fat from   my father’s steak before it was  cooked. In most cases the literature discussed marital violence between men and women,

NONDUALITY IN ACTION   13  not fathers and d aughters. Yet, in my case, both my parents and my sister participated in  the abuse toward me by blaming me for my father’s behavior.  When daily emotional issues that are problematic to parents overflow into their  interactions with their children and ea ch other, the effect on the other members of the  family are long term   (Almeida,   Wethington ,   &   Chandler   1999;   Almeida   & McDonald,  2004 ).   “Anxiety disorders are among the most common psychiatric disorders affecting  children and adolescents” (Albano, Chorpit a, & Barlow,   2003 , p. 292 )   The experience of  anxiety in childhood and adolescence can lead to a variety of negative outcomes  including antisocial behavior, academic problems, and the development of other mental  health problems   ( Ginsburg ,   La Greca, & Silver man,   (1998) .   Ira Glovinsky in a personal  communication   ( July 2019 )   stated, “Some disorders emerge in phases. We refer to this  process as staging. Anxiety is often the first signal in the staging process. We experience  anxiety and then symptoms, leading to   other disturbances of emotions.”  Theoretical Framework for the Study  .   My autoethnographic   study   seeks   to discover how   nonduality   can provide a  foundation for healing that other healing modalities will be able to work with. The  ethical stance that I am taking is crucial for the autonomy and integrity of a researcher in  dealing with a secularly cleansed model of healing.   Nonduality   does not offer a religious  or spiritual model for how to be as a therapist.   I need to assure myself and those I work  with that the nondual model of healing is not at odds with any spiritual or religious  practice they are identified with. I must not in any   way, while working with a client or  organization, exaggerate my memories, accomplishments, failures, transformational  processes or narcissistic tendencies.

NONDUALITY IN ACTION   14  Foster (2007)   Parsons (2004)   and Theriault (2005)   declared the central tenet  found in   n ondual rea lization is complete freedom from the loneliness of a separate self. (We Are Interconnected to all   L ife, para .   20)  Katz, (Ed.) (2007 ),   a nondual prac titioner, stated   that deconstruction, when   used  in   nonduality , means the undoing of the fa lse self,   wh ich he calls the separate self.   What  does it mean not to have a separate self? What does it mean to be at one with the  universe? Is it possible? Philoso pher Tomas Metzinger   (2004)   sa id , “Nobody ever had or  was a self” (p.362). I have not met anyone who is egoless or who does not live their  everyday life in a   way that demonstrates their conditioning.   Fenner (2007) proclaim ed  our everyday world is dualistic , filled with either/or choices, not   n ondual, where there is a  panoply of choices for each decision and they come without effort.  Many aspects of   nonduality   are paradoxical   (Fenner, 2007).   In non - conceptual

NONDUALITY IN ACTION   15  nonduality   something can be true and not true at the same time, good and bad  simultaneously. Our preferences for order, structures, concepts , and so forth , do not  matter during the time we are resting in   n ondual   a wareness   (p. 10).   When we can see  many alternatives, not just an either/or, our choices can be transformative.   For the  purposes of this study, the healing of early childhood trauma, I will be exploring the  Buddhist Eastern   n on - c onceptual   m indfulness   as defined by Peter Fe nner and other  expositors in this tradition.  Discussions of both Non - Conceptual   Nonduality   and Conceptual   Mindfulness  Mindfulness is important in this discussion because, as Kabat - Zinn’s   You Tube,  (2017)   definition of m indfulness stated, it is “a wareness that arises through paying  attention on purpose, in the present moment, nonjudgmentally, in the service of self -  understanding and wisdom . ”   Many people think mindfulness is nondualit y ,   and I believe  it is important to make the distinctions clear. NONDUALITY IN ACTION   85  autoethnographer is describing to look at their own problems and issues and discover  their own meaning. Autoethnographers look back at their life experience, describe and  analyze that life ex perience, and offer a way to communicate and tell a story to others  that could make a difference  There was a “crisis of confidence” inspired by postmodernism in the   ’ 80s. This  occurred after social scientists became increasingly troubled by social scien ce inquiry  limited by the ontological, epistemological ,   and axiological perspectives of that time  (Ellis & Bochner, 2000). According to Kuhn (1996)   and   Rorty (1982) ,   there was  recognition that facts and truths were fashioned by the language and paradigms   the social  scientists used to illustrate them.   Over time, scholars from various social science  disciplines speculated what research studies would become if the expectation would be  that the work would be closer to stories as described above rather than the   hard sciences.  And they suggested, the pretense of value - free research needed to end and instead the  researchers be allowed to share their values in their work (Bochner,   2014 ). My article  written as Judith S. Samuels in 1971 offered that observation with out the clarity I have  today.  According to Ellingson and Ellis (2008), autoethnography is “a social  constructionist project that rejects the deep - rooted binary oppositions between the  researcher and the researched, objectivity and subjectivity, process a nd product, self and  others, art and science, and the personal and the political” (p.451).   As a method,  autoethnography fulfills the role of the process and the p roduct (Ellis   et al,   2011). There  are many forms of autoethnography, depending on where the e mphasis is placed.

This type of autoethnography used to belong to the domain of  “white, masculine, he terosexual, middle/upper   classed, able bodied Christian”  (Denzin, Lincoln & Smith,   2008, p.16).  2.   Narrative   e thnographies:   Dissertations presented in story form which  integrate the ethnographer’s and other s ’   experi ences in the analysis of others  ( Tet loc k , 1991 ).  3.   Reflexive   e thnographies:   These   log and chronicle how the researcher changes  during the time of the fieldwork. The ethnographer, in this method, is  chronicling his/her life along with cultural members ’   lives ( Ellis, 2004, p.50).  4. This form of autoethnography  emphasized the procedural nature of research. Although similar to grounded  theory, da ta collection and analysis proceed simultaneously. CONCLUSIONS AND  RECOMMENDATIONS  We now know that memories are not fixed or frozen like Proust’s jars   of  preserves in a larder, but are transformed, disassembled, reassembled,  and   recategorized with every act of recollection.  ( Sacks,   2013. Hallucinations ,   p.15 4)  My disse rtation is a panoply of memories which appeared in my consciousness as  threads and patterns of a self - woven tapestry which focused on the research question of  the dissertation: How does the use of nonduality as a therapeutic tool assist in the  amelioratio n of early childhood trauma? The memories that I experienced occurred when  I sat quietly, took walks, paced, cried, fought with myself ,   and felt serene joy. I have  been researching and writing for a year and a half. I listened to my mind remind me of  tra uma, childhood, parents, family and then, out of nowhere, resilience.   When I shared  some memories with my sister, her experience of those moments   was   different from  mine.   I felt frightened when she didn’t believe me. I wondered if I made up my  memories.  Writing from memory created a re - experiencing and re - conceptualizing of the  different person I was /am/will be .   W hile retrieving the memories , and reliving them, I  experienced a disharmony in how I lived and still feel that at times today.   Creating a  clear tapestry of early childhood abuse was difficult. I stitched and restitched until I could  read it aloud and ask my committee to read it. Many   days   during this time .   I wished I  had pursued a different type of study such as   in - depth intervi ewing.  Writing a dissertation dealing with personal early childhood trauma revealed I am  courageous,   and I can persevere.   There were moments during these past years at Fielding

NONDUALITY IN ACTION   166  when   I wasn’t sure. For example, my recovery from a knee replace ment accounted for  more pain than I had anticipated. I lost   2   months of writing and thinking. Another  example is the experience of isolation that coincided with the completion of my classes --  where I had contact with other students -- to the pure aloneness t hat came with daily  writing.   I also discovered how much I wanted approval before I would go on. Who would  give it to me? I tried my family, friends ,   and even strangers to no avail. No one wanted  to listen to a paragraph or two without the context that cr eated this work. I paced and  walked and realized this was my contribution. I needed to own it. Eventually I did.  Memories  If this dissertation had a different focus, such as the paranormal, I would share  different memories, such as  •   Dis covering I had lung cancer through a dream  •   Having visitations by my father and friends as they die   –   showing up in a  vision and leaving me the message that all is o kay  •   Seeing what might be called ghosts at different times  These events in my lif e have always been part of my story. Yet during the  dissertation time, these memories did not appear as relevant.   So, memories, from my  vantage point   of this present time   are called to the surface of   my   consciousness when  needed, when searched for, upon   a w akening in the morning, after a good cry or laughter,  and they are not necessarily factu ally true .   Tulving (1983)   argued that “access to, or  actualization from, the episodic memory system tends to be deliberate and usually

NONDUALITY IN ACTION   167  requires conscious effort”   (p. 46).   Mandler (1985)   agreed, yet conceded that “much of  everyday memory experiences are in fact spontaneous” (pp. 10 2 – 103). Post - traumatic  stress - based memories tend to arise seemingly out of nowhere   ( Rasmussen   &   Berntsen ,  2011).   And,   although my memories were the same,   my   narratives and   stories   from the  past   were experienced differently based on   my ability to abide in   unconditioned  awareness   when I was writing them.  Suggestions for Future Research  One of my recommendations is to conduct   further research and study to  determine whether early childhood trauma memories occur similarly as PTSD  spontaneous memories. I believe not only do these early childhood memories occur  spontaneously,   but   the aftermath of the experiences over time easily determine s   the future  behavior   of the person experiencing the memories. And for me ,   my clients ,   and students,  there does not seem to be any apparent circumstance that might bring this spontaneous  memory to the surface at that time.   In other words, we cannot generalize as to what  circumstance brings the memory to the surface. This merits research th at goes beyond the  circumstance to the core experience of the trauma while gently moving through what I  call ed   Disruptive Learning Process , and now call Nonduality in Action,   I can say  anecdotally ,   and generally speaking ,   I have seen this   work with clients   and organizations.  . I have not done any   formal   research at this time ;   t hat research is a future interest and  desire.  The American Psychological Association   has suggested further research on memories  of abuse to determine how accurate or inaccurate recoll ections of events may be created.  This includes :

NONDUALITY IN ACTION   168  •   Research to decide which clinical techniques are most likely to lead to the  creation of pseudo memories ,   and which techniques are most effective in creating  the conditions under which actual events of childh ood abuse can be remembered  with accuracy;  •   Research to determine how trauma and traumatic response impact the memory  process;  •   Research to learn which people are more susceptible than others to memory  suggestions. ( https://www.apa.org/topics/trauma/memories )  Although these seem like worthy endeavors, I do not see how this research can  make a positive difference in the healing process . However, I do expect researchers to  use the data in th eir continued search for truth.   Without the self - awareness that  nonduality and self - awareness trained practitioners bring to the healing process, the  outcomes would most likely continue to be devoid of the clarity that comes from  unconditioned awareness ( the practitioner) meeting unconditioned awareness (the client). NONDUALITY IN ACTION   169  Implications for Practice  Fenner   (2007) declared the o nly experience   two people   can   absolutely   share   is  unconditioned awareness, that of nonduality. After   12   years of study and practice ,   my  team and I created a six - step process that promises to achieve the experience of  nonduality in acti on for most people who practice it. This process is not intended to  achieve the deepest self - healing that nondual practitioners like Judith Blackstone, Peter  Fenner, Brian   Theriault,   and Rupert Spiro aspire to. However, by following the steps and  doing th e assignments offered, this nonduality in action practice becomes a way of living.  Over time, new behaviors become the norm and the benefits to both the practitioner and  the client increase. The Kabbalah teaches that with any spiritual practice and medit ation,  action for the benefit of others is the most beneficial to the actor ( Rader & Rader,   1989) .  Another recommendation is that elementary school teachers and administrators  include curriculum to address quieting the mind of children who are overwhelmed   by the  demands placed on them at this time. This could be in the form of teaching kindness,  compassion and other results of nonduality. I will   also   look at this at a later date.

NONDUALITY IN ACTION   171  Definition of   t he   s ix   steps in the nonduality in action process  I will define the steps of this process and then will give an example of how it  works to achieve a   nonduality   in action   way to   liv e .  Insight:   being mindful of where our beliefs,   values ,   and points of view  originated , without   believing our truth is the truth for others. Conscious knowledge of  one’s feelings, motives ,   and desires.  Personal Responsibility : knowing that you are the   owner   of your thinking,  emotions, behaviors and min dset. It means that you are respons i ble to choose your  behaviors from unlimited options. Simply put, it is the key to creating desired results,  and, therefore, to success.  Authenticity:   being genuine, whole, and connected. Having a presence that is  exper ienced by others as congruent.  Integrity:   keeping and honoring our commitments no matter what we think or  feel. Keeping our word is simply doing what we say. If we cannot keep our word, we let  the other person know and make sure   he or she is   complete.  Cle ar Mind : occurs when our insight, personal responsibility ,   and integrity are  occurring simultaneously. At that time, there is a free choice, not one made out of a  reacti ve   type of response. There is more than an either/or alternative to any situation.  Awakened Action : allows us to know what actions to take. Awakened   a ction  points to truth, and is extremely flexible and contradictory. Each situation is unique, and  each person is unique. Only when we are relying on a clear mind can we use awakened  action . Clarity informs and points us to what makes sense in each moment with each  situation.

NONDUALITY IN ACTION   172  The   nonduality in action   process does not attempt to go into the depths of internal  transformation described by   Nixon ( 2013).   It is meant to touch the traumatic experience  lightly   while reaching   deeply, simultaneously allowing the student or   client   to attain self -  discovery without provoking another reopening of the trauma.   T his distinction between  self - discovery and provo king the original trauma   depends on what and who brings about  the “aha .”  Below is a pictorial diagram ( F igure   13 ) of the process I just described. Although  this process is taught in orderly steps with accompanying “exercises” so that the student  or   client can experience the different steps in the process, the result for the student is  systemic.  Figure 1 3 .   Another   v iew of   s ix - s tep   p rocess .  These principles began to make sense and became clear as I studied with Peter  Fenner as a participant in h is training. I noticed that many of the students in the programs  could meditate for hours until they experienced unconditioned awareness or nonduality. I

NONDUALITY IN ACTION   173  could not. After a while, I needed to take my insight and take action. I followed the Six -  Step Proc ess without thinking about the steps.  .   T his process has created   shifts in   individual and group   worldview s   from fixed  static position s   to a fluid, worry - free state that dissolves harmful recurring thoughts . Over  time, this worry - free state becomes more natural and easier to access. Even if the  thoughts do not go away ,   they are recognized as debris needing to be swept away..  As   these prin ciples   are   followed,   they   creat e new habits and a new   internal   map.  This   includ es   living   a   life with a vision of profound health,   allowing   early childhood  trauma to   be   release d   and dissolve .   This occurs when each step is followed until it is  obvious that a wakened action is required.   T he   person can then   view   hi m / herself  positively . The choices s/he makes are chosen anew from a myriad of options rather than  conditioning.  Example of Nonduality in Action  I will go through one example of the first two   principl es   and the assignments that  bring about self - awareness:  Insight:   Session 1:   I   met   with a client, a family, through videoconferencing.  They began to tell me their story.   I   listened   until something they say just   stuck   in my  mind and I   was   unable to move fo rward. For example, in a meeting with a couple within  the past   6   months, one of the partners had an affair with someone he worked with. When  his wife said she knew something was going on and confronted him with it, he   denied  everything. So, I heard the   issue of trust   rather than the affair.   She knew he was not  telling the truth, yet she did not believe   herself.

NONDUALITY IN ACTION   174  Why was that important in my six steps? It told me that both partners needed to  have insight as to their behavior that created the affair. I   know that sounds unusual to say.  Yet, I see the couple as a system ,   and each action in the system causes the entire system  to shift. Although the content of an affair can be titillating, exciting ,   and sad, I believe  the foundation of a partnership, parti cularly in marriage ,   is trust in oneself and one’s  partner.  I   g a ve   them an assignment which was to notice when they are not being honest all  the way. Only notice. They were not to make any changes in their behavior.  Insight:   Session 2 :   He shared he was   afraid to tell his wife his truth about almost  everything. He reported he felt left out and criticized when he did share. She shared how  angry he was with her when she asked questions about him and other women. He also  said his family did not speak abo ut anything personal. I ask ed   them if they saw how they  were active participants in his affair .   He said yes and she said no. I gave them another  assignment. I asked her to notice how much time she spent thinking about the other  woman. Before we ended th e call, she said she could not help thinking about the other  woman. It is mostly what she thought about when not working or being with their  children (two teens who knew about the affair). I suggested she was keeping this affair  going. He had blocked the o ther woman from his social media accounts and the wife  continued to monitor the other woman’s social media. I suggested another assignment  which was they not discuss content when they shared with each other. Instead of saying,  “I felt sad because you…”   I asked them to just say they felt sad. They agreed to this.  They reported they both saw how they were responding from their history and g a ve many

NONDUALITY IN ACTION   175  examples. I noticed they were not angry with each other at the end of the meeting. I  forwarded the recording of their meeting for them to review during the week.  Personal Responsibility: Session 3 :   The wife was angry at her husband. The  woman he was ha ving an affair with passed her on the street and “was brazen and didn’t  even look away.” Her husband felt shame and realized he has felt an undercurrent of  shame since a child. The wife did not find a connection from her history and what was  happening for   her now. Judith:   How do I let this be? How do I not tell her what I see?  How do I support her to see for herself?   I recommended she meet with the ex - lover and  let her know how she felt. When I suggested that, she expressed anger and began to share  her   history admitting this happened to her mother and father. In the middle of her  sharing, her husband gave her some feedback through holding her hand and looking at  her tenderly. I gave them the assignment to continue not sharing content but continue  just   sharing feelings. They let me know they were going away for a few weeks and felt  much better about each other. At this point they each saw how they contributed to the  affair.  I recognize this will take more than six meetings. I let them know we have  rea ched our third principle :   authenticity. If the work continues as it has up to this point,  they will see how their early childhood trauma precipitated the affair, the discovery of the  affair, the obsessions on both sides ,   and how the affair is secondary to   the lack of trust  they have recently made conscious. I do not expect them to live a non - duality lifestyle.  I   do expect them to retain what this opportunity brought them and perhaps I will see them  at another time in the future. Neither one had ev er been to a therapist. They appreciated

NONDUALITY IN ACTION   176  my honesty, my “not beating around the bush , ” and the openness we shared. I hope this  gives a flavor of my work.at this time .  Final Reflection  This autoethnographic study has been revealing both in going deep into   early  childhood trauma while understanding my personal truth about my own trauma. I am a  resilient survivor of consistent physical and emotional abuse as a young teen.   During this  process,   I realized as well how much my parents loved me. I am able to see   how the  medication my father was prescribed for his pains and heart attack changed him and my  mothe r, a s   did my misdiagnosis of mental illness that put me in a mental hospital change  me. Understanding the toll on my mother and my father shifts my perception of the past,  the present ,   and my continued dreams for the future. I no longer feel like an abused chil d.  The subtlety and nuances of a person’s life bring richness to their stories and their lives.  Giorgio (2009 ) stated, “The call of narrative is the inspiration to find language  that is adequate to the obscurity and darkness of experience” (p.270). I beli eve we need to  shine our light of awareness on our painful memories and begin to dispel the darkness  that I   fe el / felt. The memories that arose and found their place in this study were the ones  that made meaning of how and why my life was a mixture of pain   and inspiration. My  memories wove this narrative into a meaningful fabric for my life as well as the lives of  others. I pray social and cultural healing can be garnered from my experiences   as   they  touch many others.  In living a nondual lifestyle there is t he   capacity   of new beginnings and the  lessoning   of our negative ancestral consciousness.   In writing this dissertation,   I have  found the memories that   were   diffused are those I focused on.   New memories are already

NONDUALITY IN ACTION   177  asking for attention My father helping my   friends. My mother showing kindness to me  without questioning my motivations. This brings new ideas for papers and work.   As I  continue my work, other memories will show up and those are the ones that will diminish  as they are explored in their core. In t hat way my childhood trauma will continue to  gradually dissipate  I am appreciative   of   Fielding Graduate University and my amazing committee for  supporting this work   and for their concern with social justice and inclusion. I finish this  endeavor in a sta te of grace and appreciation.
